title: A Brief Intermission
subtitle: Not an episode, but the Production Team has news worth sharing.
body:
Today, this isn’t a true episode, but I owe it to you to check in.

I’ve had a rather odd, busy, and stressful few weeks. I’ve thought a lot about what I am going to say to you next, though my schedule has been filled with writing, working, and building other things.

It’s been wonderful to see that even though I’ve been busy and haven’t checked in with you, the support has continued.

To those of you who ordered my original art prints from my store, purchased my book Memoir of the Modern Heroine, and upgraded to a paid subscription, I cannot thank you enough for the love and support.

Sheridan’s Store

I want to let you in on a fun little update. It’s completed on the Substack platform, but it’s not quite ready on the official What Sheridan Said platform (will send update ♡).

I have categorized the entire series’s episodes into three categories (clickable titles):

The Heroine Arc

The main plot: the career wins, the career humiliations, the poetry that started as a coping mechanism and became the whole plot. I built this version of myself in public, badly and on purpose.

B- Roll

Not every week is life-changing, even if I’d like to pretend it is to make the episode better. This is the in-between; the chaos that doesn’t always resolve into a lesson, the errands, the four-foot aliens, the version of myself where nothing is falling up or downhill—no filter, always the truth, usually with a bow on it.

Love Interest

The cast list of everyone who almost got a happy ending — the exes, the almosts, and the ones I loved out loud before I had to write them out of the script entirely.

. . .

The production team and I (still just me and a few willing friends) have decided to make several key episodes and poems completely free. The free episodes are highlighted in the second section on the Substack platform’s main page, and will soon also be in a similar place on the WSS platform.

But for now, and for those new subscribers — welcome ♡ — these episodes and poems will remain free despite the four-week lock-in rule.

Here is the list of free poems:

Free Poems

Flowers Covered His Skin

Where Are Your Hands

Some Things Are Easy

Coke Without Ice

Here is the list of episodes (I can’t figure out the formatting, ugh):

Free Episodes

Woman Compulsively Overshares, But People Somehow Still Don’t Know Anything About Her

To The Girl Who Cries Wolf

This Is What Happens When You Don't Stay Small

So I'm Doing This Now

. . .

I have a lot of contradictions, predicaments, and resolutions to share with you — and they run through everything: the personal, the career, the dilemmas. Though that will need to wait until next week. But regarding “Sheridan the Great”, I am doing alright.

If you have read last week’s episode (always briefed at the beginning), my thought patterns, my radar for baloney, and my own intuition have only sharpened on what the truth, my truth, means. The year is over halfway complete, and has seen much growth, a lot of tears, and too many “oh yeahs” (accidental Minnesota pun). But it’s not close to being over; so much can happen in even just a day, or an hour.

More next week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: A Butterfly is a Girl's Only Friend
subtitle: Toads, Butterflies, and the Loneliness Nobody Warned Us Freedom Would Come With
body:
In honor of our angel, Dolly Parton, this episode will remain free ʚїɞ

. . .

A Butterfly is a Girl’s Only Friend

I have an idea, well let’s not get carried away because often I have several in just an hour. But this idea, I’ve been harping, praising, downvoting, and contemplating the very existence of possibilities of what it could be.

I’ve sent over a pitch deck, along with emails and phone conversations. I have an idea, and I’m testing to see if others may believe in it too.

But that’s not what I want to talk about today. Every time I try to write about something new, I end up circling back to the same friend I’ve had since before I knew what a friend was.

Butterflies.

Butterflies?

Yes, butterflies.

ʚїɞ

I love butterflies. I’m not sure why, or when it started. I grew up as an animal lover. I’d spend my weekends capturing a pet toad, and the weekdays building a makeshift home for it in my closet. Of course, I did all of this without permission — what sort of sensible parent would let their daughter turn their wardrobe into a toad terrarium? Though I never spoke to my parents about my pet toads, though every day when I came home from school, the little home I built between my soccer shorts and tank tops no longer had a toad in it. It was either the fairy toad mother, or my mother.

But I was not just a ‘toad girl,’ I was an animal girl.

I grew up in southern Minnesota, where toads roamed everywhere. They were stuck in our gutters, in our window wells, they swelled the pond down the hill, and they croaked all night long, often louder than the roosters when we woke each morning to the sound and the sun.

There were more toads than people in my town, far more toads than I had friends, and like poetry, there was more freedom in emotion, more safety in the poetry I had found, than in any one person in the town.

I had textbooks — one on dog species, one on cat species, one on mammals, one on amphibians. I remember reading the mammal textbook cover to cover several times. Maybe it’s a similar reason I gravitated toward poetry — it helped me understand myself, and feel less alone. So poetry and animals, perhaps they found me for similar reasons, or more so, perked and stayed in my interest for the right reasons.

To pinpoint when it was that butterflies flew into my favorite, I’m not sure. Perhaps they were around me the entire time; it simply took me till now to realize how important they were to me.

Monarchs loved our farm town. In the spring, they would return, and the fields would rise as the frost scorched off in Minnesota’s incoming summer sun. We had a big tree in the front of the farm, the kind with long branches that made you feel like Tarzan as a child. Across the gravel road was a pond about thirty yards wide. The toads roared and ruled that pond, the fireflies danced above it, and I watched while swinging from the front yard tree.

Fireflies at night, and butterflies during the day. For growing up in seclusion and solitude, I sure was one for escaping into the openness of nothing. I’d sneak out and sit at the top of the hill of the cornfield, where I could see the native reservation’s casino lights making a giant tepee in the sky — the only light pollution for a hundred miles. At night, it was always just me, the stars, the fireflies, and the tepee in the sky.

I couldn’t sleep much as a child, nor still as an adult. I stayed awake, hiding in my closet writing or drawing, or snuck out to sit in the middle of something, owning its own control, like the cornfield or the Tarzan tree.

My little sister sleepwalked a lot, so we had bells on each of the doors. I’d carefully walk down the stairs, placing each foot on the parts I’d memorized not to creak. At the bottom, it’s almost pitch black except for a little light in the kitchen, and the drapes are pushed to the side so I can see the fireflies dancing, telling me to hurry and join them. I’d slide on my boots, lift the bells off the door with two hands, set them on the chair nearby, turn the knob slowly with my ear pressed to catch the noises first, and creak the door open as slowly as I could to drag out the low hymn-screech it had made since Grandma and Pop moved in. Then I’d close it behind me, the toads’ chitter-chatter would fill my ears, the fireflies would dance around my eyes, and the tepee and the stars would shine bright in the sky.

These were my friends of the night.

There’s a certain kind of tree that grows in Minnesota — my favorite. They always grew in clusters; wherever I saw one, there were bound to be at least ten more nearby. They looked like pine trees but weren’t prickly or sappy, with a hollow middle where the soft thistles didn’t grow, so if you snuck under the branches and stood inside near the trunk, you had open ladders on every side. I climbed to the very top, so high there were only a few branches left above my knees, a little flimsy up there, swaying each way the wind blew. Though it was never dangerous — there was always another tree with an equally good ladder a few feet away.

That ladder inside the tree, that was where I went to be with the butterflies. And every day, when the Minnesota sun chose to be kind, you would know exactly where to find me.

Whether it was the toads and the fireflies chatting and lighting up my nights, or the butterflies landing all around me during the day — I never felt alone in complete nature. The sun always rises in Minnesota, but it doesn’t always do its job. There are days, weeks, sometimes months where the sun stares at you without ever giving you a trace of warmth, UV, or serotonin. Perhaps Minnesota raised me to be okay not leaving my home for a few weeks, though in other parts of the world that’s considered a drastic sign for help.

When the sun did choose to be kind, you’d find me in a well with the toads, or at the top of a tree, swinging in the wind with the butterflies.

Today, I tend to be a recluse. Sometimes I need complete silence; I need people not to come up and talk to me; I need to exist around you, but without you.

I find it funny, looking through this lens — I was raised in solitude, and I wanted with every inch of me not to be, but when I finally got to ‘not be’, I became the solitude amongst the chaos.

Because, well, often I feel like a butterfly.

When I was a kid, it was easy to exist, because I hadn’t known what it even was to exist, per se. I craved it more than anything — my town was my cocoon, and I was ready to fly. Ready to become who I always wanted to be, who I felt I was meant to be.

I broke out. I achieved great things. My wings grew in, the beauty learning how to light up in its own way. But like butterflies, flowers, and all other beautiful things that occur naturally, we can’t just exist around them and watch — we swat, we capture, we take, and we envy.

I didn’t know I was a butterfly. But it’s the only thing that seems to make sense.

I have friends, but they live far away, and it’s been the same pattern every time — a colleague or an employee, I leave the job, they reach out, we become friends for life. All of my closest friendships have followed this same shape.

I don’t want to talk about the loneliness you think I’m going to talk about. I want to talk about society’s new loneliness for women. My loneliness. Many of us are the first of our entire lineage to live alone. Our mothers, our grandmothers, and the mothers before them — I’m historically assuming — never lived by themselves.

I remember when I got my first apartment. It overlooked the city, and I dressed it up to look like it was out of a magazine — a girl’s apartment you wanted to be photographed in. That was the goal. It’s a funny thing, to spend so much care making a space beautiful enough to be looked at, and then have almost no one there to look.

I signed that lease just a few weeks into my new job, overseeing a theatre, bar, and restaurant for a hospitality group near Washington, D.C. I was barely out of college, scathed by it really, and I worked through the weekends, through the holidays, and soon made sure to be busy with work on Christmas, and even on my own birthday.

The friends I could have made weren’t off on the days I was, and as a very young female boss, it was easier to maintain my structure at work if I didn’t get close with my staff and managers. To be fair, my own bosses required that separation too.

It continued. At first I didn’t make myself busy on Christmas or my birthday, but after a while, that was the only way I knew how to function. It was easier to have my staff wish me a happy birthday than to sit alone in my photo-ready apartment counting texts on one hand.

I looked around at what I had achieved. I was so young, so successful — I should have been happy. But each day I’d return to my apartment, park on the ground level, and sit idle sometimes for four hours. Down there it was all empty cars, nobody ever coming or going when I was. But it was the mirage of community around me. I’d sit in that lot every single day after work, waiting for the mirage to finally lift me up enough to go inside my photo-ready apartment nobody had ever actually seen.

I should have been content. I was the first of many in our generation to do this. I lived alone; I had a successful job — so many women before me fought and clawed for exactly the privileges I was so incredibly depressed in. I felt guilty, like something was wrong with me, that I shouldn’t feel this way given the new age femininity we’d so honorably achieved.

But I was alone, and there were other reasons for it too. I had my cousin Russell check in on me from time to time; he was taken too soon. I miss him a lot. God rest his soul.

It’s not that I didn’t love what I did — I felt creative, capable, like a real businesswoman. I loved that job more than I can explain. I think the problem was there was nobody outside of work I could explain things to. There are boundaries, lines I couldn’t cross with staff and employees. Over the years, my vocabulary narrowed down to just work, and the most social time I had was with my afternoon barista.

The job had its privileges, but it had deprivations too — working through happy hour, through the weekends, my time off never lining up with the social world outside “the industry.” I was too scared the respect I’d worked hard for would wash away if they saw me two beers in on a Sunday industry night with other managers. But I couldn’t really socialize with them either, so mostly I was just afraid to go.

I hadn’t carried friends with me through college, which — like high school — I unfortunately skipped through rather than lived. I had a hard time socially, believed too easily, felt too much. Friends came and went, and things ended so badly that to avoid a bullying lawsuit they sent me to college early. As soon as I turned 18, I transferred to George Mason University in Northern Virginia, where, typical story, I let the wrong man be my boyfriend — it’s fine, ugh, lesson learned.

After schooling, I was in such a shell. I remember telling myself: the only thing I have control over is my career. This is where I shine — not socially, not at making or keeping friends. So I left school behind with that mindset fully formed: I simply wasn’t meant for friends, or a social life. I believed it for years. Some days, even today, I still struggle with believing otherwise.

I loved my work. I loved training managers, writing the theatre sketches, watching a genuine clock run efficiently across every gear and band. Giving a stable paycheck to a door girl in school, or a manager who’s a single dad — it is so incredibly fulfilling.

But I forgot I was a butterfly, not an ant.

I think a lot of us have forgotten, along the way to achieving freedom, that we are not ants. Ants survive by disappearing into the colony. Butterflies were never built for that — they’re built to be seen, to land somewhere, to be found. I built myself an anthill and then wondered why nothing ever landed on me.

In my own personal effort to reach for freedom, I forgot what else mattered. I was so caught up in being capable, in proving I’m not here for a rich husband — that I am the rich husband — that I closed off every other part of me.

I’m worried I’m not alone. I’m worried more women are doing this.

I’ve had my own particular disadvantages that landed me here, where my only friends are former colleagues who reached out. But I worry others are forgetting how dire a sense of community and socializing is to our fulfillment. I worry that while we chase this new freedom, men and women both are forgetting what makes us humans whole.

It isn’t being alone. Being human is never about being alone. Being human is about sharing — stories, thoughts, resources, emotions. We cannot survive alone; any historian can tell you that as fact.

I still struggle to believe I’m worthy of a social life, of friends, if that’s even meant for me. But as I’ve climbed out from the trenches I built myself, inside a mirage of newfound freedom, I worry others haven’t climbed out and seen it for themselves yet either. I see other cultures on this same path, toward becoming working ants or bees, and as someone who knows how detrimental that can be to your health and sanity, I hope they’re able to see the land they’ve dug around themselves.

But that is society — it will consistently tell us what to do, and whether or not you genuinely care what the world thinks, we all seek it out for advice and ideas anyway. It isn’t just work. We’re told we need one thing to be fulfilled; we identify it, hone in on it, and forget everything else that also makes us whole. I’ve seen it in mothers staying home, in a man who took a job he hates to make ends meet, and I saw it in myself, chasing the freedom those women before me worked so hard for.

We’re still in an age of extremes — in views, looks, fashion, morals. The pendulum swings both ways but never rests in the middle. Though I do see it toning down, see some of us getting exhausted from fighting for one thing, from holding an obsolete extreme, from chasing too much or nothing at all in the name of “the best.”

I was at the bar the other day. An old man sat next to me, roughly seventy-five, probably shouldn’t have had the glass of whiskey in front of him. He asked what I was passionate about, what I did. I told him, and poetry came up. He looked bewildered, straightened his back, and declared, “Now what on earth do you young thing have to talk about in poetry — have you experienced life and the world yet?”

I smiled and said, “Life is a journey of heaven and hell. I’m sure you saw both, equally, by the time you were my age.” He looked down at a bracelet on his wrist — a medical military bracelet, fairly certain it wasn’t his own name written on it — then he tucked it back into his sleeve and said, “You know what, you’re right. But I’m still curious what kind of hell a pretty young thing like you could have seen. That’s essential for poetry, right?”

I laughed again and said, “Not necessarily. I think it’s simply easier for some people to write beautiful poems from places of darkness — easier to portray the emotion effectively when you’re at an extreme, and extremes come easier in darkness. When the emotions aren’t as extreme or shaped in extreme darkness, you have to be more open. More truthful about everything.”

We talked for several more minutes. I shared a few pieces with him — one of happiness, one of love, one of darkness for good measure. It was a beautiful conversation, and I’m always curious why others assume a certain thing about me — some cover they’ve judged before opening the book. People do that with butterflies too — they assume the whole story from the wings and never ask what the cocoon was like.

Which is maybe why last time I let you see inside a cocoon of mine, when I told the world I’d broken up with my boyfriend via a poem.

Strangers weighing in, asking each other, “Is she a cunt for doing this?” The verdict was no — though usually it’s yes at first, until you actually think about who ‘Sheridan’ is.

I do love a clickbait title, but the truth is I really did send him a poem as a breakup message. Throughout that short relationship, I resorted to creative ways of expressing how I felt, because I’m often truly incapable of just saying it out loud. I painted an abstract piece of us during our first fight, and it was through that piece that he finally understood what I was trying to say, and we found our way back to each other. I wrote a poem once from a dark headspace, when he was frustrated trying to help me, and I couldn’t tell him what was even going on — but I could show him, through the poem. Through my art, we were both able to see each other more clearly because of it.

I know breaking up with someone via a poem sounds bad. But when you look at who I am, how I operate, and the moments I’m actually most honest and most vulnerable, doing it that way was the best option I had; it was the most ‘Sheridan’ — whether or not anyone else understands.

A butterfly doesn’t explain itself either; it just changes shape and leaves, and if you were paying attention, you already knew it was coming.

That’s what my poetry is. What my art is. The second any anxiety, shame, or guilt hits — whatever inherited, Christian-shaped emotion was bred into me to keep me from sinning — my throat closes, my voice goes, and art is often the only way I’ve ever been able to communicate anything at all.

I hold everything in my throat chakra. Maybe that’s why I’ve had such an on-and-off relationship with smoking — the second fear or a negative emotion hits my body, my throat closes, and I can’t speak. It’s why I crave solitude: so I can quiet the noise around me, let my voice open back up, and make whatever piece I need to make to get the toad out of my throat.

My life feels like it’s standing at the end of a fork, and everything I’ve said, done, become, is standing at my heels while I shuffle back and forth deciding which of the paths to take. It isn’t fair, though it’s more than fair to be standing here at all — fair, in that I have so many ways to go; unfair, in that everyone around me keeps telling me to turn back, that I already missed my exit a few miles behind.

Whether it’s to not have left the small town, or to have stayed with a previous boyfriend, to have said yes to a proposal when I said no, to settle down, go back, do this, do that.

But I can’t walk backwards. That isn’t what my life is going to be about.

I’ll figure out which path to take. But for now, I’m enjoying standing here, butterfly wings still a little damp from the cocoon, with all my attributes and values looking up at me — finally knowing that I am a butterfly, she’s not just my best friend, and whichever direction I fly, we’ll be okay.

I forgot I was a butterfly for a long time. I think a lot of us do. We build the perfect apartment, the perfect career, the perfect proof that we don’t need anyone — and somewhere in there we forget that a butterfly was never built to be alone in a field. It was built to be looked at, landed near, followed. It was built for company, even if it flies alone.

And if that’s the only friend some of us have some days — a butterfly on the windowsill, a memory of one at the top of a tree — I don’t think that makes us broken. I think it just means we forgot, like I did, that we were never ants.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: A Survival Guide to Men Who Love the Idea of You
subtitle: How to know when someone loves the version they prefer, and other important lessons.
body:
I don’t want this piece to be a topic of manic pixie dream girls, though I personally find that archetype of woman to be most affected by a man loving the idea of you. To those of you who are unfamiliar with what a manic pixie dream girl is, I’ll give you a brief definition:

Manic Pixie Dream Girl (n phr.)
/ manik pik-sē dreem gurl /
Originated by film critic Nathan Rabin after seeing Elizabethtown, this term refers to a pretty woman with a magnetic personality; she’s bubbly, soulful, and teaches those around her to embrace life and see the world in a romantic view.

She’s dancing in the rain, smiling with the barista, and at the sun even when it chooses not to be there. To be in love with that one side is so easy, but what happens when she’s standing in the middle of a downpour crying over a passed promotion? Or when her stomach hurts, and she orders tea in a prosaic tone? Does he leave, shun, shame, or learn to love the side he hasn’t yet seen?

A man loving the idea of you can happen to any of us women. Those stereotyped into the coined term aren’t the only ones who experience a man being devoted to only one side of you, one photograph in time, or the idea of you. Though it is the most portrayed in film and media—i.e., Elizabethtown, 500 Days of Summer, Ruby Sparks, Garden State—the idea and actuality of a man only loving the idea of you isn’t stuck to a media trope or a truly fictitious stereotype. It’s a lived relation surrounding you and me. The place of a man loving only the idea of you has your real identity with only one leg. You can stand still sometimes with ease, but to walk closer into the relationship, you grab a crutch, something not a part of you. This isn’t an ode to only women; men fall into this too. But it’s an ode to be introspective to those who first hear the words, “I love you.”

I am not a scientist nor a doctor, though I find that if you ask someone what they like about their partner and they respond with answers about how they make them feel versus their attributes and characteristics, the relationship has a possibility of only loving the idea, or to soon be shaky at the least. Maybe it’s just the easier answer at that moment, but I’ve made a habit of asking this question and taking a mental note of the type of answers. Out of those that answered my question with, “She’s amazing, she makes me feel so loved and supported, and makes the best chicken casserole,” or “He’s soooo HOT! I’ve already shared him on my Instagram; he’s also super nice, and tall,” I can personally tell you that those I’ve Instagram-checked are not together today.

Though recently I was chatting with a young man at the bar. His girlfriend was texting him, telling him he has to vote for so and so on the Love Island app tonight. So he asked if I’d do him a solid and do it too. I downloaded the app, and at the time slot I voted, and he voted for exactly who his girlfriend wanted. She sent him a text back with lots of hearts, and his cheeks immediately blushed. So I asked him the usual questions. He told me this was his first real relationship, and I followed with, “What do you like about her?” He looked up near the wine glasses hanging above, smiled, cheeks toned a hue redder, and answered, “It’s the way she solves problems, and on her worst days she’s still kind even if she doesn’t like something, even if it’s a day where she doesn’t like herself. She loves to craft too! It’s so fun watching her start all these projects; she’s cute when she’s thinking.”

But how can you tell? In all fairness, there is no true test or question to be asked to understand concretely where someone’s love is at, which should be remembered as we look at relationships on social media from the outside in. But if you yourself are questioning whether or not your partner loves you or the idea of you, what do you do?

As an artist and writer, I’m quite moody and sensitive. Through childhood, I learned where it was appropriate to show and express myself when my emotions became too much, or perhaps untrue. After having an outburst in 2nd grade over long subtraction—and not noticing my screaming rant of impatience made those who did not yet understand feel less than—my teacher talked with me, Mrs. Sullivan, and I grew as a person. I learned to grab tools to curate my frustrations, and soon found myself helping my classmates with the math I was once so incredibly mad and bored over.

I’m still quite young, an adult now, but with luckily more life ahead than behind. Though I find my days still presenting with new lessons, new emotional hurdles, and new frustrations to grow and learn from as I did with Mrs. Sullivan in the second grade. My tools now, for its portion of hell, the quiet frustrations, and the mundane things that walk the earth, are sitting with myself, writing, driving (though road rage causes another hurdle), and meditating.

There are men that love the idea of you for simply what you bring to their well-being. They can be in love with a curated version of you, the side they need. Maybe your life is put together while theirs is not. Maybe there’s a certain side of you that inspires them to climb to a level you’ve obtained, while the sides of you that do not inspire are shunned and shown concern for.

Because so many of my outlets are done solitary, with just myself, sometimes I fortuitously curate myself to those around me. It’s different when near family, friends, and colleagues, where I can wait till the evening and create a painting instead of growing frustrated in the office, or hold back from telling a friend something I’m not yet sure how to say. I want to work through these larger emotions and obstacles alone at first before having the healthy conversation. Though I’ve found myself in a few predicaments when it comes to romantic relationships. Sometimes the other partner wants to talk through each other’s emotions together, while I desire my tools that utilize solitude before saying words aloud.

When I may be first getting to know someone, those parts of me that stay in solitude as my tools—the meditation, the art, and writing—stay in solitude, and not a topic on the first several dates, if ever. I find myself more open about my writing and art now that I’ve turned it public. I’m still in the turning phases of having the things I do in solitude move more forward-facing. But in previous relationships, with those tools, projects, and outlets kept in solitude, it was typically too long before I had the thought to mention them. Slowly I learned to un-love that side of myself as they fell in love with what I chose to show. Or, the latter of this piece, unwittingly learning to love the idea of me.

Realistically speaking, it can go several ways. Sooner or later, words flow, the art is shared, and a conversation emerges. Some may react and say, well, I want you to talk to me first; I want to be an outlet; I want to be a part of this process. Some may leave, unwilling to learn and love the fuller view. While others may have clawed into the side you’ve allowed, they’re disinterested when first learning that painting is yours, or that you even paint at all. They love the idea of you.

It can be said we have audience members as lovers of the idea of us. The view of you that’s frontal public view—the woman or man that can arrive on their arm to an event, be great with the children, or perhaps just as before, the idea of you they had first learned. Through social media, I think we’ve seen this subcategory grow, but as an ode I promised, I must remind, it’s only inflated adoration. From the most visible examples of grandfathers professing their love to A.I. bots on Threads or Facebook, to the DM requests of Sydney Sweeney, to even someone as normal as just me or you, loving the idea of someone has never been easier; in public or online—it can be anywhere, to anyone.

I was in the sixth grade, and for Physical Education class we had tennis. We all lined up on the long side of the court with our rackets in hand and gym clothes on. Mr. Tedd announced, “Everyone pick a partner; just one, the freedom is yours.” It was down to me and two boys who had been fighting the entire time over who was going to be my partner. John won the intimidation match and was my tennis partner for the week. John’s family soon moved out of state, and I haven’t seen him in person ever since. Through social media we’ve reconnected, followed each other’s pages, and cheered quietly for one another as we grow and achieve new things.

My personal window for being single as an adult has been rather slim. That’s not because I’m usually in a relationship—because I’m not—but because typically I just can’t be arsed. Now that I’ve made my life a tad more public through this WSS series, he’s reached out since I announced my state of being single, publicly. Within a few brief conversations, he’s professed his love and how he knew all along, even during the intimidation match with little Tommy on the tennis courts.

But this leads me to another form of loving the idea of you. Beyond brief conversations through the years and supporting each other on social media, that isn’t nearly enough to be in love with someone. It’s a nostalgic vibe, where the idea of you is heavily curated, whether it be to that week in P.E. class or the slim view that truly does appear online. That isn’t me—not the full me, anyway.

My personal example only showcases that the idea of loving someone is rarely concurrent to just one form. Like a spider web waiting for my face in the sliding glass door, it slowly builds, entangling and latching on in different directions before you’re even awake.

Now I hate to bring you the not-greatest of news, but understanding at your emotional core whether someone loves you or the idea of you is a slow path, often through many unfortunate trials. As we grow older and learn to love ourselves in our fullness, we begin to see that those who loved only the idea of us were welcomed in, or stayed longer, because we hadn’t yet learned to love ourselves past the idea we placed in front.

This brings truth to the cliché saying of, “You must love yourself before another can love you,” but I think a better way of putting it would be: “You must love yourself in all your fullness before another can learn to love you.”

It’s important to remember that throwing the word “love” before you can be loved has its faults and detriments. And perhaps that wasn’t the best word for this narrative, because you can be loved in your fullness while not yet truly loving yourself. It still requires you to see every side of you, the sides you might like not as much, and show them to the person learning to love you for all sides.

Through this series I’ve learned to love the parts of me I’ve kept hidden, switching doubt for admiration as my lenses for my tools sharpen and turn blush with real love. It is through new communication and relationships that we uncover new versions and sides of us once shed with doubt instead of love. Still remember this: you should never feel shame or guilt for what you didn’t know, and through taking action to learn and love yourself in fullness, you are walking on two legs, perfectly forward.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: A Woman Waiting For Morning
subtitle: I woke to the windows beaded in dew...
body:
I woke to the windows beaded in dew,
the world outside fogged soft,
the sun trying —politely, stubbornly —
to thread itself through the glass
and pull me back into the day,
a day that still feels like a room
I’m learning to live in.

My iced tea waited in its crystal glass,
the one with the tiny bite missing from the rim —
where I dropped it last spring and refused to let it die.
A swirl of sweet cream and vanilla rose to the top,
curling into the morning like a quiet invitation.

Those nights on borrowed couches and guest beds —
God, the ceiling fans humming,
the soft thrum of another family’s refrigerator,
the quiet of someone else’s house settling around me.

I placed my shoes neatly by the door,
keys aligned on the nightstand,
pretending routine could anchor me.
Pretending someone might come looking.

I catch myself setting out two glasses,
like my hands know something my mind hasn’t caught up to.
Not on purpose — just muscle memory for a future
my body seems to know before I do.
One for me, and one for whoever’s meant to arrive.

I’ve started wearing perfume
before grocery runs,
letting my hair fall the way men tend to notice
when they’re truly paying attention.

I don’t know his name,but I know the shape of him —
the kind of man whose footsteps
settle a room before he speaks.
A laugh with weight to it,
a touch that feels sure, not startled,
and a quiet gravity that slips into my life
the way fog slips under morning light —
the kind of presence a home readies itself for
long before the person walks through the door.

The other day, I found myself painting —
a sure sign the noise outside me
had finally lowered enough for me to hear my own breath.
I can be in a room full of people
and still be untouched by it,
solitude blooming around me like a second skin.
The light fell across the canvas just right,
recognizing a version of methat’s only there when I’m quietly whole —
a version with room enough for someone else.

There was a second toothbrush in my cart
at Target last week.
For no reason.
Or maybe for the oldest reason of all:
my body knows something I don’t.
Tonight, I’m lighting a candle
and locking my door.

I’m turning my phone face-down
on the table.
I’m brushing my hair as a ritual,
whispering a quiet hello
to the life walking toward me.
Maybe I’ve been making room for him
without noticing.

Somewhere, he’s finishing his day,
and he has no idea
how close he is to becoming the answer
to a question I stopped asking.

And if anyone insists
this poem is about him —
that’s simply coincidence.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Animals of Projection
subtitle: She Hit Me, Yelled the N-Word, and Lied to 911… Did I Press Charges?
body:
I’m feeling perceptive today. A lot is circulating throughout my mind— some of it wise, most of it probably not. I’ve had a catastrophic week, not necessarily in the tragic sense, but chaos has sure found its way over to me.

Many of the avenues, attributes, and values circulating in my personal and work life are teetering between limbo and just above my reach. My love life isn’t the best. My personal life could use more friends. My work always seems to be waiting. Even when I do have work, I’m waiting on the next person’s word, some contract to fall into place, for the company to email me back. There’s only so much respectful follow-up you can do.

I don’t want to paint myself as impatient, but I’m reflecting on the fact that everything in my life is subject to change. I’m not sure if it’s going to change on a whim, by an email, or by a decision I make. What I do know is that I am ready, even if sometimes I feel as though I am not.

I believe in the mantra “what is meant for me will stay, will allow me to grow, and if set free and still meant for me, it will find its way back.” As everyone around me is either ending a relationship, beginning one, or— most commonly— simultaneously moving to a new place with or without ‘their person,’ I search for the deeper lessons that slide in between it all.

Wisdom, I’ve realized, is the ability to know when to withhold. Today I’m withholding quite a bit. Not knowledge exactly — more like information. There’s a difference. Knowledge is understanding. Information is just data. And I believe the people who achieve real wisdom are the ones who choose life over data.

For a long time, I operated on data over life. I’d dress scholarly for happy hour— business dress, stilettos— and position myself against the edge of the bar. I’d wait for my prey. And like clockwork, they’d appear: the ones wearing the cheapest Rolex their father could gift them. They never asked for my name. They just propped themselves next to me and started unloading facts they’d probably pre-memorized for their morning suck-up meeting.

But what was my mission? You could say I was on a knowledge war. My prey would ramble on, getting dumber, more flustered, more illiterate with every sentence. Their brain cells seemed to vanish as I stared at them in silence. And I waited — for the exact moment the fluster set in, when their rehearsed lines ran out. That, my pretty prey, is when I’d attack.

I felt okay about it at the time. Hell, they were obviously players, late-stage douche frat boys who never quite grew into maturity. They could memorize facts and swipe a credit card, so what did it matter? But when my silence forced them to outrun their script, and they finally fumbled, that’s when I’d speak— usually the first time they’d heard my voice all night. I’d calmly tell them exactly how wrong they were, then drop a piece of rehearsed data that made it very clear: they simply weren’t as smart as I was.

I see it now, the disdain I had. Even though I had somehow moralized my actions, it kept real wisdom hidden. It was just my routine to feel better after years of dumbing myself down for men who made me feel so incredibly small.

As I said before, I feel rather perceptive today. Many of the things that pain us come out in patterns of moralized disdain— whether passing a nice house and speaking ill of the people inside because their comfort highlights our shame, or seeing a woman with the figure we wish we had and instantly thinking ‘she must be starving herself.’ The reality is we are animals of projections. We stamp them on our walls, our screens, our days. We are so surrounded by them that escaping our own feels nearly impossible.

But that’s what we’ve become. And maybe wisdom is not only the ability to withhold knowledge, but the ability to see between the projections— to let the raw view come through.

I find myself noticing more of my own projections lately. Change is hard, and so many people around me are moving through big shifts in relationships and homes. With all the external pressure and new emotions, it’s easy to let projections run wild— and much harder to see what’s actually there.

Something more on the negative side of catastrophic happened this week. Among many other things, but this one topped the cake, complete with flashing lights. I was in a very public area, many cameras, many eye witnesses, when a woman, stained t-shirt, frizzy hair, a few missing teeth, and a whole lot of meat to her— slapped me across the face.

Did I deserve it? No. Her husband, also in a worn-down t-shirt with stains, frizzy hair, a few missing teeth, and not a lot of meat to him, started yelling racial slurs. So I promptly began recording with my phone as they were verbally attacking those around them. They had four or five young children, also in worn-down, stained t-shirts, running around the storage unit, hopscotching over strangers’ belongings in the hallway. There were a lot of people there that day—two families unloading, a newlywed couple, and another man minding his business. The doorways were busy, and all the moving carts were in use.

Their sons, after running a full lap, caught their breath together before walking out the doors in a straight line. A man walks around the corner carrying a bunch of things and bumps into the young boy. The man didn’t notice; his belongings barely grazed the boy’s shoulder.

I came out of the building, and there were the parents yelling, “My child was assaulted!” There isn’t much way to wiggle around the family. They demanded an apology, and when they got one, they demanded more and called 911. That’s when I began recording. Her child was not assaulted. I’m not sure who pissed in their cornflakes this morning, but this lady is full of shit. I start recording as she is talking to the 911 operator, when her husband decides to yell the n-word aloud. The wife asks if I’d like to get fucked up, and then, in between lying to the 911 operator, she swings her hand across my face. SLAP

I wasn’t sure necessarily what to do in that moment, but she was currently on the phone with 911, so I sought it best to narrate what was happening: “He just threatened him.” “She just threatened me.” “She just slapped me.”

I step aside and call 911 myself. I wasn’t sure if that was the best move, but I assumed it couldn’t hurt, as she’s transitioned into her call to “My children are being assaulted and videotaped by strangers.” The police arrive as I’m on the phone—there are around five cars and ten officers. Each one speaks to both of us. At this time, I wasn’t thinking whether or not anyone would get in trouble. I was more in the mindset of, this bitch is not getting away with lying. It wasn’t until the police watched the video of her slapping me in slow-motion that they said, “Whoa, she slapped you? Would you like to press charges?”

Every single officer watched the slap over and over in slow motion. I was shocked it was only a backhand because my god, did it hurt. Leading up to the slap and thereafter, in the video, you can see her children dancing around my feet, singing, ‘Karen, Karen, Karen.’ Which was extremely difficult not to laugh at despite the situation. They asked again if I’d like to press charges. I said to the officers, “My main concern is that they understand you cannot say racial slurs and assault people.” The officers assured me they are going to give them a difficult, stern talking-to, but ‘people like that don’t learn.’

I stepped aside from the officers and thought it over. In the end, I went with my gut. The number of times previously I wish I had followed through with a complaint, a filing, or that a friend had. I thought it over, not with a projection, but with raw reality. I didn’t want to get someone into trouble. I didn’t want children to see their mother get in trouble. I didn’t know if it would be a court date later, or if she would be taken away with cuffs in front of her little ones.

So I walked back over to the officers and asked what protocol would be, if I were to press charges. They assured me nothing would happen in front of the children, the mom would be escorted out of the building, and the officer gave me their information. With raw reality, I went with my gut and decided to press charges.

This chaotic week has forced me to look at the projections for what they truly are. The same woman who once dressed up for bar knowledge wars, weaponizing silence and facts just to feel superior after years of feeling small, is the same one who stood in a storage unit parking lot choosing raw reality over another cycle of disdain.

I could have projected every frustration from my own limbo onto her and her family. Instead, I chose to press charges not out of anger, but out of clarity. Sometimes wisdom isn’t just withholding knowledge—it’s knowing when to act from truth rather than pain.

Currently, I’m drinking a strawberry seltzer with my pup’s head on my lap, fighting for space on my keyboard. I’m still waiting on emails, still figuring out love and friendships, but I’m not waiting to become ready. Real growth happens in the moments between— when the character is off-camera, having an existential crisis while the script isn’t ready. It happens when you stop performing intelligence, stop moralizing your projections, and choose the harder, clearer path even when it’s uncomfortable.

I’m learning to lead with that version of myself— not just in the chaos, but in the quiet days too. At the end of the day, life isn’t data. It’s how we respond when the projections fall away, and we’re left standing only with what’s real.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Bitten By The Confidence Bug
subtitle: Why 98 Poems Made Me Feel More Naked Than A Nude Editorial
body:
Things have been changing rapidly in my life — ending one lease and starting another, supporting my friends and loved ones as they lose jobs, navigate this brutal economy, and watch it chip away at their confidence and sense of value in the world.

I’ve struggled with the same thing myself. The lack of a clear title sometimes makes it hard to locate your own worth, your confidence, and your self-value. At least that’s how I felt for many years.

For a long time, I was the one off working, armed with a job title that carried (what I thought) bragging weight, and for several years more, the pattern continued. I hid behind the title because I wasn’t sure where else my value was. Those of you in big cities, who live on the busy side of culture, know exactly what I mean. In my ten collective years in America’s top five biggest cities, I’m not sure anyone ever asked for my name before my job title.

It’s not per se tragic. Most of us there are working 24/7, hate wasting time, and don’t have much patience for, let’s say, the dumb. So I get how it happens. Over time, the culture made it feel more like a matter of efficiency than something rude or ingenious.

Still, I struggle today with finding value in myself without a notable career title. I’d love to answer “What do you do?” with one clean, confident swing and smile. I keep reminding myself— and my friends and loved ones— that having a tidy answer to that question isn’t what life is about, and it’s certainly not where our real value lies.

When I did have a title, I rode it like a character sheet. I let that fake confidence dance through my tone. Because I was never just a director, a manager, a model, or an actress. I was also a businesswoman, a poet, a sister, a daughter, and always that same curious little child.

Now I remind the people I love, as they lose what they thought was their forever path, that new titles, new values, and new meanings are floating around us — whether we can see them yet or not. When I got my first manager role, I proudly led with the title. But I forgot to show everyone who else I was.

I could have said, “I’m a manager, but I also love writing poetry and people-watching in cafés with new friends.”

I could have said, “I’m a sister trying to figure out how to love and support my family long-distance while managing a team at work.”

I could have said, “What do I do? I do a lot. I write, I dream, I try to be a good person… and more than anything, I like building communities of friends who lift each other up.”

These are the pieces I’m learning to lead with now. The titles are never the full story — they were just the easiest chapter to read, the cheapest answer I could give. And maybe, just maybe, the confidence I’ve been missing has been hiding in all the in-between parts I used to leave out.

This week, I got bit by the confidence bug, and maybe that light finally let me see this clearly enough to say it out loud. Sometimes I understand something intellectually, but it doesn’t sink all the way in until I write it, turn it into a poem, or hide it inside a short story that ‘supposedly’ has nothing to do with me.

So yes, this week I’ve been reminding everyone around me of the multitude of values they carry while they hunt for their next gig, next title, next career path, or bragging right. I’m telling them they are so much more than a career or a spot on a company website. Thank god they subscribe to What Sheridan Said, because they get to hear it again — and hopefully in a more beautiful way.

(And now, in complete contradiction to everything I just wrote…)

The title and career trajectory I’ve had my whole life might actually become my only one. At least I hope, but even then, I can still be a philosopher and businesswoman at the same time.

I told my mother about the bug that bit me, and later that evening, I overheard her on the phone: “Sheridan was so giddy telling me, it was like she was on a talk show couch. She kept nervously kicking her legs up in the air.”

The past few weeks, I’ve been chatting with a pretty well-established publisher. For instance, I told my mother the publishing company’s name, she pulled them up on her phone, looked at their logo big on the screen, and said, “You mean these guys? Sheridan… they’re huge.”

I’ll be completely honest with you, the way I’ve tried to be for over a year now. Early last year, I decided to put my writing, my life, the bad, the good, and all the nitty, witty, and weird details out there. I shared script snapshots and poetry previews. I’ve grown in my ghostwriting and built a network of people who simply believe in me.

Then I started getting voicemails from this publisher. Then emails. Every few weeks, another check-in. I was already quietly piecing together manuscripts and poetry collections, but I was scared and kept dodging them.

Several months later, one of the head agent’s assistants texted me. For the first time, I felt comfortable enough to respond.

And a month ago, I finally responded. I scheduled a meeting with the publishing agent. I shared and spoke about the few written projects I’m working on, signed the NDAs to protect my work and ownership rights, and then sent them my manuscript.

I didn’t send them any other manuscripts besides the 98 poems. During the meeting, we spoke about my book manuscript and other projects, but poetry really wasn’t the focus. I’m not sure why, looking back, I didn’t include the other manuscripts even though they showed genuine excitement and interest in them. Something in me held them back, and I decided to proceed with only poetry.

I’ve been writing poetry for as long as I can remember. My first poetry book is from elementary school. It helped me learn how to read, and it gave me a safe place to express myself when my diary kept getting broken into, and it still helps me make sense of this consistently confusing world.

I sat in the back of a beautiful hotel coffee shop, ordered a London Fog. I wrote a couple of good-luck poems, then tuned into my meeting, which ended shortly after an hour long. I’m hyper-critical of myself (some might say perfectionist), so I kept repeating the mantra: “Be open. Be smart.” Which meant to me, be open to criticism and different tastes, but smart about standing my ground and protecting the art I feel naked sharing.

I received what I can only call the kindest editorial review I could have hoped for. They see me as a leader in narrative poetry. I shed two happy tears.

In it they broke down projected book sales by quarter, who would buy it, and laid out an actual business strategy with what they believed were realistic metrics. After reading their ten-page review about seven times, I told them I could hop on a call the very next second.

I was eager, my god, I was so jittery I couldn’t stop crying. Was it happiness? Was it relief? Was it the thought of having 98 poems of mine out in the world, leaving me feeling more nude than any of my nude couture editorials? Or all three…

I sat on the front porch, my knees to my chest, and my feet on the chair, and told my mother about it all. She smiled and said, “I remember Mrs. Diehl at the end of the year. She brought me your three-ring binder of poems and said, ‘Don’t ever get rid of this. It will be worth something someday.’”

I shed another tear of happiness and relief, because it looks like Mrs. Diehl is (hopefully) about to be right.

My poetry manuscript was accepted. Now I’m waiting to hear back from the publisher’s board on their proposed investment. They’re already talking about book fairs, signings, and assigning me a project manager for my image and PR.

As much as I’d love to call myself a poet and only a poet, I know my value is so much more than that. My poetry wouldn’t exist without my chaotic career path, the strange life choices I keep making, and the extreme perspectives I’ve been forced to see. But my god… I never thought I’d make money from my poetry before I died.

I wrote three poems a day consistently through college and kept the habit through my career, and on to today. I think in poems, dance in prose, sing in sonnets… and apparently rant in rhythm to you.

I’m beyond excited. I’m scared. And I’m still bitten by that confidence bug.

They think my work is incredible?

I am so incredibly honored.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Boring, Happy, and Slightly Unhinged
subtitle: Poetry, Patents, and a 4-Foot Alien Named Stage-5 Clinger
body:
After years of working, skipping milestones, and surviving, I don’t really know what to do with this current chapter of my life. It’s… calm. Healthy. Slow. A little boring.

Saturday, I went to the Vienna Festival with some of the new friends I’ve made, a sentence that still feels new and good to say. We kicked off the afternoon at the Vienna Inn, this old-school diner that’s been around forever. They recently took all the prices off their menu. It felt like their way of saying: this place is for everyone. Don’t worry about the prices, just eat. So I did. We all did. Chili dogs, burgers, and bottomless fries. Then we headed off to the festival.

I’m not usually the kind of person who does carnival games. But my friends dared me to do every single chaotic one, and I don’t back down from a dare. I’ll try anything at least once.

So I find myself standing in front of that giant hammer game, you know the one, where you slam a mallet into a base and try to make the metal piece hit the bell. I look up at the guy running the game and say, “I don’t think I’m going to get very far… am I still getting a prize?” He just smirks and says, “Don’t worry about that.”

The hammer was significantly heavier than I am, a borderline medieval weapon. I lifted it, swung with all my might, and stumbled so hard I nearly knocked myself over. The guy gave me a quick tutorial and tried to correct my stance. I took a deep breath, tried again, and received the exact same result. Barely budged the thing. We’re talking two notches up. My arms may look toned, but I guess these noodles are only for show.

I turned around to my friends, who were filming me and cracking up, and when I turned back around, the guy handed me the biggest prize on the rack: a four-foot-tall rainbow alien. I absolutely did not deserve it. But he gave it to me anyway. And now I’m walking through the carnival with a massive alien on my back like he’s my little clingy boyfriend. He was wrapped around my body like a stage 5er, while everyone kept pointing and laughing. He was a hit.

I carried that alien around for three hours. We were inseparable. My new boyfriend and I. I now have him in my house, and I’m unsure where he lives yet. Guest bedroom? Living room mascot? Emotional support plushie? I’ll keep you posted.

Otherwise, I don’t know, life just feels a little boring right now. Not in a bad way. More like a healthy way. I’ve been growing a good group of friends. Slowly. Organically. I even turned down a gig recently, a background actor role in a music video. It wasn’t my vibe, but it still made me laugh. Like, of course, I got asked to be in a random music video when I’m trying to lay low.

What else? I’ve been writing new poetry more consistently lately. My poetry book needs to get to at least 200 finalized poems before it’s published. I still have several more notebooks of old poems to go through. Some of them are from middle school, and, as wise as I was in my early years, the emphasis on the early years sometimes shows too much. So I’ve been reworking some lines, editing others, and adding new ones when the moment hits. I have about 117 finalized right now. I would love 250, but maybe we’ll just have a second poetry collection book. Editing old poetry is like cracking open a time capsule. Some lines make me proud. Some make me want to crawl under a weighted blanket and hide. But it’s all part of the process.

Work is a little slow right now, which is kind of peaceful and kind of maddening. I’m used to sprinting. I’m used to solving things, building things, fixing things. Right now, I’ve just… rested. Taken long naps. Cleaned. Reorganized. Read books. It’s lovely. It’s strange. It’s dangerous. Because now I’m feeling the itch. That itch to do something new. Something chaotic. Something for the plot. Maybe it’s a new job. Maybe it’s a creative project. Maybe it’s buying a funny pink hat and seeing where life goes from there. I’m open to suggestions.

The truth is, I don’t really know what I want right now. I just want to have fun. I want to be more of myself every day. I want to keep learning. That’s what matters most. That’s always been the goal.

And despite the slowness, I’m still doing things. Big things, actually. I’m about to have my name on hopefully multiple patents. I’ll officially be a patented inventor. Which is wild. Being this young and holding patents is no small thing; hell, holding patents at any age is no small thing. I’ve worked hard for it, and I’m proud of where I’ve arrived.

So yeah, that’s where I’m at. (:

Life feels good right now. Calm. Slightly boring. Deeply funny. I’m happy. I’m not in survival mode. I’m not climbing out of something. I’m just… here. Living. Planning. Laughing. Writing. Carrying giant aliens around carnivals. And maybe that’s the plot twist.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Chaos, Couch Legs, and the Words That Saved Me
subtitle: I missed graduation, nearly cried over furniture, and remembered I’m still a poet.
body:
My baby sister graduates from college this weekend, and I’m not going to be there. I’m sad. I’m proud. I’m also overwhelmed. My schedule is chaotic right now, and as much as I want to teleport myself to hug her and act like the emotionally responsible eldest daughter, I just can’t make it work. And it sucks.

This week has been heavy with a sense of fatigue hard to shake. Everyone I know has been sick, physically, emotionally, or energetically. People are canceling, rescheduling, and rescheduling again. I tried to hold onto structure, but it felt like grabbing water with my hands. I ended up taking multiple naps, like it was part of my job description. My body gave up before my brain did. And when I finally allowed myself to collapse, I felt it: the exhaustion. Sometimes, surviving the week looks like sleep, tea, and lots of soft clothes.

Somewhere between quietly melting into my third or fourth reheat of the same cup of tea, I reminded myself: my poetry book is almost here. It’s happening. A real book. With my name. With poems I wrote in isolation, out of emotional survival, out of understanding the world around me, out of pain, and pure joy. I wrote when I didn’t want to talk to anyone and didn’t want to lie either.

I never started writing poetry because I thought I was good at it. I started writing poetry because I didn’t want anyone to read my diary. It was the safest way to say what I needed to say without handing anyone the full story. It was my therapy before therapy.

I grew up in a world where feelings weren’t explained; they were endured. I learned early how to fold a breakdown into a sentence. Poetry gave me that. In middle school, I used it to escape. I wrote about places I hadn’t seen and futures I didn’t know how to get to. People I met in passing, or stories I thought to be entertaining. In high school, I began writing more. I filled notebook after notebook with poems, and still to this day I’m finding more that I had completely forgotten. By the time I was living on my own in D.C., it was more than just my consistent ritual. I’d scribble verses while waiting on a bus or write full pages during 3 a.m. panic spirals. I have poems written on the backs of receipts, concert flyers, and matchbooks. Most of them I never shared. I didn’t write them for anyone. I wrote them because poetry is my longest friend.

Over time, I got better. Sharper. More honest. Less afraid. And now, years later, I can trace my growth back through these poems like a trail of breadcrumbs. Poetry cracked me open. It softened my anger. It gave my silence a voice. And it taught me how to see the world and myself clearly without flinching.

Now, it’s not just mine anymore. I’m building a poetry collective, a creative container for people like me, who need somewhere safe to say something real. A space for the poems that don’t rhyme but hit anyway. Where poetry can be practical. Where feelings are functional. Where truth has a stage, even if it’s trembling a little.

So here’s one of the poems from the upcoming collection. It still stings a little to share.

« ADD LUXURY EATS ME LAST »

And just for fun (and to show you how far I’ve come), here’s the very first poem I ever wrote. I find it quite adorable.

Okay now. Let’s talk about this couch I just bought.

I bought a couch off Facebook Marketplace because, of course, I did. It was a great deal, perfect color, beautiful shape. The only issue? I live in a very charming, very narrow, very unforgiving cottage-style house. My front door doesn’t open all the way because it hits the stairs at a dramatic two-thirds swing. The side door goes through the kitchen, which is essentially a hallway with cabinets. So that left the back door.

My driveway is basically a vertical slide for cars. We backed the truck up to the top and slowly inched the couch down like it was a baby grand piano. We made it through the back door. Into the dining room. Then we met the hallway.

Tom, who offered to help because he didn’t yet regret it, was standing there silently calculating the square footage of his mistakes. The hallway is the size of the couch. Exactly. I mean that in a literal sense. The couch entered the hallway, but it wasn’t coming out. It just sat there. Blocking everything. We tried angles. We tried swearing. We tried walking away. At one point, I accepted my fate: I guess I have a hallway couch now.

But I don’t give up. Not on couches. Not on metaphors. I spread my optimism onto Tom like butter on slightly stale bread, and we got back to work.

That’s when it hit me. If the couch stands perfectly upright, feet forward like a zombie marching to its death, it just might fit. But only if it was perfectly, and I mean perfectly, straight. One centimeter off, and it wasn’t going.

So we tilted. Lifted. Repositioned. Took a breath. And in one beautiful, excruciating moment, the couch slid through the doorway like it was always meant to be in that living room. And there it sits. Triumphant. Beautiful. Absolutely not a hallway couch.

Anyway, that was my week. I missed a milestone. I grieved a little. I slept a lot. I remembered who I was through poems. And I fought a couch and won.

More next week. Probably from bed again.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Coke Without Ice
subtitle: The girl who bullied me // had greasy skin and half-moon nails,
body:
The girl who bullied me
had greasy skin and half-moon nails,
drank her Coke without ice,
leaned bow-legged against the wall
like she knew what beauty cost.
My bully was me.

I had no friends—
only obsessions,
mostly older girls who smelled of iris
and something black-tea bitter.
Sallys. Tamaras. Dollys.
Names that made the air look glossy.
They floated by lockers
like cigarettes in slow motion,
while I studied posture, timing, tone—
the science of what cannot be learned.

I wanted them to sense me,
the quiet cool of my knowing,
but I was giving awkward,
I was giving wrong century.
When I opened my mouth,
everything lovely leaked out sideways.

I knew colors like lovers—
pink lava-lamp flesh,
spaceship silver,
sunset bruised orange-lilac—
but none of it translated.
Words abandoned me mid-sentence,
leaving only the echo of my effort.

Sometimes, before sleep,
I replayed the conversation with Sarah.
You must understand—
she was the kind of rich that smells clean.
Her family fostered children,
and wore philanthropy like silk pajamas.

I wanted her to like me,
so I tried to sound bright.
Too bright.
The space between us tightened—
even the silence looked away.

Sometimes I still see her—
greasy skin, trembling straw,
that Coke sweating in her hand.
She drinks it warm, like punishment,
and smiles as if she finally
deserves the burn.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Crying Over Directions & The Art of Forgiving Yourself
subtitle: America's Chicken Noodle, Family Whiskey, and Trusting the Messy Middle
body:
Last week ended up being a half-episode because I wasn’t feeling well, and normally, when something like that happens, I do what I’ve always done: push straight through it. I keep working, finish whatever needs finishing. I also have the deeply unhelpful habit of skipping the ibuprofen, skipping the vitamins, and basically ignoring anything that might actually help me recover, because somewhere in my brain I’ve convinced myself that productivity is medicine.

This time, though, I didn’t do that. I actually took it easy. I rested, stayed in environments that were helping me recover, and stopped working when I was supposed to be recovering, which turns out to be the entire point of being sick, who knew? The strange thing is how quickly everything turned around once I stopped fighting it. I got better in what felt like record time, which was almost annoying because it forced me to acknowledge something I already knew but clearly don’t practice enough: sometimes the fastest way to recover is to stop trying to outrun the problem.

Part of the reason resting feels unnatural to me is that I’m the type of person who likes to know exactly what’s happening inside my body. If something hurts, I want to know where it is, how much it hurts, what it means, and whether there’s some explanation that makes the whole thing understandable. I like knowing things. I like the mechanics of things. I like the illusion that if I understand the system well enough, I might somehow control the outcome. This time, I didn’t chase any of that. I didn’t analyze every symptom or interrogate every sensation. I just let it be what it was, and it turns out my body handled it perfectly fine without my supervision.

This week, I rested, took vitamins and ibuprofen, and I even had an amazing man make me homemade chicken noodle soup. Spoiled. ♡

Speaking of chicken noodle soup, being sick reminded me of something that happened several years ago that still makes me laugh every time I think about it. I had been seeing this guy for a few weeks; he stayed with me over the weekend, and that Sunday, he wasn’t feeling very well. He was on the couch, wrapped up in a blanket, looking absolutely miserable, the full sick-day setup. At some point, he mentioned chicken noodle soup, which is basically the universal sick food, so I went into the kitchen to see what I had.

The only thing in the house was a can of Campbell’s chicken noodle soup. So I grab the can opener and open the can. As I’m standing there with the can still in my hand, he walks into the kitchen. Mind you, I bought my first pot and pan at age 25/26 so I’m not sure if that was even in this kitchen at the time. Also, my oven was being used for extra shoe storage (I know).

The really nice king-size blanket is wrapped around his shoulders, dragging across my hardwood floor, reminding me I should have vacuumed the dog hair. He gets to the kitchen, stops, and looks at me. Then he looks at the can. Then at me. Then at the can opener. Then back to me.

Finally, he said, completely serious, “You think I’m a fucking cat? Why are you giving me canned food?”

Completely confused, I stood there holding Campbell’s chicken noodle soup, trying to understand what he meant. I said, “What do you mean? This is America’s chicken noodle soup, Campbell’s, see?”

He keeps eye contact like I’ve launched the biggest insult of the year.

“I’m not a fucking cat,” he says.

At that point, I’m contemplating whether or not I should explain to him that this is actually meant for humans, not cats. Eventually, I just say, “Well, this is all I have.”

He nods and says, “It’s cool. I’m headed out.”

He grabs his bag, lays down my king-size blanket that has swept up my floors from being a dog hair carpet back to its hardwood glory, and he leaves, within a few moments, closing the door behind him.

I immediately started laughing hysterically the second the door shut. I’m still standing there in the kitchen, staring at the soup, trying to figure out how America’s Campbell’s chicken noodle soup insulted him that badly?

So last week, as I was fed and cared for, and saw what true homemade chicken noodle soup is, I hate to say it, but maybe I am on his side now?

Not really, but I do understand the classism he had, though I don’t respect it or like it. But hey, you won’t ever catch me eating canned spam, or Wonder Bread, but also, if I’m at someone’s house and they make me a sandwich and all they have is Wonder Bread, I’m not saying anything. I will eat that sandwich with a smile, like goddamn Wonder Woman.

All jokes aside, I suppose I have empathy for the chicken noodle soup buffoon, or maybe, just maybe, I’m getting used to being spoiled.

Aside from that bizarre story, this week actually ended up being really good in ways I didn’t expect. I got to spend a lot of time with family and people I love, which was exactly what I needed after not feeling well. My beautiful mother’s birthday was this week, so I have to give her a shout-out because not only did I get my amazing, voluminous, bouncy hair from her, but no matter where I am in the world, no matter what my relationship status is, she will always be my first love and my first home. I love you always mom ♡.

Yesterday was also Uncle Brian’s birthday!! Brian, I love you so much. You’re truly the big brother I always wished I had.

To throw in even more family members into this week’s episode, my great aunt was visiting town as well, and it was really nice to spend time with her. I think we shared a whole bottle of whiskey, um.. the details are blurry. The whole week ended up feeling relaxing and rejuvenating in a way I didn’t realize I needed (even the whiskey hangover).

Of course, right as all of this is happening, as my health becomes intact, my PMS decides to arrive, which means I have been crying about absolutely everything. At one point, I cried wiping down the car, and at another point, I cried because I felt like I was never going to understand my left and rights correctly.

I was driving the other day with a friend, and she said to turn right. I naturally got into the furthest left lane at the twenty fucking lane stoplight intersection. I make my turn and drive straight a few blocks before she says, “We were actually supposed to turn the other way at the stop light, but you looked so confident, I didn’t want to say anything.”

I immediately started crying. I guess I felt stupid? I also wasted an extra five minutes making more turns to get back on the correct route, and I could have been eating my burger at the bar a whole five minutes sooner, which my PMSing, hangry self did not have much self-control to account for. So I cried, calmed down, ate a burger, then definitely cried later over something obviously not worth crying over.

Truly, when it comes to 50/50s, I get them wrong 50% of the time; it has, unfortunately, always been like this. I remember, in sixth grade, we were taking a science test, and everyone else had finished. The bell had rung, the entire class was already in the locker room getting ready for the next period, and I was stuck, sitting at my desk, with the teacher staring at me, frustrated, with one dumb final question left. It was a true-or-false question about whether a proton was positive, and for some reason, my brain just would not commit to the answer. My teacher saw how frustrated I was and came over to sit next to me. She looked at the question, thought about it for a moment, I swear I saw her smirk a little, then she asked me the same question in a different way, instead of framing it as true or false (as a 50/50). The second she asked it like that in a new way, I knew the answer immediately. She smiled and told me to write “true” on my test. I remember thanking her over and over again because it felt like she had rescued me from something unnecessarily frustrating.

I had actually hoped to have a lot more news to share with you this week, and I’ve been a little stressed about that because there are so many timelines in my head right now that I haven’t even written down. They mostly exist in my brain, and I’m constantly trying to mentally hold myself accountable to them without actually having them organized anywhere, which is a strange way to live, but apparently, it’s one of the systems I’m currently operating under. Part of the reason for that is right now, I’m in a position where I really should—well, need—to say yes to consistent ghostwriting gigs that are, well, sending consistent paychecks. That work has taken priority, even when there are several other projects I’m excited about building at the same time.

It’s been a weird balance because a lot of what I’m working on right now is about elevating my own writing career, and sometimes it feels like I’m my own worst enemy, biggest fan, and harshest critic all at once (it’s fun inside my head). I had hoped to be able to announce the release of my book this week, in this episode—everything is completed on my end—but even that timeline shifted because of things completely out of my control and unrelated to my ghostwriting gigs.

At the same time, I’m still working on the location for my short film (I’m so picky it’s an issue), and I have so many smaller projects that I’m excited to share with you once they’re ready. I know that eventually all of these things are going to support my career in ways that make sense, but right now they exist in that strange middle space where you’re building everything at once and trying to trust that the pieces will eventually fall into place together.

With forgiving my hidden timelines, I’ve also been thinking a lot about what it means to become a person inside your own writing. Not in an ego way, but in the sense that writing forces you to step outside of yourself for a minute. Stepping out of your own shoes, stepping into someone else’s, hopping into another that’s just a bystander—I think it’s about taking the small picture, the big picture, and all the other sizes in between; that’s how you create a world within your own writing. By understanding the world, or at least actively learning what it looks like from every picture size, and from every person’s shoes.

That’s always been the strange magic of writing for me. It lets you zoom out just enough to see that the chaos, the timelines, the crying over left and rights, the projects moving slower than you want them to—none of it is actually the end of the story. It’s just the middle of it. And if the middle of the story right now involves resting when I’m sick, forgiving myself when things take longer than planned, and occasionally discovering that a grown man thinks Campbell’s soup is cat food, then honestly… I think I’m doing just fine.

Anyways, I’ll talk with you next episode ♡.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
