title: Every Unhinged Thing I Had to Do to Be Taken Seriously at Work
subtitle: On bronzer, fur coats, pants, mom cards, and the toolkit that kept me alive in rooms full of men twice my age.
body:
Last week, I told you about how I lied about my age to get the job I wanted. I was nineteen, pretending to be twenty-seven. The part I didn’t get into was how I pulled that off. A lot of you asked me that, and honestly, it wasn’t one thing. It was everything. I smelled like an old lady. My perfume wasn’t fruity, flirty, or playful; it was powdery, mature, the kind of smell that clings to velvet drapes and pearls. And I wore pearls, always. My shoes were closed-toe stilettos; I never wore sandals, never peep-toes, always sharp and pointed. My coats were fur, real, the coat was a statement, and there was only one statement I wanted to make: you are not dealing with a child. My wardrobe was built around old-school business dresses and tailored suits, the kind of thing you picture in faded photographs from the seventies when offices were still full of cigarette smoke.

Even my makeup played a role. Bronzer has always aged me, in a strange way I don’t fully understand. So I piled it on, letting the warmth shade me toward an older version of myself. My speech matched the look. I was clipped, declarative, never too eager, never bubbly. I understood that when all the senses line up, when you look older, smell older, sound older, people stop questioning you. They take you as the person you are presenting, because every detail points in the same direction. That was my secret; it was a performance in flesh.

But that story is just part of the beginning. Pretending to be older was only one of my unhinged career hacks I’ve learned and carried with me. Over the years, I’ve collected a whole arsenal of them, tricks born out of necessity, survival skills for navigating rooms that weren’t built for women like me. They are not always glamorous, and they are not always fair. You may not like all of them, but here they are.

One of the biggest is creating a uniform. And I don’t mean wearing the exact same outfit every day as a cartoon character or Steve Jobs. I mean building a silhouette, a formula, a look that becomes your visual brand. Margaret Qualley did this in Honey Don’t; every outfit was basically a high-waisted pair of trousers and a button-up shirt, with small feminine touches like a belt or boots. That’s the genius of it: you can create endless variations while still presenting a consistent, unmistakable shape. I’ve built my own version of that, and you can too.

It’s not just about branding, though that part matters. It’s about sanity. If you’re like me, someone who obsesses, someone who wants perfection every time, then choosing outfits can become a spiral that eats away at your energy before you even step out the door. By sticking to a thumbnail uniform, I free myself from that mental tax. The creative juice I would have wasted deciding between a thousand different skirt options is now used to build stronger pitches, sharper ideas, and more profitable companies. My uniform doesn’t just save me time; it redirects my energy toward the things that actually matter.

And sometimes it’s tactical. In male-dominated industries, especially in the hospitality industry, I only wear pants. Always. It’s not that I don’t love skirts or dresses—Believe me, I do—but to certain eyes, no matter how professional or modest the skirt is, it will still be reduced to “a little skirt on a little girl.” Wearing pants takes that weapon out of their hands before they can swing it. Some battles are fought with silence, others with fabric.

Another unhinged hack I learned very early: cite your sources. When I was first starting out, I was always the youngest in the room, always the only woman, always the only one under the age of fifty. And whenever I spoke, people demanded evidence. My title wasn’t enough. My place at the table wasn’t enough. If I made a point, I was asked to back it up with three reasons, three facts, three data points. So I built the habit of speaking in triplets: outcome, mechanism, proof. I became evidently bulletproof. Once the field was level, once people started listening to me as though my words had weight, I could drop the act and go back to normal conversation. But in those early years, that armor of evidence was what kept me standing.

Not every trick is steel and sharpness; some are about amping up your stereotypical female traits for the greater good. Sometimes, it’s called pulling the “mom card.” Sometimes, in new offices, I’d run into the man who seemed to box me quickly into a stereotype, who dismissed everything I had to say. So I stopped trying to fight him outright. I’d let him run his experiment, let him argue, let him do it his way, so long as it wasn’t catastrophic. Then, when it failed, he’d come back to me. And I would meet him the way my mother used to meet me: patient, empathetic, calm. I’d show him the right way, walk him through it, and guide him into the path that actually worked. And suddenly, that man would become one of my strongest allies, a better employee, a better listener, even a better leader. All it took was picking my battles, letting him fail a little bit, and waiting it out.

I’ve even experimented with optics when it came time to negotiate for a raise or promotion. This one might sound manipulative, but I’ll be honest: it worked. I would dress just a touch richer, subtle changes in jewelry, in shoes, in hair, and in nails. Nothing obvious, nothing gaudy, just enough to spark a thought in my boss’s head: she looks too expensive for what we’re paying her. Visual branding, baby. Sometimes it’s louder than words.

And then there’s the sales lesson. One of the quickest instincts I’ve had to hone is knowing whether a man wants to do business with me or just wants to see me again. It’s not always obvious at first when you are just beginning in your career, but you learn the difference: does he care about the contract, or the next time you’re stopping by? Do they want the company I represent, or my company? It’s a survival skill, especially when you’re young and female in environments where those lines are blurred far too often.

There’s also a truth I can’t ignore: the safety rules aren’t the same for everyone. A man might finish a project and grab drinks with his boss without a second thought, but as a young woman, I’ve always had to pause and calculate what’s safe, what’s smart, what’s actually business, and what might not be. Those quiet calculations become second nature. They turn into another piece of the unhinged toolkit, not glamorous, not something I wish were necessary, but survival all the same.

To straighten any arrows, I would love more than anything to tell you that you can always show up exactly as you are, in any outfit, in any tone, without ever needing to strategize. But the truth is, not every room is sound-minded, and not every set of eyes will see you without bias. That’s why I’ve learned to collect these unhinged hacks over time, because sometimes it takes bronzer, or a uniform, or a carefully pulled “mom card,” or even a sharpened sales instinct to navigate a room that wasn’t built for us. Pretending those dynamics don’t exist doesn’t make them go away. What you can do is decide when to lean in, when to deter, when to let patience work for you, and when to let the fabric, or the silence, speak on your behalf.

At the end of the day, none of this is about disguising yourself. It’s about claiming space in places that were never designed for me, or women like me, and refusing to let anyone mistake confidence for invitation. If there’s one lesson in all of it, it’s this: don’t wait for the world to give you permission. Wear the fur coat at nineteen. Build the uniform. Pull the mom card.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Flowers Covered His Skin
subtitle: It smelled nice, hid the cigarettes // And when he forgot to brush his teeth.
body:
I drove across town
And met a fugitive in a small shop.

I knew his crimes. Still I sat,
Talking with the man whose jail tag
Wore a dollar sign as cheap cologne.

But flowers covered his skin
They made him look gentle, from afar.
It smelled nice, hid the cigarettes
And when he forgot to brush his teeth.

I ordered something sweet,
Him a dark drip. The walls
Were painted black, but somehow
His cup was even darker.

Maybe it was the caffeine,
Or my hyper positive smile,
I convinced myself he had a light
But I think really he was just holding mine.

He lies awake all night,
Thumbs twitching toward war,
Chasing ghosts that always respawn,
Then dreams through
The sun’s bright rays.

He cleans his teeth with white Colgate
And spits hot red, staining my sink.
Dishes stack like unpaid debts.
Dust collects where his hands don’t reach.

I read him a poem after he runs
A head into a brick wall. Blue fog
Lingers. My London tea is bitter,
Too strong.

We walk, the sun seems to skip him.
The trees dance opposite his way
Fire follows, and the birds all pray.
What damned you be this way?

s.g.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: From Mugshot to Miracle: My Harrowing Journey for My Shadow
subtitle: Inside the late-night seizures, roadside chaos, and an emotional low that only a Dinosaur could fix.
body:
Let’s get one thing out of the way: yes, that’s me in the mugshot.

And no, I didn’t miss last week’s newsletter because I was journaling from jail. I wasn’t scribbling haikus on the walls of a Washington County holding cell or bartering eyeliner for Wi-Fi access. Though honestly? That would’ve made for a hell of a story.

But I was arrested, well, not really.

Technically, emotionally, spiritually, cosmically, sure.

One minute I’m driving south on I-81 with both dogs in the backseat, singing to a playlist that could’ve resurrected Amy Winehouse herself, and the next it’s lights in the rearview and an officer asking, “Do you know how fast you were going?” I did. And I didn’t. Because isn’t that how these things go?

It was very much a “shit, I’m speeding… shit, that’s a cop… shit, he’s behind me” moment, followed by “Well, Sheridan, I hope you enjoyed freedom.”

Now, before anyone clutches their pearls, no, I wasn’t thrown in a cell or handcuffed in front of my dogs like some suburban outlaw. But in that moment, heart racing, hands shaking, Shadow looking up at me with those eyes, asking, “Is everything okay?”—it felt like the kind of day that deserved a mugshot. So I made one. Obviously. Because I’m definitely not ✨dramatic✨ in any way, shape, or form???

The truth is, I was barely going over the speed limit. And honestly, it was a slow day on the roads, so I get it: my long streak of good luck had to tap the brakes once in a decade.

I was driving from the East Coast to southern Tennessee. While the morning roads were eerily empty (just me, the trees, and the existential dread), the evening was absolute chaos, bumper-to-bumper traffic snaking along the edge of a mountain, semis tipped over like dominoes, every car crawling as if we were in line for the apocalypse. I didn’t get to my destination until 10 pm, five hours later than planned. So yes, I missed the newsletter.

To everyone who asked if I was okay because your favorite drama series, What Sheridan Said, didn’t air on schedule, thank you. Consider this my apology letter, complete with a fake mugshot and a very real story I finally decided to share.

If you haven’t realized it yet, I’m a massive fan of dogs. But I want to tell you about my mother’s favorite “Grandpup,” Shadow, and why I would drive 500 miles in the middle of the week just to hand-deliver him to my parents for safety.

Because when your dog has epilepsy, when he’s had four seizures in two hours, when you cradle him into a vet’s arms while mascara streams down your jawline, suddenly, every mile feels like a prayer.

It was a little over a year ago, maybe around 3 AM, when I woke to Shadow kicking me in the back. At first, I thought he was dreaming; he’s an active dreamer who howls in his sleep (I know, fun). But as the movement became more aggressive, I realized he was seizing, full-body, uncontrollable. It was terrifying.

He had four more seizures before I could even make it to the ER. I woke my mother, and with one eye barely open and my arms wrapped around Shadow, we drove straight there. When I arrived, I stood in the center of the waiting room and said, “He’s had four seizures in two hours.” Then everything blurred, vets rushing toward us, arms reaching for him, clipboards thrown aside. I will never forget the way they looked at me: like I had just brought in a baby who was close to death. Because I did.

Shadow was quickly diagnosed with extreme epilepsy and began taking heavy medication twice a day, “he’s stoned 24/7,” as the doctor put it, so as his guardian, I take my role very seriously. I don’t know how long he will be with me. The medication is so strong that I have to get his organs and all of his insides checked out once every six months. I’m hopeful he will live a long life, even if it’s been shortened by his medical diagnosis.

Shadow isn’t just a dog. He’s part of my “before and after.”

I got him when my first dog, Fendi (actually named Fendi), was roughly five years old. He was the best dog you could ever ask for. Fendi was a dachshund/chihuahua/terrier mix who looked like a Duck Dynasty extra, and of course, Shadow’s best friend. Then one day in my Houston backyard, the cruel circle of life appeared, and an owl swooped down and killed Fendi.

Just like that, gone.

Shadow saw it all happen. He ran inside through the magnetic screen door, crying in a way I’d never heard before, and hid under my bed. I sprinted outside and found Fendi’s body, covered in blood, breathless.

Instinctively, I climbed the nearest massive tree, convinced whatever did this was still up there, and that I would kill it and have it for dinner. Picture a clumsy panda flailing and falling over and over, refusing to quit.

Eventually, I wrapped Fendi in a blanket and drove to the emergency vet. They shortly confirmed that an owl’s claw had punctured his lung, ending his life in an instant, assuring me it was fast and painless.

If you didn’t know, owls kill and leave their prey, then return later to eat.

I don’t care what anyone says: a dog can grieve, a dog can suffer from extreme depression. And Shadow didn’t just grieve Fendi’s murder; he spiraled into a deep depression.

He stopped eating entirely, and for over four months, he wouldn’t touch a toy. When I finally took him to the dog park, I’m not even kidding, he went up to every single dog, did his little “sit dance” (raises a leg, sits, and smiles), and they all turned away and walked off. After trying every dog, there were dozens, he sat by the exit gate and let out a howl/cry. It wasn’t until I brought home Dinosaur, Dino for short, who needed a home and was free, that Shadow instantly cheered back up. He just needed a friend.

That’s why I don’t trust anyone else with him besides my parents. That’s why I packed him and Dino (a Golden Retriever/Chihuahua mix, if you can believe that contradiction) into the car, kissed the East Coast goodbye, and drove all the way to Tennessee to drop them off, before flying over an ocean for my next adventure. Didn’t I say I’m “definitely not ✨dramatic✨?”

So no, I wasn’t arrested last week. But I did hit pause on everything. I drove, I wrote poetry, and wrote some other things I’ll soon spill details about. And I didn’t even get a speeding ticket; Dino’s cuteness distracted the officer, who turned out to be extremely nice. It was my first time getting pulled over in almost ten years. So, yeah, I dropped off my best friends and whispered, “Good luck and safe driving only,” to myself before driving straight back home to pack. Then I made a mugshot, just to be dramatic.

But today? I’m not driving across the country, flying over an ocean, or performing at a poetry slam. I’m here, talking with you all, whom I’ve loved sharing my life with these past several months.

And no, officer. I won’t do it again. Scouts honor.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: How I Lied My Way Into Power Before I Could Legally Order a Vodka Soda
subtitle: Proof that audacity beats qualifications every single time.
body:
Let me tell you about the time I lied about my age just so I could run restaurants, fire bartenders, and evade the police, all before I was legally allowed to order a vodka soda.

When I was nineteen, I pretended to be twenty-seven.

Yes, twenty-seven. Not twenty-one. Not twenty-two. Not a little white lie to scoot past a technicality. I skipped right over legal adulthood and planted myself firmly in “established professional” territory. Why? Because nineteen-year-old me looked around, saw a world that wasn’t going to hand her a seat at the table, and said: Fine. I’ll just forge my own damn chair and show up anyway.

And I sold it. I sold it so hard that I ended up running restaurants, bars, and a theater on the East Coast.

Most of the people who sat on the board of directors I reported to are now deceased. The businesses themselves have been shuttered for quite some time, so nobody’s left to be implicated, maybe except me.

Of course, my reign wasn’t without hiccups. There were moments when the illusion wobbled, when furious bartenders, recently fired for stealing, decided the best way to get back at me was to march to a police officer and announce: “She’s lying about her age!”

The cops showed up, and I braced myself for collapse. Then, I walked away scot-free.

Because here’s the thing: the cops adored me. They never even asked to see my ID. I was nineteen, with a neat bun and a notepad, playing twenty-seven with such conviction that armed officers shrugged and let me go back to running the liquored establishments.

Think about that for a second. That’s not just audacity. That’s sorcery.

Now, let’s discuss my bosses. They were Army Special Forces veterans, which sounds glamorous until you realize what that means for employee training. They didn’t just teach me how to run venues; they broke me down like I was in boot camp.

They had this drill, pure psychological warfare disguised as “training.” I’d start at the front door of a restaurant and march in a straight line to the back, eyes locked on the exit. I wasn’t allowed to look around, not even a glance. But I was expected to notice everything.

The napkins that had dwindled down to two. The barstool leaning on a bad leg. The wood paneling scratched by some drunk’s wedding ring. A customer sliding their table three inches to the left.

When I hit the back alley, I had to yank out my notepad and list it all. Every flaw, every offense, every negative change in the room. If I missed even one detail? Back to the front door. Start over, again, and again. Until my legs ached and my pride cracked and I found myself crying in a broom closet, wondering if this was actually worth it.

And then, something shifted. Perhaps after a week of drills, my peripheral vision turned into a weapon. I could clock a missing coaster, a lipstick smear on a martini glass, and a drunk weaving toward the bathroom all in the same sweep, without ever breaking stride.

It was hell while I was in it, but it hardwired me. Now I walk into a space and instantly know what’s wrong before I’ve even thought about it. Which, honestly, is less of a “superpower” and more of a curse when you’re just trying to enjoy brunch.

Do I recommend this to anyone? Bending the law to achieve your goal? Absolutely NOT. Don’t lie about your age, don’t risk arrest, and definitely don’t put yourself in situations where your only escape depends on charisma and war-veteran-trained peripheral vision.

But, and this is the part that matters, I will never regret it.

I was a nineteen-year-old girl on the East Coast. No connections. No family money. No reason anyone should have taken me seriously. The only way I was going to get the job I wanted was to create a Sheridan big enough, bold enough, and old enough that the world had no choice but to believe her. And I did it. Not because I was qualified. Not because I had experience. But because I refused to hear no.

The regular path isn’t always the right path. If you wait for the world to tell you you’re ready, you’ll be waiting forever. There will always be a credential you don’t have, an experience you’re missing, a box you haven’t checked.

So here’s what I want you to take away:

  • Send the pitch you’re scared to send.

  • Apply to the job you think you’re underqualified for.

  • Make the audacious ask.

The worst thing that happens is someone says no. And I promise you — that hurts a lot less than spending your life wondering what would’ve happened if you’d just had the nerve to try.

I wouldn’t be who I am today if I hadn’t marched into those venues at nineteen and pretended to be twenty-seven. It was reckless, it was insane, but it was also the crucible that shaped me.

That was then. These days, the battleground looks a little different. I’m not dodging bartenders or fooling cops anymore; now it’s just me, a laptop, and the constant negotiation between ambition and sanity. The drills have changed, but the chaos? Still alive and well.

This week I worked, I went to the dog park with Shadow and Dino (a lot), and I questioned my sanity (a hobby at this point).

I also sent out some very ballsy pitches, the kind that made me laugh when I hit send, because who the hell do I think I am?

But then I remembered: the same girl who once lied about her age just to get the job she wanted. That’s who.

So yes, I recommend you do the same. Be legal, but be unreasonable. Be audacious. Because who knows who you might become?

Don’t wait for permission. Don’t wait until you’re “ready.” Don’t let “no” be the end of your story. I was nineteen, running venues with forged confidence and sheer nerve. You can do the thing you think you can’t do. You can apply, you can pitch, you can walk through fire.

And if anyone doubts you? Walk straight to the back door with your eyes forward, take notes with your peripheral vision, and keep achieving your goals.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: How Poetry, Go-Karts, and Three exes Took me out in the Same Week
subtitle: This Week I Blacked Out (Twice), Got Hit with a Mallet, and Accidentally Took Out a Couple on a Date
body:
I want to bring you back to Thursday, because that’s when the trouble began. I went go-kart racing with two friends, yes, in a summer mini dress and heels, because why would I EVER choose function over fashion? These weren’t kiddie go-karts either; these things go 60 mph, no padding, just a helmet, and the big man above crossing his fingers for the daredevil inside of me. The track had three big turns shaped like a snake. First round out, it’s me, my two friends, and this couple clearly on a date night joyride. They’re taking it slow. I’m not...

But then it happens.

Right before the big S-turn, my heel gets caught under the gas pedal. Full throttle. No way to move it. I’m flying into the turn at 60 mph with my foot jammed to the floor, and this slow, romantic couple just strolling, making googly eyes at each other, in the middle of the big, crazy S-turn. So I make a choice, I see a slight opening, and I go straight between them, thinking I’ve got the clearance.

I don’t.

I hit both of them. They spin out. I get yelled at for being “too aggressive,” and I just nod sweetly because I don’t want the staff looking too closely at my shoe situation. I mean, I have several more races in my system for the night. After that race ended, the couple bowed out, and they waited for me to be done before going back out on the track. Understandably so. Meanwhile, I went two more rounds. That’s called commitment.

And let’s be real, I wasn’t racing to win. I was racing to figure out exactly how fast I could take those S-curves without spinning out and crashing. I was collecting data. 💋 For 30 minutes, I flung myself around that track like a pinball just to test the math of speed, angle, timing, and how long it takes for your brain to start enjoying whiplash.

Later that evening, I peeled off my clothes to find welts across my back and bruises blooming on my hips. I looked like I’d lost a fight to a flight of stairs. My friends were like, “Was it worth it?” “Absolutely?” I answer with a smirk. I want to go fast. I want to test my limits. Even if it means walking like a Victorian woman for two days after.

Friday was quieter. I got some work done, mostly keeping up with startup advising and the nonprofit I’m working with. Saturday, I went full Americana and grabbed burgers and root beer floats with friends before heading to a karaoke bar. The kind of karaoke bar where you don’t sing, you people-watch.

That night’s headliner? Adam Sandler’s long-lost twin. He had the wraparound shades, the baggy T-shirt, the basketball shorts, and the slides. He danced like no one was watching (we were). He was the moment. There were also some Navy boys doing rap songs, and honestly? They ate. Iconic. 10/10. Zero notes.

Sunday was a reset, my favorite deli, some long hours reading and writing, and mentally preparing for what was about to be the most vulnerable 48 hours of my entire creative life.

Enter: Open Mic Monday.

It was a small, cozy poetry open mic night. Not many people, just a group of strangers in a café-style room sharing work, and I was terrified. I showed up early and met this girl, Anne, who immediately gave me a vote of confidence. She signed up third. Told me to sign up fourth. “You won’t be first,” she promised. And she was right.

I went up and read two poems. I blacked out the whole time. Like, truly blacked out. I don’t remember hearing anything. Not the applause. Not my voice. Not even my heartbeat. When I sat down, people told me I was good. A few even asked for my contact info to read more. Anne was so kind. It all felt very safe, very lovely. But I was still shaking the whole night.

And maybe I should’ve left it at that. But I don’t know how to do things halfway. So I signed up for another poetry night the next day, Tuesday, yesterday. Only this time, it wasn’t low-stakes and cozy. It was the BIG leagues.

I showed up at 7 PM sharp, hoping to sign up early and maybe catch a few warm-up poems before the nerves kicked in. What I didn’t expect was to walk into a full-blown event with over 300 people packed into the room.

Congressmen, senators, activists, the owner of the venue chain, and me… wearing a tiny green dress, shaking like a leaf. The venue was hosting a geopolitical panel before open mic called U.S. Attacks Iran: What Happens Next with Mehdi Hassan and Representative Ro Khanna. Between my nerves shutting off and on, I tried listening in to the panel, but truly, my mind was in no vacancy.

At some point, I started talking to the owner of the venue. He finds out I’m performing. He’s nice. Supportive. And somehow, I end up going up fourth again — just like the night before. I don’t know if it’s fate or a curse, but I blacked out the second my name was called. No memory. No internal monologue. Just silence and white noise and my feet moving on their own.

I read the same two poems I’d done the night before. Everyone else had a strict time limit, but the host, Glo Shines, a radiant poet and hip-hop artist, let me run a little long. That felt generous. But as soon as I sat down, I could feel it. The panic is building. The nerves are swelling. She had the crowd thank me again, and then she cracked a joke about Beyoncé (I think?) — I don’t remember a single word of anything she said after I read. I was just trying not to cry in front of 300 people. But as gravity does, the tears fell, and I had to sneak off to the bathroom. There I paced in circles and tried every grounding trick I knew: smell something. Touch something. Curse at the ugly poster on the wall. Count the tiles. Breathe. Repeat.

Ten minutes later, I came back out. A comedian was onstage. He was good. People were laughing. I tried to laugh. But then it hit again. The crowd. The lights. The vulnerability of having just read something real. I started crying all over again. So I left. Sat outside for a few minutes, thinking fresh air might be what I needed, but it wasn’t. So I went and sat in my car and cried some more.

I’ve been crying a lot lately. Not because I’m sad, not really. I think it’s about writing. About the weight of it. About the terrifying honesty it demands. I’ve had people lately look me in the eye and say, “You’re a writer. You need to own that.” And every time I try to say it out loud — I’m a writer — something closes up inside me. Like there’s a frog in my throat, ribbiting out loud, and I can’t tell if he’s warning me or welcoming me. “Don’t you dare.” or “Finally, you’re here.”

Maybe it’s not fear. Maybe it’s grief. The kind you feel when you realize that calling isn’t always convenient, that writing doesn’t come with a wardrobe stipend for my heels and jewelry addiction. That poets don’t get the kind of applause you can spend. That’s when you spend your whole life being good at pretending, boardrooms, business pitches, taking the stage as someone else, the scariest thing in the world is being asked to just be yourself.

But I still do it.

Even if I cry in the bathroom after. Even if I black out under the lights. Even if I have to leave early and sob in the front seat of my car. I still get up and I read. I still write. Because my soul doesn’t give me a choice. Because this, this-this messy, gut-wrenching thing, is the only time I’m not pretending.

And then, just for fun, the universe tossed in a little twist: All three of my exes ended up in the same city as me on the same day.

Yes, THREE. One moved here recently. One lives here already. The third? Randomly visiting from across the country. On the same day. I don’t know what message the universe is trying to send, but it better be a warning and not a setup.

I mean, sure. I get it. I’m magnetic. But I can’t be dodging emotional landmines and reading poetry and healing in public and dealing with back welts from my go-kart lifestyle.

It’s been a week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Didn’t Make a Resolution and Somehow Did Everything Anyway
subtitle: Failure, ambition, abs, and a brief attempt at self-restraint
body:
Viewer Discretion Advised.

This season contains unresolved tension, inconvenient truths, questionable decisions made with good intentions, and a narrator who is self-aware enough to know better, yet keeps yappin’ anyway.

. . .

You know what? 2026 is going to be filled with more failures than 2025, and I think that’s a beautiful thought; the mistakes— all of it. Because even when something isn’t technically a mistake, maybe it’s just an unfortunate hurdle dropped directly into your lane, we still have to adjust. We learn how to jump, how to slow down, how to change lanes without wrecking the car entirely. Those lessons don’t disappear. They settle somewhere permanent, lodged into the brain like muscle memory for survival.

That’s why I keep saying ‘mistakes’ on purpose. Because trying matters. Failing matters. Failing with glory matters. Because a failure isn’t a failure, it’s effort. And effort costs something. It takes energy, courage, ego, and time. It takes a willingness to look stupid in public. It takes actual movement.

I know I’m from the generation of participation medals. Everyone gets a ribbon, everyone gets a pat on the back. I truly hated them as a kid. I was competitive and thought participation medals were society’s quiet downgrade, a collective agreement to stop demanding excellence. But the older I get, the more I realize it wasn’t society that downgraded. It was— effort. Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, we stop trying as hard and call it realism. Those stupid medals taught us something we forgot how to do: how to show up and still be proud of ourselves even when we didn’t win, even when we make mistakes and score for the wrong team.

So for 2026, I didn’t make any resolutions. I’m a stickler about that. Any real resolution should survive the moment it’s born. It should have the strength, desire, and discipline to exist without a New Year’s permission. Maybe I’m not a stickler, and I just want my participation medal to be extra shiny this year?

Either way, people keep asking me what my resolution is, and every time I answer the same way. “I’m not sure. But I’d love to know yours?”

A few particularly audacious people suggested that going to the gym should be mine. These people need glasses and a reality check. I have abs, and I did three pull-ups at the club over the weekend. Puh-lease be serious.

That said, I did go to the gym this week.

Just not to work out, but as a stand-in model for a friend.

Thursday looked like writing, dog park, Starbucks—obviously. It also looked like me yelling at Shadow to be a gentleman and stop licking his private parts. Ugh. Men.

I also stayed awake until eight in the morning because I physically cannot sleep until an issue is asleep, and the issue that night was a brand redesign that needed immediate intervention. The business owner was making decisions, bad ones, my advice was required, and cleanup was urgent.

Now, ugh, ok, I know I spent the last half of 2025 swearing off my business and tech career. I’ve been intentionally quiet about my advisory background because I want to stay small. I want to write. I want to just be Sheridan, who loves mini skirts and a manic pixie attitude, and pretending she doesn’t know how a backend system works. But unfortunately, if I see a problem—a hole, a missing link in a strategy, a broken sequence in a business or project—I have to solve it, or I won’t sleep. So despite my best efforts, I haven’t been able to keep my mouth shut. People keep discovering my former career inside my new one, because once I solve the problem I do know how to solve, it unlocks the beast that becomes obsessed with all the problems she doesn’t yet understand.

Am I a businesswoman or a scientist? I’m not sure. I try to bite my tongue. I try to leave the room. I try to mind my business. But I care easily and deeply, and if there’s a clear path forward sitting right in front of me, I can’t pretend I don’t see it!

Somehow, with this diva strutting around in jeans and stiletto boots—Atlanta is not emotionally prepared for Sheridan in a mini-skirt yet—I’ve wiggled myself into yet another opportunity to sit as an owner in a few different companies. Broken record, but I’ve been trying to leave my business career behind because frankly, I’m heartbroken by it. Still, maybe walking in as a creative and closing the door behind me with a business brain isn’t the worst idea I’ve ever had.

What I want more than anything is to be completely and unapologetically myself. In my career over the last decade, I couldn’t be. I trained my dialect. I trained my wardrobe. I trained my mannerisms. I even trained how I laughed. The first thing I was ever made fun of for was my clothing. I was a strange kid. STRANGE. I remember one Minnesota winter showing up to school in a sundress and rain boots. My teacher called me to her desk, worried about frostbite more than fashion, and asked what I was thinking.

“Mrs. Carlson, I just feel like a storm cloud in the middle of sunshine today,” I told her.

That’s always been me. It’s why I fell into branding, psychology, and fashion. I wanted my clothes to speak before I could. Even now, as I am able to articulate exactly who I am, that doesn’t mean I want to shut that part off. Sometimes I feel like Audrey Hepburn. Sometimes Paris Hilton. Sometimes, a terrifying Slavic woman who will probably murder you in your sleep. It’s a balance.

Friday, I spoke with my good friend and business lawyer. I don’t know what I’m going to do yet—what companies, what my involvement looks like, or if I even want it. What pulls me in is the idea of paychecks I can turn around and give back with. That, and buying more expensive shoes. As a woman with a taste for wealth, an unwillingness to give sugar to a sugar daddy, and biologically born to a kind middle-class man, I unfortunately must work for my money.

Saturday was more work—coding, automation, writing—and then UFC!!!! BLOOD!! GORE! Incredible fights! Truly. And I hesitate to say this because I’m supposed to champion women’s sports, but once the women fighters came on, my god. Snooze fest. Were you afraid to punch each other? That is literally your only job. The men brought gore, heart, war, freaking blood. The women salsa-danced with enough room for Jesus to walk between them all the way to the bell.

I would have put my money on Paddy Daddy, and thank God I didn’t.

Sunday, I wrote again. Worked on scripts. Wandered from coffee shop to coffee shop. Thought seriously about reentering the business world and in what capacity. Then, Monday was industry night. I went out with all the local industry hotties. I was just a hottie, not an industry hottie, if you were wondering. Tuesday, I tried to figure out what to say to you—which of my million thoughts were actually worth sharing, which ones made me look sane or crazy, and when that has ever mattered.

Today—Wednesday—I had calls with my closest, most trusted colleagues. I solidified advisors and mentors for every step of this transition, including the very important transition of not living in someone else’s house. And can I pause to stress that I’ve been curating outfits from a single suitcase? All of my things (my shoes, my fur, my books, and my volumptuous attitude because my personality is the only fat I have) are locked nine hours away. And yet, have you seen me repeat an outfit? No. You haven’t. And if you did— No—you didn’t.

I’ve made slight progress since last week on securing a location for my short film. Everything else is set. I just need the place, I’m close. I just need a string pulled!

While writing scripts, networking in Atlanta, and deciding how, when, and if to reenter my business career(with my attitude mandatory this time), I’m also putting together a digital, audio, and hardcover book of the entire first season of What Sheridan Said. I’ve updated my website, listed an old painting for sale as a print (just in time for Valentine’s Day, hehe).

The failures, the effort, the business I keep tripping back into, the writing I refuse to stop doing, the version of myself I’m finally letting exist without sanding her down, I’m not exactly sure what it’s all adding up to. I just know I’m going to always try, on purpose, and with more honesty than I used to allow myself. If nothing else, this year already feels like a year where effort counts for something, even when the outcome is unclear— maybe, especially then.

Thank you for being here while I figure it out in real time, suitcase outfits, bad sleep habits, opinions, sassy attitude, and all. I’ll see you next Wednesday.

Participation medal or not, keep showing up.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Didn’t Want To Break Up Over a Poem
subtitle: I didn’t want to break up with you // over a poem, // the truth is
body:
I didn’t want to break up with you
over a poem,
the truth is
I could not get these words past my mouth.

It’s not you. It’s not me.
It’s the place we’ve reached
where the road runs out.

When you touched me, I felt continents
shift into place — a country I never earned
until your arms carried me home.
You gave me safety like a man
who had never known it himself.
That mercy was real. I carry its heat.

But mercy cannot pay rent.
Mercy cannot keep the lights on
or quiet the landlord’s fist at dawn.
I hate the Catholic girl who lives in me.
She was raised on roofs that did not leak,
on dinners that did not arrive by miracle
or last dollar.

I loved your stories—
the luminous strangers you collected between disasters,
the way every press credential was a boarding pass
to somewhere no one had planned for.
Every tale ended the same:
another motel, another borrowed tank of gas,
your last dollar spent arriving somewhere.

I didn’t notice how often that dollar was mine,
or borrowed from tomorrow.
I wanted so badly for the velocity of falling
to be destiny.

You learned the exact shape of the love I warned you I needed—
my silences, my noises, the particular way I flinch—
and you stayed anyway.

I didn’t want to break up with you.
The poem arrived first.

I cannot be your friend right now—
not while the wound is this fresh,
not while your voice would unmake me.
When I’m stronger—
maybe colder—
I may reach for whatever remains.
Until then, give me the quiet.

I cannot bear your crying—
not because it doesn’t move me
but because it does.

I cannot swear my heart doesn’t love you—
that would be the only real lie here.
You taught me how to be loved safely.
You could not teach me
how to build a life safely.

I am not yet strong enough
to carry both of us through.

My own life is already a half-finished scaffold,
swaying downtown in the wind.
We come from different centuries.
I’m sorry I cannot be the one
who fixes what first broke in you.

I didn’t want to break up with you
over a poem—
but it was the only room left
where I could say it.

Thank you for the safety.
The bruise is mine now.
I will learn to walk without leaning.

s.g.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Don't Know How I Like My Eggs & Toast
subtitle: Oversharing, Bad Exes, New Love, and the Small Panics of Building a Beautiful Life
body:
A lot has changed in my life since we finished season one. Many of the things I’ve been waiting patiently for have finally started happening, but I’ve been holding back from sharing any of it with you. I’ve needed so much external validation before I share it — I want it to feel like it’s actually my reality for a couple of months first. Or maybe I just need certain factors to solidify that this thing is really true for me.

I’ve been really wary these past several months about even talking to my own family and friends about my goals. I see this pattern so often. If I speak a goal or an ambition of mine out loud too many times to somebody else, it sometimes just doesn’t happen. Sometimes it does, but I spent a lot of time thinking about this. I think some of my motivation and drive comes from the surprise of it all. Finishing a script, starting a new company, or completing an art project feels powerful when I keep it to myself until I can showcase it.

Another annoying habit I’ve noticed is that my creative projects turn out better when I don’t tell people. I finish them faster, I pour more into them, and I feel more eager to make them the best they can be, so I can finally share the finished version and talk about it with real excitement.

Because of all this, many things in my life have changed, progressed, and moved forward in ways I never quite expected. I’ve stayed quiet about them because I wanted everything to feel true. I wanted it to be real, and I wanted it to be completely mine.

I’m still hesitant to share how close I am to the next stage with my short film script, but I will. I’m in the middle of conversations with people about its potential—different creative houses, industry folks I’ve already met, and others I’m working to meet. I can’t share too many details yet, but these conversations have been genuinely exciting. It feels like I’m back in my startup days, pitching all over again—talking through the story and the real impact it could have on society and the people who experience it. This is a story I believe is incredibly important to share right now, and I’ve been safeguarding it more than anything else because I’m so motivated to make it exceptional and get this narrative out there!

I’ve also been a bit quiet about the other important things that have progressed in my life, the projects I’ve been working on, the goals I’ve been trying to achieve, slowly I will tell you everything. I promise.

So, um, to make a transition here… if you haven’t noticed already, sometimes I have boundary issues. Well, it’s really only once you’re in my inner circle. I will tell you anything and everything about myself. I’ll pee with the door open. Given this, I am picky, and I heavily vet my friends before they become friends. So it’s not just anybody that hears my stream from down the hall because I didn’t want to stop mid-conversation just because I had to pee… I’ll just leave the door open and continue chatting with you like normal.

Duh.

Society often tells us women not to share anything bad about who we are, what we’ve been through, or the messy parts of past relationships with potential romantic partners. We’re supposed to leave all of that out completely so it doesn’t get foreshadowed or repeated.

Several months ago, I made a new friend. We started hanging out all the time, and really hit it off. We met up at coffee shops to work together. We stayed up late into the night on our computers, each doing our own thing, simply enjoying each other’s company. Before long, he had entered my inner circle. I was peeing with the door open, and he knew everything — the good and the bad about my past and my current life. He had crossed that bridge. Then we kept hanging out more and more until I started seeing him as a potential. But I didn’t know how to make that step.

A big part of me kept listening to all the societal advice that says if he already knows about those things, he can’t be someone worth romantically pursuing. I pushed back hard in my own mind and built up many walls. Some of the specific bad parts he learned were everything I discussed with you last season — how my career hit the fan, how I had to go to court and protect myself from dangerous people. That alone is a lot.

Then, as he became even deeper in my inner circle, he learned about my last boyfriend. I dated him for almost two years. This isn’t something I’ve shared online before, but the entire relationship was serious. We were early in our mid-20s, and we had plans to be engaged right before we both turned 30. He was the first person I ever saw myself wanting to marry.

After about two years, he sat me down. He was a very wealthy guy — I’m only sharing this for background information. He put his hand on my knee and reminded me of how dead set he was on me being his wife, but that he hadn’t been completely honest. He said he wanted me “to be too in love with him to say no,” and that the whole time he had been looking for another woman who was as worthy as I of being his wife. He then says that he had finally found her, and that he wanted me to meet her the next day.

I was in utter shock. I wasn’t living in Utah, he wasn’t Mormon, so this isn’t something you look out for or are even paranoid of, like cheating would be. At first, I didn’t know what to say. Then I just wanted to ask why — why do you think you get to do this? Why do you think you can have this? Just… why? After a few minutes, I realized there was no getting through to him. His mind was made up, and my thoughts didn’t matter to him. So I stopped asking questions. I closed my mouth, and we fell asleep — well, he did.

I laid awake for about an hour and a half until I knew he was deeply asleep. I went into the bathroom first, blocked him on everything, deleted his number, deleted my access to his front door, and then I walked right out the front door, locking it behind me. That was the end of my last relationship.

So, my new friend? He knew all of that, plus some other fun things — the good and all the bad — because sometimes I just get chatty and I can’t shut up.

We had developed such a strong friendship before anything romantic even started, that I eventually learned to break those walls down because the advice isn’t always true. Someone unhealthy or unstable or simply not meant for me would see all the bad parts of me and everything I’ve been through, then consciously or subconsciously repeat those patterns. But somebody that’s good, stable, and meant for me… wouldn’t.

In the past several months, I’ve been waiting to share any of this because I needed it to feel true. I needed it to be mine and to exist as my reality before I said it out loud. But I have been shown — by the world, by him, and by all of you who listen while I overshare every single week — that my good traits, my bad traits, my quirky traits, and every good and bad thing that has happened to me, because of me, at me, or around me should have no negative influence on the right people. If any of it does influence them in the wrong way, consciously or subconsciously, then they simply aren’t the right people.

It has been so refreshing to grow in a relationship that started as a genuine friendship. It feels good to grow alongside all of you, too, and to keep learning that the right people will stick by you no matter how good or how bad things get. None of it changes the way they treat you.

So, might I finally share? Sheridan the Great has found herself a great boyfriend.

I have also found meaningful projects, solid friends, and I’m slowly building a great life. Through all of this, I’m building what feels like normal for the first time, because I have never really had normal. I have been a loner, a ‘loser’, and a workaholic for most of my life. Building this life — not rebuilding, but truly building it — has reminded me that I’m on a steep learning curve. I’ve caught myself being over-forgiving when I make mistakes with small talk or figuring out how to navigate adult friendships and life in general. I’m not used to being in a relationship with someone who wants to make me breakfast. I’ve never had someone make my toast before.

When he asked me how I liked my eggs and toast in the morning, my mind completely shut down, and I started panicking. I don’t know these things. I don’t know how to allow people to do these kinds of things for me.

Going to a restaurant and picking something off the menu feels very different. Which reminds me of my Italian sandwich dilemma.

I have no idea what’s actually on an Italian sandwich, and there are only two sandwich shops I will go to because I know I can just say “Italian sandwich,” and they will give me exactly what I want.

About a year ago, I was with a friend who wanted to go to a different sandwich shop than my normal two selections. They assured me I could order an Italian sandwich there. So as I walked up to the cash register to order, there was a long line behind me. The place was busy and loud with noise and chatter everywhere. I got to the register and said, “I’ll take an Italian sandwich, please.” The lady asked, “On what bread?” I panicked a little, but figured it out by picking one that looked closest based on the pictures.

Then she asked, “And what do you want on it?”

I replied, “What do you mean? I want an Italian sandwich.”

She repeated, “No, what do you want on your sandwich?”

I said again that I wanted an Italian sandwich. She asked one more time what I wanted on it. I stood there completely dumbfounded. I had no idea what was on an Italian sandwich. I just know that I eat it. I have never looked at the components of it before; all I know is that it tastes good, and I know I like it. Nowhere in my brain are any of the ingredients. It’s something I’ve never had to think about, and it’s something I usually avoid because I stick to my two safe sandwich places.

I’ve never been to a sandwich shop with a friend before. I’m not someone who has done a lot of things with friends or gone out. I’ve gone out by myself a lot, so after a long time, I created habits of going to the same places. It felt like my safety net. Especially as a hundred-pound, cute little girl in the city, sticking to the familiar makes me feel a lot safer. Over the past years, I’ve developed this bad habit of relying on my routine of comfort, efficiency, and safety, which is why I didn’t know what was on an Italian sandwich.

My friend ended up looking at me like I was crazy and asked if I was serious. The place was so loud I couldn’t think straight. I started panicking and just looked at them, saying, “I don’t know — can you please order for me?” They looked it up on their phone and read off all the ingredients. Not to sound entitled or like a ‘Karen’ or ‘Jennifer but I think the lady at the register should have done that herself. If there isn’t a single button for “Italian sandwich” or a list of ingredients right there on the menu, she could have looked it up on her phone, the same way a bartender figures out a fancy cocktail they don’t know.

Yeah… I felt so dumb. Everyone around me made me feel dumb, including my friend.

This only happens in a good way when I’m getting pulled over, but I cry when I’m stressed, scared, or feeling dumb. Naturally, I started crying right there in this weird sandwich shop that apparently couldn’t just make me an Italian sandwich the easy way.

So, when my boyfriend asked how I liked my eggs and toast in the morning, the same panic hit me. I don’t have this information stored. These aren’t things I’ve ever put in my brain or thought about before. I don’t really go to breakfast places. If I do, I just order something straight off the menu and get my eggs sunny side up. I submit to whatever selections they have.

When he asked me, I had no idea what to say, and I felt so stupid. I tried to cover it up and ended up saying the wrong thing completely. I didn’t realize I had said the wrong thing until he brought me my eggs and toast. That made me feel even dumber. It reminded me that this was the first time someone had ever asked how I wanted my eggs and toast. This vocabulary simply isn’t something my brain has ever had before.

Even though I’m reminded of the learning curve at hand, I will always do my best to learn, to grow. I will keep moving forward and building a beautiful, fulfilling life. I feel so grateful for all these amazing new friends and for my boyfriend, who is incredibly patient and understanding with me.

Some days, though, I’m equally as sad as I am grateful. Especially in the quiet moments, like the first time someone asked me how I like my eggs and toast in the morning.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Don’t Know What I’m Doing (But It’s Working?)
subtitle: Wrapping up TV episodes, abandoning my notebook, and realizing my voice matters more than the packaging.
body:
I sat down to write this week’s episode knowing I wanted to write, but not knowing exactly what I wanted to say, which feels like the most honest place to begin. Last time I mentioned that I wrapped up scriptwriting, and while that wasn’t untrue, it also wasn’t the full picture. What actually happened is that we finished a few episodes and will be picking back up at a later date; however, we’re still not entirely sure when that date is. I think I was a little unclear and brushed over it, but if I’m honest, my vague-to-professionalism ratio remains just right for where I am. I’m excited, I’m proud of the work, and I’m looking forward to continuing it into the next set of episodes or possibly even a second season. I’ve had a small taste of show business before—one theatre role, modeling through high school and college—enough to understand what the culture can be like, but not enough to prepare me for this. As someone who is deeply addicted to learning, being dropped into an industry where everything is still unfolding, and the limits aren’t visible yet, feels incredibly energizing.

At the same time, I’ve noticed that I haven’t written in my journal in quite a while, and I miss it in a way that sneaks up on me late at night and early in the morning. I’ll feel the urge to write and then hesitate, not because I don’t want to, but because the notebook itself feels wrong. It has no spine, it’s bulky, it doesn’t fold down into a single sheet, and it hurts my wrist because I write like a Notre Dame monk whose only remaining value to the world is her cursive. It also gives me paper cuts that make me look like a teenager going through quite a terrible time. It’s a beautiful notebook, leather wrapped, textured recycled paper, but maybe that’s exactly the problem. It’s built for permanence, and I think I’m currently in a phase that requires something a little less sacred and a little more forgiving. So maybe I’ll get myself a new notebook for my birthday this Saturday. One that bends, perhaps, one that doesn’t injure me.

I’ve been thinking about whether I should bring the voiceovers back for each episode, which is ironic considering my voice is currently cracked, gone, and spiritually located in California on fentanyl. At the beginning of this series, I recorded myself reading every episode because I thought it might give the series a little extra leverage and help me reach more people: readers, listeners, anyone willing to stay. The truth is, recording myself each week wasn’t really adding anything. It didn’t change how the writing landed, and it didn’t change how people connected to it. I also wasn’t sure I wanted to turn this into a podcast and upload the audio elsewhere, because that isn’t what this story wants to be right now.

After skipping the audio for a few episodes, I put up a poll and asked all of you whether I should continue it. With the sweeping number (or more accurately, the number swept quietly under your rug), responding, I decided not to. It also made sense practically. Writing an episode from rambling to sending usually takes me about two to four hours, depending on how critical I am of myself that day. Recording the audio took roughly the same amount of time but required a far more controlled environment. You need a quiet space, solid equipment, and in my case, three different softwares programs to clean, revise, and tune the audio, because yes, I am a perfectionist and no, I am not interested in pretending otherwise. Throughout the week, when I have a notebook that bends and doesn’t cut me, I’m constantly jotting things down for the episode. By Wednesday, I usually have an outline built out, and from there I ramble, adjust transitions, revise, and then cross my fingers, close my eyes, and send it to your inbox.

I know I’ve said before that I created this series as a way to open up, get social, and let people see what I’m doing and who I am, but what I didn’t anticipate was how much it would change the way I move through the world outside of it. I’ve caught myself mid-conversation with strangers, thinking, Oh my god, Sheridan, did you just overshare? And then I realize that I didn’t actually overshare at all. It only feels that way because of how much of myself I kept reserved for so long, how used I was to keeping my inner life contained and carefully managed, like something that needed supervision.

I used to believe that branding was everything, and in some ways, I still do. I was an odd kid, and if I noticed my peers, parents, or siblings shying away from something, I often did too, or I learned how to keep it hidden, like hiding in my closet to play with my sister’s Barbies because I was the football-playing tomboy daughter. I carried that instinct with me for years. My first semester of college, I was so quiet and reserved that people thought I was a Russian exchange student, and the fact that I wore fur, pearls, and stilettos every day definitely didn’t help clear that up. I actually spent two weeks alone in my room trying to teach myself a Russian accent. When I failed, horribly, I might add, I decided to let the rumor die with the semester and kept up my mute act.

As women, we’re taught not to let anyone know we’ve been treated with anything less than perfection. We’re taught that if we reveal negative patterns in our lives, we risk inviting those patterns back in, consciously or subconsciously. This isn’t to say that I became reserved because of a bad boyfriend—that’s not the story here. What my life has shown me instead is that I learned to rely on restraint as power. I stayed quiet. I stayed composed. I used my outfits, my hair, my posture, and my body language to control the image people formed of me. Whether that meant pant suits with a clean ponytail and no lipstick at work, or showing up to a local creatives bar in a silk necktie, stockings, and a blouse that suggested I wasn’t American, I understood branding deeply. For a very long time, it was the primary way I knew how to enter a room.

This year, though, has shifted something internally. Landing a new writing gig, finishing new pieces, and having publishers reach out weekly this month has forced me to recognize what’s actually carrying me forward. The branding I curated so carefully does its job when I need it, and I’m grateful for that, but it isn’t my greatest strength. What’s carrying me now is everything underneath it—my voice, my curiosity, my willingness to be seen without armoring myself first.

So for my birthday this Saturday, I plan on being the queen of the dance floor. I’ll blow out my candles, wish for my writing career to continue growing, and thank all of you for staying with me through what has been an absolutely insane, dramatic year, one that still doesn’t feel real.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Dumped My BF Via a Poem
subtitle: I Hit Walls, Opened Doors, and Broke Up With Him Via a Poem
body:
I’ve hit many walls this year, and I’ve also opened so many doors. This year we watched me learn how to love safely, how to build more openly, how to make friends, and how to continue to be better in every avenue I walk through.

I think that’s important. Not chasing perfection — though I openly admit I have this issue — but consistently striving to be better in every category. I’m not looksmaxxing, I’m curiousmaxxing. Okay, I really hate myself for typing that. I’m sorry. But when I write these, I usually let what comes out naturally stay in. Because why would I mask how cringe I can be sometimes? This is WSS after all…

What I mean is I find it difficult to move alongside others who aren’t at least chasing that growth in a couple of categories. Yes, I obviously want to continue to get hotter as the years go on. And while I’m slowly headed for a collagen collapse, I know my beauty will shine through with all the smile lines, the frustration lines, and the eye wrinkles. What I’m not cool with, however, is having the number one imprinted in my forehead. I’m number one, I know that, I don’t need my forehead to also tell the entire world that I’m number one. So as I continue to grow and soon grow older, I will be getting Botox between the brows. For obvious spiritual reasons.

I want to continue to grow in curiosity, my knowledge, my understanding of others who are not at all like me. I want to be better, healthier. I want whatever gizmo and gadget that promises me better hygiene. I want it all, forever and always. But I know what you might be thinking, so let me put a stop to it real quick. It’s the learning, it’s the growing, it’s the story of how I got there that is the most amusing and fulfilling to me. How I can say I read a full textbook cover to cover, and this is what I’ve taken away from it. How I’ve met someone from a culture I’ve never experienced before, and I’m a more understanding human because of it. Cheesy, but whoever coined the saying, “It’s not the destination, it’s the journey,” you are my shaman.

Things have halted, changed, and adapted in my life. I’m now single, hiding in my parents’ basement, I don’t have a publishing deal, and I’m juggling between being heartbroken and motivated.

But as you know me, I’m better at writing my emotions than speaking them. So to ode to the title, yes, I did break up with him via a poem.

I cry a lot — at someone startling me, at someone stealing my last french fry, at puppy videos, and sometimes while writing. I’ve never been great at processing my emotions, or better yet, formulating words that leave my mouth to express anything I need, want, or feel. I’m a bit enamored by it. I freeze, and the only motions are the visions behind my eyes and my fingers’ ability to speak for me.

I’ve done this a lot. I wasn’t the best child, and I mean that in the sense that I was terrified of expressing my love, let alone saying the words “I love you.” It wasn’t until after I was an adult that I expressed that in writing first.

But that seems to be my pattern: feel, poem, vocalize. And until I’ve narrowed down in my own turtle shell what exactly all these things mean — if they even mean anything, or if I’m just projecting onto the situation — I need a lot of quiet, uninterrupted time to write my emotions before I can act on them, let alone vocalize them to another.

So when my boyfriend lost his job and his place of living, things just continued to go under. My emotions continued to go under. I was losing my own self in the process of not having the time, the quiet, to even understand what I was feeling.

He left and drove states away to stay with his sister. I felt guilty, but I needed the space. I needed to understand my own emotions as the groundwork we laid broke down underneath us. I needed quiet, and I needed him away for a while so I could simply catch my breath and listen to what my heart was trying to write out for me.

I spent a few days without replying to his texts or answering his phone calls. I wanted to answer, but each time I remembered the ‘us’ I loved so much did not exist anymore. I asked him for quiet and just said I was sad. I’m not sure if he took the full sign there.

It had been a few days, and I spent the morning staring at my notebook. I cried and wrote a poem that was 10 pages long. Too long. I stared at it for several more hours. I wrote so many different versions. It’s not ten pages long anymore, but two phone screenshots long.

I opened the texts I had only read the preview of. My read receipts hit our messages, and I clicked on my recent photos, and I sent him the poem, titled “I didn’t want to break up with you over a poem.”

« Click below to read the poem Sheridan sent her now ex-boyfriend, or continue scrolling to read the rest of the episode. »

I Didn’t Want To Break Up Over a Poem

I told you I’ve been going back and forth with a publishing company. I shared my manuscript of poems. There were promises said aloud, and I was waiting for the board to finalize its investment offer.

Well, the wait is over and… It’s not happening. There is no investment offer — at least not right now.

When I learned and saw the Oz behind the curtain, my heart was absolutely crushed. So much so that it took almost a week for me to even cry about it. I’m slowly making my rounds to those closest to me whom I shared this news with intimately. I wanted to sit with my own emotions first, write a poem about it, understand it, before sharing.

But what I’ve learned — what I’m taking away from this — is that all those around me had complete faith that my work was good enough for a deal like this. Those who have read just a few pieces, those I’ve endlessly annoyed with “but what about this line instead?”, those I’ve met through poetry and writing groups, and those who love and support my work even if poetry isn’t their thing and they’ve never read a true word of mine. That’s the takeaway I’m choosing to hold onto. Not that the deal wasn’t real, but that my work being good enough — that was extremely real.

So what now?

Well, I’ve got a few ideas up my silk white sleeve. Ways to give back, ways to grow, ways to collaborate with others.

Life is meant to teach you. It’s not just the moments, it’s the people. Whether it’s a colleague who only lasted a day on the job, a best friend you’ve lost touch with since growing up, a romantic relationship, a quiet crush, the barista who barely says a thing, or the family you sit around the table with. Often the lessons aren’t that moving — unless you’re me and you’re wired to find the deepest lesson in just a second of sitting.

It’s about noticing things. Noticing the barista loves leather bracelets. Noticing that she prefers to wipe before *and* after making a cup, whereas her coworker only does before. It’s noticing why and how the colleague was let go. It’s not a lesson of blame or shame. It’s a lesson of noticing all the visible and invisible things that make us decide to walk that way, to say yes or no.

Relationships, life, and every moment have something worthwhile to teach you. That’s what my last little while has been about. It’s been soul-crushing, as I was dancing around like a happy ten-year-old who just wrote her first poetry book. That was the hardest part. Telling her, not no, but not yet.

So now she’s sitting in the corner, pouting a little bit, but that ten-year-old girl is writing another poem and strategizing how to make this deal real. Because even if relationships, friendships, a business deal, or any sort of promise doesn’t actually happen, it doesn’t mean it’s not real. It *was* very real. But most of the time, it’s not real in the way we think it to be.

That’s what I’m learning. That’s what I’m grieving. It’s always real, but not for the reasons you may think. My ex and my relationship, my book deal — it’s all real. Just not in the way I hoped.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I Was Going To Write This Sooner But Life Said No
subtitle: From Tesla to RAM, from meltdown to rescue, this week was a movie I didn’t ask to be in.
body:
Yes, I’m late. This was supposed to go out already. But right now, I’m writing this from bed, still wearing the cut-off leggings and one-sleeve white tank I drove across the country in. I feel comfy, sexy, and absolutely a little smelly after 12 hours behind the wheel. It’s fine. I’m fine. Sort of.

This month has been a blur of Google Maps reroutes, gas station coffee that tastes like regret, and the kind of middle-of-nowhere truck stops where being a hot girl feels like walking into a saloon in a Western, every man turns, none of them blink, all of them dumbly drool. I think this was my fourth or fifth cross-country drive; I’ve lost count at this point.

Someone, please buy me a jet.

Normally, I bring my dogs, Shadow and Dino, with me. If they’re not coming, I’ll drive them out to Tennessee, leave them with my parents, and fly out from there. But this time, I thought I was being efficient.

A longtime friend needed a place to crash while his house was under construction. Perfect timing. I’d be gone, he could stay in the guest room, take care of the dogs, and keep the house locked up. Win-win.

Until it wasn’t.

I was halfway to Florida when my phone started blowing up. My landlord was calling. Every single neighbor had contacted her because my dogs were howling in the backyard, and had been outside alone since 11 a.m. It was now 11 p.m. No water. No shade. A small backyard. Shadow can jump the fence. Dino can dig underneath it. Anyone could’ve taken them. They could’ve escaped. Someone could’ve called the cops.

And then I find out the house was left unlocked.

Someone could’ve walked right in.

I was driving when I found out, hands on the wheel, eyes on the road, and suddenly my phone lit up a few too many times for comfort. I let out a scream that didn’t sound human, more like a throaty, survival noise ripped from somewhere deep in my body. The kind of scream that makes you swerve just slightly, grip the wheel like an ex that wronged you, and make every man at the gas station look up like they just heard a wild animal crash through the door.

I was panicking. Fully spiraling. My heart was pounding. My stomach was in knots that wouldn’t let go. The only thing I could think of: Shadow will have a seizure and die. Dino will escape or get stolen. These aren’t “just dogs.” They’re my children. I’ve driven across states for them. I’ve missed events for them. I’ve structured my career around their well-being. And now this?

The worst part? I shouldn’t have even needed to say it. Don’t leave the dogs outside all day in the heat, unsupervised, without water; that’s not a “just in case” reminder. That’s basic human logic. I did specify that Dino must be kenneled when no one’s home, or he’ll destroy anything that smells like me. That Shadow takes medication twice a day. That they both have specific needs. Routines. Sensitivities.

Trauma.

And he just… left them.

Everyone in our friend group is disappointed in him. I’m disappointed in him. I wish I had stayed calm. I wish my tone had been softer, cooler, more graceful. But the truth is: I care. And I cry easily. And I’m working on it. Okay?

What pulled me back from the edge was my best friend. He dropped everything, drove over, made sure the dogs were okay, and slept in the guest room like it was his full-time job. And on the one day he couldn’t be there, two other friends stepped in. Made sure they were safe, hydrated, and that Shadow had his meds. My people showed up for me. For them. And I’m so incredibly thankful.

Why was I even driving to Florida? A friend’s parents had just had an estate sale and generously gifted me some stunning art and a few pieces of furniture. I drove the Tesla down to meet a potential buyer, and thankfully, the sale went through. So I handed off the Tesla and rented a 2024 RAM truck to bring everything back up the East Coast.

And I don’t care what anyone says, the sound of an engine tingles my heart. I love a Tesla. But there is nothing, nothing, like the rhythm of a truck engine shaking itself alive beneath you. I needed that feeling. That grounding. That noise. I needed something real to carry me home, with priceless artwork in the backseat and the weight of the week fading slowly behind me in the rearview mirror.

I still don’t feel fully settled. Like a part of me is still out there, somewhere on I-95, mid-scream, mid-panic, mid-fury. But when you’re the one who always holds it together, there’s never really a clean end to a crisis. You just go home. Unpack the car. Feed the dogs. And write it all down like the story isn’t still living in your body.

So now I’m back. I’m in bed. I’m tired. I’m okay. And yes, I’m still a little mad. But mostly, I’m thankful my dogs are safe. That I have friends who show up. That I get to write this down and send it out to people who care enough to read it.

More next week.

Until then, hug your dogs. Lock your doors. And maybe don’t trust everyone who says, “Don’t worry, I got it,” even if they’re your friend.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
