title: I'm Back and Baby I Brought Context
subtitle: Because a lot has happened, I look hotter, and I’m thinking clearer than ever.
body:
I’m writing this week’s episode of What Sheridan Said, whether I’m ready, you’re ready, the world is ready, or not…and I already know it needs context. This is the first episode of season two, and I haven’t written to you since just before my birthday (December 20th, put it in your calendar and send me flowers). The following Wednesday was Christmas Eve, then the next one was New Year’s Eve, and then the week after that, I didn’t write at all because I was mentally spiraling, something we will get to later. There are reasons for the gaps, I don’t want to pretend there aren’t, but I also don’t want to rush past them just to arrive at something cleaner or more convenient.

So, my birthday.

As you know, my birthday sits right next to Christmas, which is one of those things that sounds minor until you live it year after year. People are busy. Plans are already made. Everyone is traveling, exhausted, or mentally checked out, and you learn early not to expect very much. This year, though, something different happened. I went out with new friends I’d made at work, and we actually went out— drank, laughed, celebrated— in a way that felt normal, grounded, and human. That might sound small, but it isn’t. I can’t remember many birthdays where I wasn’t working, navigating unexplainable chaos, or simply surrounded by people who weren’t really available or my friend. Christmas birthdays will do that to you. So will a life that has never stayed still.

It felt good— genuinely good. I don’t want to overstate it, but I also don’t want to minimize how much it mattered to feel present on my own birthday instead of treating it like something to survive, a day to make it through.

New Year’s Eve happened in Atlanta. I don’t need to spill the juicy details to you publicly. If you know, you know. If you don’t, you don’t need to.

The first season, the last season of What Sheridan Said began on what felt like a real high. My career was moving in the right direction. I was working as a business and startup advisor, lining up opportunities, and living in a home I genuinely loved. I had friends. I had routines. I had a sense that I was growing into myself instead of constantly shapeshifting to fit whatever environment I was in. It felt like momentum; I felt like I earned it.

And then everything fell apart, slowly, then all at once.

My safety became a question— not metaphorically, not emotionally, but practically. Logistically. Enough that I had to make fast decisions that weren’t dramatic so much as necessary. I ended my lease. I packed everything from my three-bedroom house into storage. I left my city. I bounced between friends and family while trying to keep my nervous system regulated enough to think clearly about what came next. There was no grand plan, only running into a fire with triage.

I’ve talked before about sexism in business and about the way pretty privilege operates as a double-sided sword that people love to oversimplify. Yes, it exists. Yes, it opens doors. But those doors are rarely free, and the cost is seldom acknowledged by people who benefit from pretending the tradeoff isn’t real. When things are handed to you because of how you look, they come with strings attached—expectations embedded, assumptions baked in. You’re expected to be easier. More agreeable. Less complicated. Your competence is often treated as optional, your struggles as unlikely, your boundaries as negotiable. There’s an unspoken belief that attractiveness should insulate you from hardship, that if life is generous with your exterior, you have no right to be messy, exhausted, or affected. Emotions soon become inconvenient. And when you fail to live up to that projection, when you have real problems, real limits, real consequences, you are met not with empathy, but with confusion and resentment. That kind of distortion can be isolating and dangerous. And it can make you profoundly lonely in ways that’s hard to translate unless you’ve lived inside the contradiction of being both highly visible and fundamentally misunderstood.

At the same time, I don’t want this season to live entirely in that space. What matters now is that I’ve found my way back to my creative self— not in a nostalgic way, but in an honest one. Creativity was never something I discovered later in life. It was always there, even from the beginning. As a kid, I won awards for my drawings, and my teachers encouraged me to write history essays as poems instead of forcing them into MLA format. Creativity wasn’t extracurricular for me; it was my natural state.

That instinct eventually took me into fashion. I modeled and worked with small brands and magazines. I loved it, but the industry was brutally narrow then. I’m petite by fashion standards, and even when I lied about my height (somehow managed to sell the fib that I was 5’8” and not 5’6” to my agent), it still wasn’t enough. Mind you, this was before body inclusivity, before flexibility, before any meaningful conversation about expanding what was allowed in the modeling and fashion industry. About 90% of casting rooms were closed to me before I ever walked in, even with my lie of two inches (that’s what he said).

I was emancipated from my parents and went to college early. By eighteen, I transferred to George Mason University and took out a forty-thousand-dollar loan to pay for one year of school. One year. I never really wanted to go to college, and I still believe that if you’re not sticking a needle in someone, you probably don’t need a piece of paper to prove you’re capable. That’s my personal belief. But I also understood the system well enough to use it strategically.

I looked at my modeling paychecks. I looked at the business world and its long-term potential. Then I looked at my own position— what I had access to, and what I didn’t. I had a Minnesota public education. I was advanced, sure, but I was on my own, and I understood that very early.

So I made a decision. I chose a school strategically, based on proximity to power and connections, not prestige. I got an internship, turned it into a job, and didn’t look back.

When I transferred to George Mason, the contrast became unavoidable. Suddenly, I was surrounded by peers who came from oil money, elite private schools, and dinner tables stacked with mentors and inherited access. Their backpacks were Birkins. Their cars were Lamborghinis in rotating colors. That was the moment I could see, in real time, what I was actually competing against, and how differently we had all been resourced.

I started in marketing and haven’t held a marketing title since. I’ve been C-suite adjacent or above, and that climb required edits. I deleted social media. I asked magazines and brands to take down my name in their campaigns. I curated my image carefully because I needed to survive in business spaces that do not tolerate complexity in women. It worked, but it also took something out of me.

That’s why I started What Sheridan Said. I have a bad habit of not opening up, of not letting people understand who I actually am, because I spent so much of my life making complicated decisions in environments that didn’t favour honesty. Maybe I am complicated. Maybe I want more than the world is willing to offer. Both things can be true.

What’s new is that I’m happy I am writing again. I’m getting more gigs. I’m working on scripts, a play, and a short film— my own short film! I have my team and my crew lined up, and I’m excited to refine my craft without it feeling conditional.

I do want to mention something, because people can misread me: But I hope you know, when I’m arrogant, it’s comedy. It’s actually my armor. If I’m being cocky, it’s usually because I don’t feel confident at all, and I’m turning that discomfort into humor before it has a chance to swallow me whole.

“Sheridan the Great” is a bit, but it’s also a wish. Part humor, part manifestation, part self-defense. I know what I carry. I know the walls I built to survive my business career. I know what changed when I moved to D.C. and saw power up close, every version of it, every sin, every corruption I wasn’t prepared for. That kind of exposure changes you, whether you want it to or not. Calling myself great isn’t a claim; it’s my way of hoping, a way of reminding myself that I have greatness within.

Last week, I was working nonstop on set, and when I got home with twenty minutes to spare before I normally write and publish, I didn’t have it in me. I write close to posting because I want these episodes to reflect my actual week, not a sanitized version of it. If I had written that night, it would have been a raw rant about how overwhelmed, exhausted, and emotionally spent I was. That didn’t feel useful or honest in the way I want this space to be.

So I didn’t write. Not because I didn’t care. Not because I was avoiding you. Sometimes, restraint is the more responsible choice. You don’t need every spiral in real time; you just need to know that I’m still here.

This past year, last season, has been about ripping off every possible Band-Aid. Writing to you every Wednesday has been such an incredible part of that. I know I contradict myself. I know things don’t resolve neatly. But I’m committed to staying in the process instead of pretending I’ve already arrived.

There’s also a lot happening practically. I’m putting season one together as a digital and printed book, likely hardcover, with an accompanying voiceover so you can listen to me rant on the go. I’m solidifying the location for my short film, about twenty minutes long, which is small by industry standards, but enormous to me. For most of my career, my success was measured by how well I made other people successful. This is different; this is me applying everything I’ve learned to my own work.

So here we are, Episode one of Season two. Definitely not a clean reset, but a continuation with sharper awareness. I’m still dramatizing my life, because frankly, it entertains me, and I might as well let it entertain you, too. But this season, this year, I’m doing it with clearer boundaries, steadier hands, and a deeper commitment to telling the truth as I actually experience it.

And that feels like the right place to begin again.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I'm Off To Atlanta. Also: I’ve Been Proposed To Four Times. Life Is Wild?
subtitle: A little life update, a little chaos, and a few confessions I probably shouldn’t make online.
body:
Hi (: I have so much to tell you.

First off, Happy Thanksgiving! I hope you had amazing food spent with loved ones last week. Also, Lilly the rescue puppy, is now Ὀία (she’s Greek and boujie and better than you now, so watch out)! She was adopted by a newlywed couple who moved in just a few doors down from my current safe house. And while we’re here, I should probably update you, because it’s been quite some time since I’ve heard anything from any of the men who once had me worry about safety enough to pack up my things. Silence can be such a luxury. My safe house is in the country of Tennessee, giving me a perfect excuse to tap into both Nashville and Atlanta’s creative industries, and honestly, the quiet here is good and bad.

It was Thanksgiving last week, and as someone who grew up without technology— an honorary millennial, but definitely not by age, because I am still young and hot, sorry—I had to take my brother and his fiancée out for Blackout Wednesday. And yes, typically I write to you the night of because I want everything to feel true to the week I’ve had. I don’t like lying to you or holding anything back. So last Wednesday, instead of writing my newest episode of What Sheridan Said, I did what I had to do: I got blackout drunk.

I ruled the dance floor. I stole a couple of hats off some innocent men mid-dance move (am I sorry? No. But if you see this and subscribe, I might consider giving them back). Then someone slapped my ass. He’s lucky security took my machete out of my boot before I walked in, because honey, I cut. I’m kidding (maybe), it was a light tap, and he was with his girlfriends, and he apologized and blamed getting caught up in the moment and slapping their butts too while they were getting down. I let it slide. He was nice and glittery✨. Maybe it’s ridiculous, but even that night felt like another reminder that joy and chaos always show up for me in the same breath, like they’re conspiring to keep me awake to my own life. Yes, therapists, chaos is a big part of my personality; you can un-analyze me now. I do it enough myself.

I mentioned before how I felt as though the world was telling me to give up on my business side, even though it’s always been such a huge part of me. My earliest dream in that tiny farm town was to move away to the big city and be the best businesswoman they had ever seen. And in many ways, I did that, and I’m so proud of myself and every life I’ve helped, in a big or small way, like providing someone with a consistent paycheck. But throughout this year, writing to you has forced me to keep acknowledging that writing has always been a major part of me. I mean, hell, this girl, Sheridan the Great, earned a perfect score on her ACT essay. Before all you kiddos had robots writing hollow sentences for you.

Well, I also have some very cool news to share with you, and it’s part of the reason I’m writing this on Tuesday and letting the scheduler handle the rest. Your girl, Sheridan the Great, is officially a TV script writer!!! Yes, you can be jealous now. I can’t share any other details, but I’ve been developing relationships in the entertainment and creative industries because, as I keep repeating, I want my words to selfishly surround your entire world. So I’ll be in Atlanta all day when I normally write and share with you.

I suppose pretending this is a dramatic TV show all year actually paid off.

The confidence of this new gig pushed me to finally move forward on my other projects, too. I mentioned before how I took numerous storytelling and scriptwriting courses during quarantine and after. Well, I’ve been sitting on a very intense plotline for quite a while. I’ve tried writing it as a pilot, then a film, then a novel, but a little while ago I thought, selfishly, that becoming a playwright would feel as prestigious to me as having the letters ‘D’ and ‘R’ in front of my name. Not the same, obviously, but the level of prestige is similar in my mind. I’ve co-written a theater script before, a medieval British comedy with an ode to Monty Python, but since then, I haven’t tried my hand at another. So I began writing the horror story I’ve kept in my back pocket, but this time as a play.

And I finished it.

It’s two plays, both three acts each. The story is a realistic, dramatic horror. I wanted the story to showcase how if you partake in evil, you can’t just forget or shove it down; you have to grow and forgive, otherwise a new evil world will swallow you whole, leading to you being just as evil, if not more.

As the perfectionist I am, I need to revise it one more time before I let anyone peek at it.

Between this episode and the last, I wrote and published a new poem. It started as a simple ramble about my morning, but as all great poetry does, it dragged the truth out of my subconscious and became, unknowingly, a love poem. I mentioned last episode how men are my Plan B, and how I often get hate for that. It’s still very true. I, myself, will always be Plan A. And if a man comes along, fantastic. If not, I have enough random men on the streets and online offering to change my tire and calling me beautiful to keep life entertaining.

A Woman Waiting For Morning

Can I tell you something rather unhinged? I’ve been proposed to four times, and I’ve said no every single time. One man proposed after I had only kissed him. One proposed for obvious citizenship reasons. And the other two… we don’t need to discuss. Can I tell you something even more unhinged? I don’t have any of those rings! Not a single one! What a shame! I feel like I should at least be at one out of four, right? Not because I’d ever say yes to any of them, they’ve barely seen the light of me, except for the occasional Google search in the past years, but because I think it should be courtesy. I’ve had to say no four times!!! I deserve one of those damn rings free and clear for dealing with men who think proposing without ever discussing the seriousness or longevity of “us” is appropriate. Like boy… catch your breath. I know I’m breathtaking, but let’s settle down and see if I actually like you back before you go and purchase an engagement ring. Alright, buddy boy?

I tend to be overly honest, which men sometimes take as a game. I also think and operate equally like a man and a woman, depending on the environment or situation. Basically, I’m a baddie who can play ball. I get it. Trust me, I’m turned on too by myself after taking a few selfies. BUT CALM DOWN.

Speaking of dating and the great lengths men have gone to earn my love, I shared a very romantic date I had in the past. No, it wasn’t a top ten date; men going all out on first dates for me is fairly standard, but this one has always held a special place because he showed so much effort with only about $20. And the story has now gone minor-viral on Threads. It’s sweet to see, truly, but I hate getting messages congratulating me on experiencing a date ‘like that,’ because that kind of effort has always been pretty normal in my world. It’s probably why I’m cautious about whom I say yes to. lol.

SEE POST

I suppose I’ve gone on a tangent, but all of this is to say: I am Sheridan the Great. I have so many iconic moments. I’m not forgotten. For instance, I was going on a first date a couple of years ago. I was sitting outside the café waiting, while he was walking from a few blocks away. I could see him. And I kid you not: two different men walked up and tried asking me out. Each time, I pointed to the man walking toward me. The second guy even waited to shake his hand and congratulate him on his date with “this beautiful woman.” Still to this day, every six months or so, he texts me: “You planned that shit, right?” And every time, I remind him: I am Sheridan the Great.

Things just happen for me when I’m confident, which is why some people (yes, I know who they are) prefer me when I’m down. And that’s okay, to an extent. I know there are people in my life who only feel comfortable talking to me when I’m either thriving or struggling, depending on what makes them feel less alone. The important thing is being aware of their energy. I truly believe that telling your plans to someone who doesn’t wish success for you will harm your outcome. Their thoughts interfere of maybe just their own insecurities. So I keep certain boundaries in place. Some people are only meant for certain conversations, certain activities, certain versions of me. And to keep things positive, those lines have to stay where they are. It’s hard at first, but with intuition and practice, it gets easier.

I know it sounds cliché, but life really is a balance of energies, finding the things that keep you from going insane with boredom, and finding the people who fit the different sides of you, knowing not every person is meant to see every side.

Okay, maybe that’s a little hypocritical considering I’m literally sitting here telling all of you about every side of me. But don’t compare yourself to me. I am not normal. I have not had a normal life or career. My life probably confuses you. Don’t worry, it confuses me too. I just know I was put on this earth to fuck shit up and make shit happen. As were all of you, in your own ways. You are not me, I am not you, and none of us are our neighbors. Don’t compare yourself to me, don’t compare yourself to anyone. I’m sharing my lessons and my “fucking shit up” so that it doesn’t stay silent, because silence would make all of it completely pointless.

I left college at 18 to run marketing for a startup. I bursted out of anger about how terrible their app design was, then took over the entire project. I’ve been working consistently ever since. I’ve run theaters, nightclubs, bars, and restaurants. I’ve built companies to millions a year. I’ve started my own. And I am still in my twenties.

When I was little, I lived in films and photography. Meanwhile, the most “fuckable” guys in my high school called themselves the Camo Crew because, you guessed it, they wore camo every day. While the coolest girls chewed tobacco and used the ‘back door’ for religious purposes. There, in this farm town, I was in pearls, fur coats, and stilettos, trying to survive long enough to escape. I was lucky in a way; the difference between me and everyone around me was so drastic that it was almost laughably clear that comparison was pointless. Not in a negative way; just in a “we’re meant for different universes” way. I can still smell the metal of the lockers, the cow manure from the farm next door, the diesel fumes from the camo-wrapped trucks in the parking lot, an entire world I was never meant to belong to. And that’s the thing: we’re all meant for different worlds, different stages, different impacts. That is the sameness we actually share. The yin and yang, the holy trinity, the compass pointing north.

So take inspiration from the fucked-up shit I’ve had to endure, learn from my lessons, and know that even though this year has been chaotic, I’m going to keep telling you what’s happening. Because someone out there needs to hear it. I know younger me desperately needed a voice like mine. I remember opening Google for the first time and feeling like the universe finally cracked open. I stared at the search bar for ten minutes, thinking of every single business idea I ever had, before panicking and typing: “What is the average American family income?”

My mother told me years later she found my first search history and laughed. I was the only kid who didn’t believe in Santa anymore, so the whole “we’re poor, but Santa brings bouncy houses and Xboxes” storyline was rather dead to me.

If you’re reading this right as it comes out, hi, I’m in Atlanta, being a hotshot in the entertainment industry, kidding, I’m starting at the bottom and absorbing everything possible. But I’m excited, so be excited for me? And if you’re wishing bad juju… I’ll know. And I’ll return the energy, booboo.

I think you know by now I’m not a scared person. I’m not scared of starting over or starting small or starting late, because every time I’ve jumped into a new world, somehow the ground formed under my feet. I don’t know if that’s faith or delusion or destiny, but either way, I know it’s mine as long as I have the confidence to claim it.

It’s annoying, honestly, how divinely inconvenient my destiny is and has been. But here we are. A new city, a new industry, a new world that has no idea the amount of impact I may have, and I suppose neither do I. But if this year has taught me anything, it’s that my story only gets louder when I lean into my chaos.

So let’s see what Atlanta makes of me. Or better yet, what I make out of Atlanta.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: I’m Tired of Being an Anomaly
subtitle: Notes from a Firecracker; What Nobody Tells You About Skipping Every Rung on the Ladder
body:
I’ve traveled to a new city not because I wanted to, but because I needed to. I’ve moved across the country by myself several times now. I’ve existed in millions of spaces, rooms, and restaurants where not a soul knew me. But I’ve also existed in millions of places where every single soul knew too much about me.

Where I grew up, when I share the stories of my youth, people are utterly shocked that such things happen in the United States. I’m constantly reminded how much of an anomaly I am— with my family, my peers, the people I went to school with, everyone I’ve crossed paths with.

I find myself feeling more alone when I share the reasons that I am an anomaly, but these are just facts about myself. I’m very keen on behavior, on minor flinches, on that split second of true emotion sandwiched between two masked ones. So when I share why my life has been curated to keep me not on a pedestal but at a completely different table from everyone around me… it hits different.

I feel like I’m inspiring. I motivate people. I exude creativity onto others. But what’s left for me? I crave learning others’ anomalies.

It’s an exhausting thought— to lie normalcy with death in a world of sameness.

I remember the first time I spoke to a licensed therapist. I watched his eyes cower, flinch, smile, and even laugh as I shared the strange phenomena that has been my life. This is my normal, but when I look at what’s actually considered normal, I sit alone, wondering how I became so strange, or if perhaps I was just this strange from the beginning.

I wish more people spoke. I wish you spoke more. I wish you wrote more. Perhaps I feel like an anomaly because I’m still only beginning to share who I am behind the big hair and red nails. Or maybe I just haven’t heard the right people speak yet.

It’s a difficult thing— offering others creativity, stories, absurd notions, and anomalies while quietly starving for one in return. Maybe that’s why I dove headfirst into the internet so young. I found the anomalies that enriched me by wandering as the digital man on Google Earth streets and devouring countless stories on socials and blogs.

It’s hard to meet anomalies in real life. Maybe I’m not near them, or maybe they’re a lot like me— scared to share, scared to talk.

So that’s why I left the small city in Tennessee, just for a minute. I’m craving anomalies. I’m craving extravagance. I need my version of normalcy.

That is to say, I’m not in an extravagant city, but it is new. Greenville, SC, is peaceful and quaint, surprisingly busy, and, more importantly, there isn’t a soul here who already knows who I am. I can exist as an anomaly while the people around me make guesses about who I am.

For being a Z-rated celebrity, I’ve dealt with an unusual amount of “paparazzi.” Growing up in a town that thought camouflage was a color on the color wheel, I was the firecracker who refused to change herself to please them. And for all the right reasons, I grew into an anomaly.

The lesson that standing on your morals could cost you those around you was ingrained in me very early. I’ve always known true right from wrong. Small towns in seclusion, communities in seclusion, make it dangerously easy to lose that definition—especially when everyone around you is screaming one way or the other. But I never did. I became the outlaw.

As painful as it was, that became the core of why I will not back down; why I am so confident in my values, my morals, my decisions. I was sixteen and couldn’t go to the coffee shop, Walgreens, or walk the school halls without someone snapping my photo to blast online, ridicule, or keep tabs.

So, as I switch cities and travel between places that have yet to discover what a true firecracker anomaly I am, I’ll keep blazing the trail I believe in. Because when the hell have I ever backed down? For fuck’s sake, I took my boss to court last year for a protective order after he attempted to physically harm me.

Don’t fuck with me.

Woman Compulsively Overshares, But People Somehow Still Don’t Know Anything About Her

This little city in Tennessee has started to get to know me—through friends, through my attitude, my loud mouth, and stilettos. It’s fun letting a new city slowly acknowledge your existence. I’ve been escaping down to Atlanta quite routinely for work, but the acknowledgment there hits different.

Consistently, I’ve gone to shake someone’s hand on set, or at another professional setting in Atlanta, and before I can share my name with them, I’m cut off by them announcing that they already know me.

After the seventh person, it clicked: maybe I’m as much of an anomaly on the outside as I am on the inside.

I’ve let my inner anomaly spill out into my fashion and overall style. To say the least, I love equally confusing and impressing people. So no, I haven’t been in any movies. The notable editorials and runway shows from my short-lived modeling career had my name scrubbed after I personally audited every photo online when I stepped into business.

Yes, I emailed and called every photographer and publication myself because I was determined to be taken seriously. And to fill you in—excuse my French—my titties are apparently extremely high fashion. I never did anything provocative or revealing, but yeah… my side boob is in a lot of those old photos. (I also had black hair back then—I wouldn’t even recognize myself.)

I’ve never truly taken little steps. I’ve never placed one foot in front of the other on the chronologically society-agreed-upon ladder. Every single time I have jumped from the bottom of the ladder, up several steps. I don’t know what those first three steps actually look like—they could be silver, black, or maybe even rusted and rigid?

I skipped through high school and went into college early. I left college early for my career. And now, as I’m still figuring out how exactly to catapult my writing and creative side, I know that the advice I’m going to be given is probably not the advice that I need to follow.

Many things I’m god-awful shit at. Many things I’m okay at. But for some things, I am an anomaly.

I’m writing this rant because I don’t want to stay one of the few who openly share what makes them an anomaly, not when I know you have powerful, beautiful, incredible anomalies inside you too.

I think the world would be a better place if we shared our reasons. What makes us special? Isn’t that what makes the world move—inventions, discovery, the future?

I’m tired of being an anomaly, but mostly because I haven’t heard from the rest of you.

I’ve been making great strides in my writing career; I’ve somehow been able to consistently earn money, network new gigs, and continually grow in my written collection in the worst freelancer market known to us in the past few decades.

Last night, over a Southern soft serve dessert, someone asked me what got me into writing. Per my routine, I started telling them how I launched What Sheridan Said as a way to open up and finally start writing again—but mid-sentence, I cut myself off and realized I’ve actually been writing this whole time.

I suppose I’m a bit sensitive to my ladder and anomaly analogies because I was told earlier this week by a family member to get a real job. Though this is a different kind of leap.

I’m certain I won’t be standing at the bottom of the ladder, carefully stepping onto the first step as everyone expects. Because over the past ten years, I’ve built an incredible written collection.

So maybe we aren’t always anomalies. Maybe we’ve been climbing the whole time—placing our feet from the ground to the first rung, and then the next. It’s just that we couldn’t see it; we didn’t know we were on the ladder. We didn’t know that part of the story yet.

But there’s my argument again for us to talk, share, and speak more. Because maybe sometimes we aren’t that much of an anomaly. Maybe it’s just that not enough of us have told our stories yet.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Let’s Make a Sandwich Out of It
subtitle: Caterpillars on My Face, a Southern Twang in the Supermarket, Kyle’s Sad Little Fern, and Banana Pie: The Secret Ingredients of My Favorite Sandwich.
body:
Somebody, the other day, a stranger in the supermarket, spoke Farsi to me without being prompted by a thing. I looked at him, confused but not entirely — mostly because I’ve been around the language enough to recognize that yeah, he was definitely speaking Farsi. So I hit him with a little Southern twang and said, “Now I’m so sorry, sir, I only speak English.”

His smile adjusted into another smile, and he goes, “Oh ma’am, I’m sorry, I thought you were Arab like me.”

Me, now curious as hell, said, “Can I ask what made you think I was?”

He didn’t even pause for a full second: “Your eyebrows… and the way you move and walk. You’re very elegant and slow with the way you carry yourself.”

I said, “Thank you.” Checked out at self-checkout, then marched straight to my car, flipped down the sun visor, and studied my eyebrows in that tiny vanity mirror.

The next day, that stranger was still taking up space in my head. So I texted one of my friends who actually speaks Farsi and is Arab, and typed this whole chaotic paragraph:

“sooo.. the other day at the supermarket, well yesterday, this random guy came up and started speaking Farsi to me because he thought I was arab and spoke Farsi, so I asked him what made him think that, and he said ‘your eyebrows’ umm.. so what is it about my eyebrows that say im arab?? can you help? lol ok thanks, my mind won’t stop wondering about this.”

He hit me back in thirty seconds flat: “They’re very hairy and very straight.”

I replied faster than lightning: “Oh… cool lol. thanks”

Now, what I like to do when firing an employee, breaking up with a boyfriend, or just pointing out negative attributes — I say, “let’s make a sandwich out of this situation.”

But what I mean is let’s make a compliment sandwich.

Thank you so much, Adam, for this new Birkin purse. I love it! You’re such an attentive, thoughtful man—I really admire that about you.
(Pause)
We’ve both made such great strides in our lives: me with my book, you with your career. But I think it’s time we go our separate ways from here.
(Pause)
Oh, and Sarah’s going to take over your office and move in. I already talked to your buddy Jared—he has two spare rooms ready for you and your stuff.
(Pause)
I’m really excited to see what you’ll achieve next, Adam. When you really focus and put your determination into something, you can do anything. Now you’ll finally have the space to make it happen! I can’t wait to watch your company take off!

Or this example:

Hey Kyle, I just wanted to say, you are incredible at showing up on time every single day. Seriously, the punctuality is chef’s kiss, and your desk is always so tidy, like we could actually perform surgery on it.
(Pause)
That being said, we’ve decided to go in a different direction with the team. We’re letting you go today. Oh, and HR already packed your stuff—your sad little fern is in this cardboard box right here. We also canceled your Slack access and your parking spot, but good news: the vending machine still takes your old employee code for one more free bag of chips on your way out!
(Pause)
I’m so excited for whatever comes next for you, Kyle. You have this amazing… energy. When you really apply yourself to something you actually care about, I have no doubt you’re going to crush it. Can’t wait to see your LinkedIn glow-up!

I’ll stop with the examples because I’m pretty sure you’re getting my drift now.

So when that stranger explained that my furry straight eyebrows plus my slow, elegant mannerisms are what made him assume I was Arab, I declared the whole thing a compliment sandwich. The main bread and condiments are the fact that I, Sheridan The Great, am elegant, poised, controlled, and feminine with my mannerisms — major chef’s kiss. The sad bologna in the middle is that I have caterpillars on my face. But the other piece of the sandwich that smashes that nasty bologna down is Cara Delevingne, the British supermodel who made furry eyebrows hot. To you, my queen, I thank thee.

I mentioned earlier that my abs were coming back in, and overall, I’m a fit person — any indulgence usually gets followed by a week of moderation. I’m saying all this as I stuff my face with a box of Kraft mac and cheese and banana pie, because let’s be real: 95% of this body is straight genetics.

The past few months, my social media feeds have been filled with women posting about my body type, asking, “How do I achieve this? Please only realistic responses and only respond if you have this body, please!!!! thanks, babes! No hate!”

I’ve refrained from commenting, but I scroll through the replies quite frequently. Some are giving advice that may or may not actually be harmful to their health in the long run, some comment to troll and to hate, and others — I find a small fraction — are commenting with the reality: it’s just genetics.

It is genetics, but it’s also style. It’s a trend. It’s what the media, what society, what you and I collectively say is… “goals.”

Fashion is a funny industry, and as I like to famously say, “It’s the only industry where the trickle-down effect actually occurs.” Beauty and body trends run on a predictable cycle of about two decades. I didn’t know who Paris Hilton was until my late teens, so I’m truly blessed to have been sheltered growing up in the country of Minnesota throughout the early 2000s. Back then, my naturally thin body with slight proportionate curves was one of the most desired looks. Women were starving themselves and making themselves throw up to achieve it. Tabloids, Perez Hilton, and TMZ called every roll of bad posture “fat and ugly.” It was dehumanizing.

Today, twenty years later — slightly after BBLs, slim thick, and “curvy is queen” — we’ve turned the page to Ozempic, Mounjaro, and Ro (oddly sponsored by Serena Williams). I’m really mad I tossed all my skinny jeans, because I know they’ll be back every twenty years like clockwork… and so will my body. Thin is apparently in right now, but guess what — that’s just for the moment. Soon, “curvy is queen” will cycle back, along with some new fat-surgery placement solidified by media and the Kardashians. —Ozempic and thigh gaps will be yesterday’s news.

At the end of the day, whether it’s random strangers reading my face like a map, my body being “in” or “out” every two decades, or me having to fire Kyle while praising his sad little fern — everything’s better when you slap two big slices of compliments around the ugly middle. Life hands you bologna. You add bread and condiments, and suddenly it’s… edible.

So next time someone speaks to you wrong, or the internet tells you your body is trending (or not), just smile, hit ’em with that Southern twang (fake it like I did if you need), and declare it a compliment sandwich. Then go eat the damn pie.

Running into that stranger makes me wonder what other assumptions people are making about me that I’ll never hear. In college, I was rumored to be a Russian exchange student. In D.C., people often assumed I wasn’t American until I spoke. But what does the lady at the gas station think? Does she think I’m quiet and mysterious because I move slowly? Does the barista at my local coffee shop assume I’m high-maintenance because of the rings on my fingers? Hell, maybe someone out there even sees my whole aura and decides I’m a secret agent (kidding, we already know they do).

And the funny part? Most of those stories are probably way more fun and interesting than the real one. I’m not elegant on purpose; I just think too much before I move. I’m not ‘goals’ because I earned it; I just won the genetic lottery this decade and lost it the one before. None of us are the main character in anyone else’s movie, and rarely are we even the one in our own.

So yeah… I’m gonna keep stuffing my face with banana pie when the mood hits, keep my eyebrows exactly as furry as I want them to be, and walk however slow and elegant I damn well please. Trends will flip again — thin, thick, straight, fluffy, whatever Vogue says is hot — and my body and my face will still just be mine. Sometimes the best reality checks come from the produce aisle, no physical sandwich required.

You know me — I’m the girl who’ll show up to a biker bar in a ball gown and full glam because I genuinely don’t care about the perceptions, I just want to be myself. Still, it’s refreshing to sit at a café in stilettos, a loose blouse, and a skirt, place my purse on the hook under the table, and glance over to see the woman next to me rocking stilettos and a silk skirt too.

And with that, I’m off to finish this banana pie and practice my Southern twang. I’ll see you next episode.

title: Lie of Tomorrow
subtitle: That the air will taste crisper, my sheets will feel softer, the sun brighter, and my mind easier.
body:
My tongue lies and says,
“I’ll do it tomorrow.”
But the lie isn’t in putting off.
The lie is in pretending
tomorrow exists.

Like I will wake up
in a different bed.
That the sun will find its way
through the darkening curtains
I hung to keep it out.

That the air will taste crisper,
my sheets will feel softer,
the sun brighter,
and my mind easier.

I braid my guilt like a to-do list,
spit out a mouthful of wine,
and lie again that tomorrow
will wait for me.

But my tomorrow isn’t a loyal dog.
There is no pretense.
There is no dog.
There is no tomorrow.

And still, I speak it,
as if the act of saying
can summon what never comes;
what I’m too afraid to bury.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
The Official Poetry Collection of WSS

title: Lipped Pearls
subtitle: I love dolling up. // Twirling to music as I smack my lip stain,
body:
I love dolling up.
Twirling to music as I smack my lip stain,
the red seeping into the cracks.
It’s going to be such a fun night.

The mirror swallows me whole—
split in two: girl and ghost.
The pearls at my throat are tight-lipped,
they gleam like teeth— waiting.
Perfume pools in the hollows of my collarbone,
sweet rot, sugared decay.
My heels click against the tiles—

Tonight, I will shine.
—I will vanish.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
The Official Poetry Collection of WSS

title: Luxury Eats Me Last
subtitle: Her shoulders stopped living near her ears...
body:
I spit out my feelings like watermelon seeds,
small and useless —
meant to be discarded, like the M.R.S degree
I ‘supposedly’ moved here for.

I climb the staircase
and realize the rich have two,
when my reflection didn’t check me back out.

The carpet tries to swallow my feet,
lower me below the chandelier,
whispering, “Join in, money’s fun.”

I’m tired of men who touch like they’re counting.
Tired of women parading titles, counting stones,
thumbing themselves around
like the livestock I showed in 4-H.

Sadness smells like lavender detergent
and tastes cleaner served in a crystal glass.
They smile and say, “Drink it down,
It tastes of salvation.”

I make it up, and in the marble tub,
cradling my insides,
I wonder how long luxury will keep me alive.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Maybe I’m Just a Late Bloomer
subtitle: After years of working, skipping milestones, and surviving— I proved to myself I didn’t miss the moment.
body:
This past Saturday, I hosted my first party. I mean, first party… ever.

Not a little dinner. Not a cozy catch-up with two friends and a bottle of wine. A real party. A backyard full of people, food, music, string lights, and laughter. I sent out a last-minute invite to almost everyone I know and respect, around 50 people total, and to my complete shock, 25 of them showed up. That might not sound like a lot to some people, but for me? It was everything.

Here’s the thing: I’ve never done this before. Not in high school. Not in college. Not as an adult. I’ve never been the girl who hosts. I’ve never been the one who says, “Come to my place. I’ve got it covered.”

Growing up, I skipped a lot of things people think are normal milestones. I skipped through high school. I skipped college. By the time I was 18, I wasn’t playing beer pong in dorm rooms or planning spring break trips with friends; I was managing people twice my age. I moved to the East Coast, took on real jobs, and started building a career before I ever really had a chance to build community.

When you’re the boss at 18, 19, 20… when you’re running meetings, hiring people, making decisions, and carrying weight, you don’t exactly have time for girls’ weekends. You don’t stay out late with coworkers who see you as their manager. And when your one real day off a week is used to run errands, clean, or just breathe? Hosting a party, let alone making friends, feels like something that belongs to someone else’s version of adulthood.

But lately, I’ve been realizing something: maybe I didn’t miss those moments. Maybe I just wasn’t ready yet, my life wasn’t ready yet. But things are different now.

So I planned a dinner party. A big one.

I spent a full week prepping (between my already packed schedule), I cleaned every corner of my house. I trimmed the backyard. I made a giant charcuterie board, actually three.

And then, the sun came out. It was 72 degrees, not a cloud in the sky. Which, if you know anything about the week we had here, was a gift straight from the weather gods. It rained before. It rained after. It’s literally been pouring ever since. But that day? She was perfect.

My backyard was glowing. I strung up lights. People filtered in slowly, drinks in hand, hugs on arrival. Everyone brought something: snacks, flowers, drinks, and good energy. There was music. There were children running barefoot through the grass. There were conversations that actually, intellectually, mattered. We played oldies, and around midnight, I turned the music off out of respect for the neighbors. But the funny thing? One of my neighbors told me afterward that she and her friends were listening from their window and loving it. They were jamming in their living room, windows wide open.

We grilled hot dogs and stacked nearly 80 burgers. Yes… 80 burgers. I have no idea how, but they all got eaten. I thought I overdid it. I guess I didn’t.

At one point, a few friends gave a toast. Just a quick little moment of gratitude, thanking me for bringing everyone together. I nearly cried. I couldn’t believe I created something that felt like this.

Because for a long time, I really believed this wasn’t in the cards for me. I didn’t think I was the kind of person who had a backyard full of people who wanted to be there. I thought I missed that window, that by throwing myself into work so young, I had sacrificed any real chance at building friendships. Deep, rooted friendships. Ones that didn’t just happen by convenience, but through intention.

But then I looked around. And there they were. A table full of people I love. People who stayed until midnight or until dawn. People who helped clean up. People who showed up even when I invited them at the last minute. People I want to know for a long time.

And maybe I’m not behind. Maybe I’m just blooming on my own time, and in the end, my milestones will even each other out.

It’s not easy to be vulnerable about something like this. I get embarrassed about it sometimes, often because I’ve never done this before. That something so normal for other people felt impossible for me for so long. But I’m proud of myself. I really am. For pushing past the fear. For hosting. For laughing. For letting people see my space. For not being perfect.

There was no noise complaint. There was no awkwardness. There was no mess I couldn’t clean up. There was only sunlight, music, grilled food, and people who made me feel like maybe, just maybe, I’ve found my place.

I’m excited for more. More memories. More milestones. More slow, soft, late-blooming joy.

Because maybe I didn’t miss anything at all. Maybe I just started a little later. And maybe that’s okay.

title: My Upper Lip Is Fake, My Career Is Real, and My Birthday Is Still Cursed
subtitle: A deeply unserious update about Botox, writing, divorce, and being an ordained minister with a tragic 0–1 record.
body:
Last week I told you about the men who disappeared, the city I’m loosely hiding in, and the scriptwriting job that fell into my lap. And now, the first season is already wrapped on my end, anyway. I keep waiting for someone to tap me on the shoulder and tell me this was a very expensive misunderstanding, but until that happens, I’m choosing to believe I belong here. Which is why I’m already plotting my next move, whether that’s slipping into the writers’ room of Nashville 911, convincing more media companies to hire me, or finally selling a story of my own. I’m not sure what will happen yet.

Anyways... I got shot in the face today! Twenty times! I’m dramatic, remember? So, I drove to the bougie side of town and got Botox. And no, I’m not outing the med spa because I had to pay for this, and if I’m paying full price, then confidentiality is my gift to myself. Technically, I paid for it six months ago, which is even funnier, but I figured with my birthday coming up, why not go get stabbed a few times?

I’ve never gotten filler, and I’m really scared of it. I started getting Botox a couple of years ago because I hate how my top lip tries to hide whenever I talk or smile. So if you’re scrolling through my Instagram wondering why sometimes my lips look bigger in some pictures vs others, it’s literally just the Botox being fresh. Nothing mysterious, nothing sinful, just science, little pain, and vanity.

The first time I ever got Botox, I fully fainted, and now I just squeeze stress balls and squeal like a little b*tch. We call that growth! I also swear it helps my hormonal chin acne. Not sure if that’s medically accurate or if I made it up, but anytime I get Botox in those areas, my acne calms down. Maybe the cortisol can’t flex through the muscle or something. I don’t know. I’m not a doctor. But back when business was booming, and I had extra money to throw around, I’d get a little chin Botox if my acne flared up, and it genuinely helped. Not recommending it; I am just sharing what happened and what worked for me.

My birthday is a few days before Christmas, which means I am contractually obligated to be a grinch. I don’t love artificial holiday cheer. It’s not even the holidays that make me a grinch; it’s that my birthday has never once been convenient. People are traveling, at parties, with their families, doing anything other than celebrating my existence.

For a few years, I stopped planning anything altogether because watching things fall through felt worse than pretending my birthday didn’t exist. I used to purposely schedule myself meetings so I wouldn’t get disappointed. I know this sounds anti-Christian, but I swear the birth of Jesus has overshadowed my birthday every single year. And what if the books are wrong? What if he wasn’t even born then? Truly, what then? Also, my cousin was actually born on Christmas Day, and he’s not nearly as dramatic as I, so… maybe I am the problem.

Anyway, these past few weeks of shifting writing from a hobby to a career have been wonderful and also a little difficult. I was talking with a friend about how I always turn my hobbies into paid gigs, which made me wonder if I’m supposed to go out and find a new hobby or if I can just separate the writing I do for work from the writing I do for myself, or if it even matters at all. I’m still bouncing between Nashville and Atlanta and loving both cities for different reasons, but now with this gig wrapped and no timeline on anything future-related, I need to keep pitching myself and finding new creative work because apparently I am a full-time creative now.

I was supposed to go to Art Basel to help a friend, but once I landed this gig, they were nothing but supportive, which made it easier to stay focused even though I really wanted to go, and felt bad saying no.

Side note: I wish I could spill all the details about the show, but that would be unprofessional of me.

To everyone cheering me on, with this new writing gig, thank you! ♡

It has been such an exciting experience, and I hope I get to be involved in the next season’s script. In between everything else, I’ve also been revising my play, which I first mentioned last episode. I’m almost done with play one, then I’ll read through and revise play two, and after that, I guess I’ll learn what playwrights do after they write plays. As far as my other writing, I haven’t written any new articles or poems this week, but a lot is happening in my head and a lot I’m working on quietly, so don’t worry, there’s more coming.

title: Non-Perishable Items
subtitle: Perishable or not, black or white, and the colors I added later
body:
When I think of non-perishable items, you might think of food, but that isn’t where my mind takes me. I think of my mother’s phone number I’ve had memorized since grade school, I think of the worn-out paperback book I’ve reread a countless times, I think of the candle I refuse to light because of the petals beautifully placed inside the wax, I think of the first poetry book I ever wrote, and I think of who the world, or a higher power, says I am destined to be.

If you drive straight on I-35, starting roughly at the southern border of Texas, and drive just over 1,000 miles straight, on one single road, you’ll meet a little town that’s grown up a little now, but when I knew it, everything was labeled as perishable, or non.

No phones at the dinner table, never start eating before everyone has sat down and filled their plate, always memorize your safety route; itemizing where things are for an emergency go-to bag run. A mantra I’ve never said out loud, and the ones I wish weren’t ringing throughout my ears. A grudge with an ex I decided never to spend, my playlist of 12 songs I’ve listened to on repeat. My favorite pen, the only one I chose to ever write with.

Maybe in a certain lens, these items, these attributes, things, are all perishable, in one way or another. Though they have no expiration date to me.

When I think of non-perishable food items, I think of rice, pasta, flour, oats, canned goods, fats & oils, nuts, and the seasoning and baking basics. There used to be a cornfield where McDonald’s now stands. Behind my house was an abandoned cow farm, and my grandparents were surrounded by nothing but corn and bean fields. In this little farm town, there were non-perishable items, and there were perishable. There were the town people, and there were those who were not welcome. In school, there were the cool kids, and of course the ‘losers.’ All throughout the town, we labeled each other, each item, each packaged good in the local grocery store as perishable or non-perishable.

I revisit home when I can, though so much has changed. The cornfields have been shredded into concrete Pizza Huts, and the pastures into youth sporting facilities. Though if I step into one of the few bars covering its delicately charming Main Street, I’m greeted with an impromptu class reunion. The basics were simple back then, in the town, disposable or not, perishable or not.

Perishable food items such as corn or beans are the foundation of roughly every single food item in your grocery store. More realistically, it’s roughly over 40%, hence the dramatic argument still standing sound.

If you were to start driving on I-35N from the southernmost Texas city, drive straight for over 1,000 miles on the same road, you’d land in Minnesota, just over the border into the southern part, where all you see is flat land, covered in low grass bowing away from the wind, or a farm and fields, usually quaint. Sometimes, when you just drive over the border in Minnesota, you might see buffalo, and cows, horses, and the most charming single-story houses paired with a 50s-style barn. But mostly you will see corn and beans.

On one of my last visits back home, I drove. It wasn’t straight through I-35N on a 1,000-mile gas trek from the southernmost Texan city. Though it was comparable, just as tiresome. I have an impending desire to always have several shoe options on hand. Each one with the stiletto, toe, and shine interchanging between my choices. I will typically pack twenty pairs of shoes for a seven-day trip, so as a non-perishable item, my desire for shoe options, plus I wanted to bring my two dogs with me; driving was the only thing that made proper sense. It had been some time since I visited before this trip, and when I crossed over the border into Minnesota, I was reminded of something I’m not sure I ever noticed.

There are flat grass plains, and flat farming fields, pastures without a hill to climb, and roads that look like they just… end… in twenty straight miles. I’m not sure if I noticed this while I was a child, but if the earth were flat, it most certainly is in southern Minnesota.

It’s a warmth in a hug as it feeds you a sleeping pill. Revisiting southern Minnesota, after what was my longest time away, I felt a warm feeling as I arrived in town. This was it; this was the community I was (sort of) a member of. It’s where my family is, and even though I used Google Maps to get from the house I grew up in to Main Street (clinically geographically challenged), it was still the most familiar. But when I got to Main Street, I could see it again. I drove past the only stoplight, and when I peered out onto the road in front of me, it looked as though the world just ended, and if I were to continue driving, I might prove a flat-earther right.

That’s the version I saw. The graph that I grew up on, and boy was I a little wiz with calculus. But this graph had two colors, black and white, perishable and non; it had where it was and where it ended. I could see each of these things clearer than the snow in December. Maybe I was frustrated growing up; I knew there was so much gray, so much color to the world; it’s just that I couldn’t see it yet.

As a visual person, this became my non-perishable. A part of me will always associate southern Minnesota with putting constraints on what my world could be, but it’s not the town, it’s not the farm, nor the flat fields of corn, or the perishable or not. It’s simply a non-perishable item for me to have my world, visually, have no end meet.

The graph and its dotted points were quite harsh. Perishable or not, disposable or not, cool or lame. It’s not saying the town was like this or even is today, but it is the version of the town that got to know me. There are rumors of blue, and yellow, and maybe even purple dotted points added into the graph today, and perhaps the graph is now beautiful if I were to study its paint.

It is, however, to say that the graph that knew me, the perishable or not, laid a framework for my initial thought patterns, my dreams, and, dare I say, who I am as a woman today. The corn and beans our grandfathers grew and shared that make up almost half of all the food we consume. It lays a foundation for Thanksgiving dinner, for a celebration dinner, and a regular family meal.

If you didn’t know already, you can drive straight, on one road (I-35N) for over 1,000 miles straight from the southernmost Texan city to reach southern Minnesota. The fields wave at a friend opposite the wind, the cornfields lay flat till the sun kisses the stalks’ tassels, and the cows truly pay you no mind. The people as I knew them rarely left or drove the road that appears to just ‘end.’ And those that did rarely spoke about the world beyond the field.

Back then, a few dozen more cornfields and a couple of corporate takeovers ago, the world seemed simple; it appeared black and white. Perishable or not, it had an end, and corn and beans were the foundation of our health and meals. I labeled my hobbies perishable or not, my desires as disposable or not; in moments of growth, often my own sanity teetered and shared its role between completely lame and allowed.

I always knew a graph with many colors was far more beautiful than one of two, and that gray bounced between thousands of hues in every moment of our lives. For me, it wasn’t until I drove past the road I couldn’t see. I still label things on my graph as black and white, perishable or not, and those have created such a beautiful foundation for my desires, my motivations, strengths, and what makes me. But I’ve added in beautiful colors; there are purple and blue dots, maybe a giant red line pointing upwards, and some sprinkles of pink scattered randomly.

I am a visual person, and in the most introspective way, I took things as metaphor, as face value, or as a challenge in every detail that surrounded me. I have many non-perishable items: my love for poetry, my insane need for countless stiletto options, beautiful voluptuous hair, a feeling of charitable virtue, and never creating an end to the world surrounding me.

I studied the way the lights in the theatre shone against the fabric walls for the majority of my first movie theatre experiences, rather than watching the funny cartoon. Maybe it is that I look at the world a different way, at least my world. I believe each of our worlds is different; we first learned the world through a graph that doesn’t correlate to the world you are in today, or maybe the world that you desire. We each learn labels from the townspeople that define who we are, whether it’s limited to perishable or not, or a kinder tone; we each start the world with different non-perishable items, with a different graph.

This was mine, and how it shaped me.

(Please don’t eat expired food, though. Metaphor only. I’m not responsible for anyone who gets food poisoning trying to eat a perishable item as a non-perishable.)

Sheridan Guerrette

title: Ordained, Deranged, and Dangerously Into Yogurt
subtitle: A completely unsolicited list of things about me that reveal both character and probable brain damage.
body:
Let’s keep it light this week. In the past few episodes, I’ve shared my thoughts on betrayal, ambition, and deep emotional damage, so today, I’m giving you the version of me that people usually only get after the third glass of wine or a 12-hour drive across the country. These are the unhinged facts. Things that don’t really matter, but somehow explain everything about me. You don’t need to know any of this. But you’re going to be so glad you do.

Let’s start where I recently left off: I hate sweating. Hate it. I think I might be allergic to my own sweat. When I do sweat, it itches so bad I want to tear my skin off. Oh, and also, I’ve literally never been to the gym.

Don’t worry; I have plenty more unhinged facts.

My mother didn’t believe in the flu shot growing up, so I had to bring a note to public school every year that said it was “against my religion.” Yep. That’s how I walked into first grade. And while we’re on childhood humiliation, my first concussion was in art class. And then later I stabbed myself in the thigh… also in art class. Apparently, art class is deeply dangerous for me. I was in seventh grade when the concussion happened. I was big into eyeliner. I had it caked all around my eyes and then fell off my chair, got a concussion, and the principal had to wheel me out of the building, through the lunchroom, where the eighth graders were having lunch. I looked like a raccoon who had been hit by a bus.

Another fun fact: I was in swimming lessons for three years and never passed level one. Still really can’t swim, even though I grew up in the land of 10,000 lakes. Minnesota, baby. I did, however, water ski and kneeboard like a maniac. I’d strap myself into that kneeboard like a Velcro-wrapped idiot and flip upside down every other run, unable to unstrap myself until my mother would jump off the boat to save me. And I just kept going. I didn’t care that I was almost drowning over and over; I just wanted to ride.

And please don’t ever try to share food with me. My name is Sher-idan, but I do not share. Do not touch my fries. Do not take me to a restaurant where the only options are “shareables.” If you reach for my plate, I will slap your hand.

I also don’t use lotion. It freaks me out. It’s cold, mushy, slimy. I hate the feeling in between my fingers, too. So instead, I use green salve, an old wives’ tale from my family that’s not FDA approved but absolutely works better than any store-bought moisturizer. And if you want a little healing trick? Black salve. Use it on zits, scars, warts, whatever. It draws stuff out. Don’t Google it, just trust me.

I wore stilettos every day from age 16 until maybe a few years ago. I walked 12,000 steps or more a day in them, six days a week, consistently for four years. Yes, I even walked my Chihuahua in stilettos. RIP Fendi. Now that I have two big dogs, I’ve eased off the heels. But no one warned me back then that wearing stilettos long-term would eventually destroy the arches of your feet so badly that you’d need Botox in them just to walk without pain.

So now I wear… kitten heels. I know. I never thought I’d say that. But here we are.

I refuse to use public transportation, besides the scooters. My favorite snack is yogurt with Ritz crackers. I use the cracker as a spoon, eat it, and then use another one. It’s delightful. Don’t knock it till you try it.

I’m extremely particular. About my routines, my outfits, my environment. If you mess with my morning routine, you’re going to meet Mean Sheridan. And when I pack three suitcases to stay at your house, please know I am doing this for you. If I don’t have the outfit that matches my emotional weather that day, I can’t function. So yes, thank you in advance for carrying my bags.

Speaking of emotional weather: one time in middle school, in the dead of a Minnesota winter, I wore a black turtleneck, black long johns, a strapless sundress with umbrellas all over it, and rain boots. Because I woke up and felt like “sunshine in the middle of a storm cloud.” So I dressed accordingly. Thank you.

I never owned a pot or a pan until recently. Yes, I know that’s utterly shocking. But you have to understand, I’ve somehow always had a chef nearby; hospitality life. There’s always just somehow been someone around who just… made me food. I think when your employees love you, and you don’t have an ego about anything, they end up doing things for you out of pure love. That includes feeding me like a royal toddler. I mean, if I’m the kind of boss who scrubs toilets next to you when the restaurant’s short-staffed, then yes, I’m also the kind of boss who gets a salmon filet handed to her on a porcelain plate mid-shift. Love you, chefs. Always have, always will.

I once ate spaghetti for two weeks straight and would absolutely do it again. I make the best spaghetti in my family, and everyone knows it; they just won’t admit it. I’ve challenged them to a spaghetti cook-off, and they always find a reason to dodge it. Cowards.

In everyone’s phone in my family, my contact name is “Sheridan the Great Guerrette.” I changed it myself when I was 10 or 12. And they’ve all kept it. So… I think it’s safe to say, you too need to address me as “Sheridan the Great”.

I became the leading lady of a theater without ever auditioning. I was helping run the business side of a medieval-themed theater, and two hours before the show, both the lead and her understudy bailed. I was the only one who fit the gown, but I’d never acted in a single play before, so my colleagues said, “Sheridan, the show must go on.” And so it did, we told the audience what happened, and I didn’t even use the script, and finished with a standing ovation. They never let me off that stage again.

I’ve moved across the country five times. I am not afraid of change. I am not afraid of starting over. I know who I am, and I can be that wherever you drop me.

I’ve never passed a reading test in my life. I learned to read late, and I still remember my first day at a new school in first grade: the teacher handed me a Clifford the Big Red Dog book and asked me to read it aloud to the class. I didn’t even know how to read “I” or “am” yet. So I stood there, staring at the pages, tears welling up. Yeah. That was fun.

I’ve never had a cavity. Blessed be the tooth fairy.

I drink way too much Diet Coke. Like, it’s my one true vice. But I take my vitamins, eat clean, and structure my day like this: start with water, then coffee (because it’s mostly water), then Diet Coke. A couple. And then water again at night. It’s a system. It works.

In high school, I won a McDonald’s eating contest. I think I ate something like 17 McChickens, 10 McDoubles, and a mountain of nuggets. I was the tiniest thing. I’ve basically been the same size since seventh grade, which is why my wardrobe is so massive now. You never know when a corset from 2009 might come in handy.

I am terrified of ladybugs. Don’t argue with me—they bite. They do. I had two on my arm as a kid, and they bit me at the same time. Mortal enemies ever since.

I don’t know how to snowboard. I can ski. But sideways? No. I fall every time. As a kid, I watched luge in the Olympics and thought I could teach myself. So I took my SpongeBob skateboard, laid on it head-first, and launched myself down our incredibly steep driveway. I did this often, convinced an Olympic coach would just happen to be in our small town and discover me. I did the same thing with figure skating, shoveled frozen ponds, practiced spins all night, then mimicked the moves on rollerblades around town. I really believed someone was going to find me and say, “She’s a prodigy.” Disney Channel really raised me, clearly.

I’m an ordained minister. Yes. Legally. Spiritually? Unclear. But I did once officiate a wedding between a dancer and a Marine, which, frankly, felt like the most holy union I could ever be asked to bless. I stood there, clutching my little binder, absolutely winging it. And somehow it worked. They cried. I cried. The audience cried. I said, “By the power vested in me by the internet and probably the state of Nevada,” and then I married them, a dancer and a marine. One year later, they are now getting divorced.

I lied about my height for years. I’m 5’6”, but when I was 17 and doing castings in Minneapolis, I told everyone I was 5’8”. Then I thought that sounded too suspicious, so I downgraded the lie to 5’7”, you know, to keep it “realistic.” The math didn’t matter. I quit modeling in 2016, right before things got inclusive. Timing’s never been my thing. But delusion? That I’ve always had in spades.

I love dogs more than humans. All of you reading this? Love you. But not more than my dogs.

I’m not aging. I’ve decided. I don’t want to be called old; I reject the premise. I’ve chosen to be an angel. Not a vampire, I don’t want to eat people or drink blood, unless it tastes like a good dry cab. I just want to float through life, radiant and ageless, like the heroine in the final scene of a movie that never ends. Thank you. Please continue clapping in awe.

I don’t go to Korean BBQs anymore. I’m five for five on getting into a fight. I don’t know what it is about the place, any of them. Doesn’t matter the city, the people, the vibe. I walk in calm, and by the time we’re grilling short ribs, I’m in a full-blown fight. Every single time. So I avoid them. Out of respect. For myself, and for the beef it brings.

My entire library is filled with textbooks, and I don’t think I’ve ever actually ever read a true story book before. But a textbook? I love those. My current favorite that I keep rereading is a Harvard business law book. Unhinged and sometimes boring?

I quit hurdles freshman year, not because I was scared, but because I had peaked. I biffed it on the final curve of a 300-meter hurdle race, laid flat on the track, and when I opened my eyes, the two hottest senior boys, Foster and Zach, were standing over me in the sunlight. Literal angels. They scooped me up like a damsel. Some girls chase medals, I chase moments. That was it, that was my curtain call. I never ran hurdles again, and I have no regrets.

Last unhinged fact, for now: I drove across the country six times in the month of July. I don’t want to talk about it. I was feral. And I probably will be again.

Anyway, that’s enough for one week. If you made it this far, I applaud your endurance and question your sanity. You now know more about me than some exes do, and honestly, you got the better deal. I’ve laid bare my green salve habits, my hatred of sweat, my refusal to share food, and my ordained minister credentials, which I’ve only used once, to marry a dancer and a Marine, as God intended.

But I also know some of you saw yourself in my past few episodes, where I got a bit deeper with you. And for that, I love you more than I love Ritz crackers dipped in yogurt, which, if you’ve been paying attention, is saying a lot.

Until next week, stay hydrated, stay unhinged, and don’t touch my plate.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Papers Don't Mean Sh*t
subtitle: I had to give up my favorite home, my city, and my sense of safety because a piece of paper couldn't protect me from a man with a tracking app.
body:
“Now things have settled?” I’m laughing at myself, because it did not indeed ‘settle.’

A lot of times, we believe a protective order is a ‘hard stop’, that the intimidation and threats will halt with the wave of a judge-signed paper. But as some of us have learned, some papers don’t mean JACK SHIT.

For a few days, it was great. I successfully Legally-Blonde’d my way through the courthouse. I was happy, I shared the news… and then the silence was shattered. That flammable, thinly-sliced paper gleamed with flames, then settled into dark ashes. The system’s limitations became violently clear.

It started with a confirmation for a subscription to a men’s hunting magazine, delivered to my address. It felt weird, but I wrote it off as spam. Then, a welcome email popped up from a family locator app, the kind used to track your kids or your spouse. The username was a string of numbers, but the connected phone number was mine.

He wasn’t just telling me he knew where I lived and where I hung out. He was showing me he was trying to digitally anchor himself to me, to make my location his business. It was a quiet, technological violation that made my skin crawl.

I called my tech friends to wipe everything needed, and I called the police. They took the information, filed another report for “violation of a protective order,” and told me they’d “look into it.” But they also said what I already knew: without catching him in the act, an arrest could take time. Time I didn’t have. The evidence was circumstantial, but my fear was not.

The dread became deafening. It was a physical reality. Every creak in my old 1930s home was an intrusion; every time the ice maker dropped a new batch, my heart dropped even more. Every floorboard groan or my dog Shadow sneaking a drink of water in the middle of the night was a deadly threat. I wasn’t sleeping. I didn’t feel safe or comfortable.

So I decided to leave.

Over the past weekend, I packed my bags, my pups, and all of my things. With this man knowing where I lived, and having failed to land a new client who wouldn’t rather date or stalk me, I told my landlord my situation and asked to break my lease.

I’ve moved many times in my adult life, alone, a total of six times across the country. The home I was renting was a quaint cottage, but it was my favorite home so far. And while I’ve been emotionally conditioned to pack up and start anew, this time I didn’t want to move. Thankfully, I’ve had amazing friends by my side through this chaotic journey, and as I placed all my belongings in temporary storage, I felt more okay with them by my side.

What now? Now… I’m literally at my safe house in a remote location. I’m off the grid with my dogs, enjoying writing, seeing the stars at night through an unpolluted sky, and breathing fresh air that doesn’t smell of homeless sewers and cheap Sauvage cologne.

As for work, I’m continuing my side hustle of ghostwriting and creating automated communication systems for companies. But my confidence in advising business owners and investors has drastically gone down.

This situation I’ve shared is just the most extreme example. I’ve ghosted several potential clients and blocked business owners over the course of this year alone. To be humble, as a beautiful young woman, I’m having a difficult time convincing prospects that I’d be a better business partner than a romantic partner.

I change what I wear, how I present myself. I’ve cut, dyed, and restyled my hair. I’ve tested different brands, different dialects, and different scenarios. I’ve avoided even non-taboo topics to try to shift my value in their eyes from beauty to business. I’ve even tried making myself purposefully ugly, for fuck’s sake.

Maybe it’s the cities I’m networking in, or that I’m shooting too low or too high—I’m not quite sure. But I do know I’m frustrated and over it. Hence, my pivot mid-spring into my full-blown diva creative self.

So here I am. I traded my favorite quaint cottage for a security system made of trees and silence. It’s a bitter trade, one that tastes like a nasty injustice sandwich. But I want to be clear: I’m not hiding just because I’m scared (well, I am, but that’s not the point). I am here because I am choosing a safe environment after the one I was in had continually proven it wasn’t. The protective order was a tool, not a solution, not a lightsaber or a magical shield. And when it failed, I had to become my own superhero.

For now, my office is a porch overlooking Mother Nature, and my only networking is with my dogs. This feels like a strategic repositioning. I won’t be hidden away here for too long; I think I might travel the country for a minute, or go visit a few friends I haven’t seen in a while.

The work of rebuilding my life may be slower than I’d like, but I know that whatever happens, I’ll end up in a better position than I could have imagined. Because a man may have taken my sense of safety in my home, but I’ll be damned if I let him take my voice, my business, or my beautiful future.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
