title: Rejections, Resumés, and the Return of Sheridan Guerrette
subtitle: Sheridan applies to a thousand jobs, reflects on power and purpose, and shares the preview of her newest song, Honey and Hay, a Hallmark Film-style love track born from her poetry notebook
body:
Let’s start where we left off. I’m officially at my second safe house, cat dander-free and thriving, and I’ve had so much time to think, write, try new things, and apply to roughly 1,000 jobs. But something peculiar has been happening, and I wonder if you’ve ever experienced this yourself: I can’t, for the life of me, get hired for a low-paying, entry-level position.

Now, I know. I’m the only Sheridan Guerrette in this world, and at least 700 of you already know that I am that bitch—F A M O U S—but still, I have not been able to land a single hostess or server gig since I was eighteen.

I’ve been here before. When my CEO suddenly passed away, I lost everything: a mentor, a paycheck, and a promising career. During that time, while applying for salaried roles, I sent out applications to every server, hostess, and front desk position imaginable just to keep my income flowing. I was denied left and right. I tried adjusting my resume and excluding any titles and responsibilities that might make a hiring manager feels small in comparison. Still, rejection.

Even at the intermediate level, it’s been the same story. One major nonprofit told me outright: “You’re too motivated. You’ll get a better offer soon.” And they were right about that. But what most people don’t understand about me is that my motivation has never come from money. (Shoes don’t count.) I’m driven by the desire to produce good work, for others, for a mission, for something that actually matters.

Give me $70,000 a year doing meaningful work over $250,000 doing something soulless.

Every. Single. Fucking. Time.

Maybe it’s just how I’m wired, but I’ve never understood how power and money make some people’s morals dim. For me, the opposite happens: the more power, the more money, the stronger my sense of responsibility becomes. Maybe it’s because I finally have the confidence and means to do something about things I witness or come across. Every story of challenge and triumph I’ve lived through has started the same way: my morals refused to stay on the sidelines. I had to step in, to make it right, to make it work, for everyone. I don’t care about credit or recognition; I care about fixing what’s broken.

So yes, I’ve applied to biker bars, regular bars, swanky bars, and everything in between. I’ve toned down the gold jewelry, relaxed my diva wardrobe, and even tailored each résumé to sound a little more… approachable. I even threw a bit of dumbness into one interview for good measure.

What I really want, though, is balance. To keep writing and help grow someone’s business, venture, or little corner of the world. Maybe that’s as a consultant, or maybe it’s behind the bar of a biker dive, honestly, I’d take either right now.

It’s just hard to pin down a résumé when you’ve been everywhere. For a minute, I had the itch to prove myself in every possible arena. I wanted to see if I could take what I know about business and drop it anywhere—startups, logistics, fashion, hospitality—and still make it work. And honestly? I did. But now I’m wondering if that little experiment has run its course. Maybe the quest continues, maybe it’s time I turn back to my true love, hospitality. I don’t know yet. But either way, I’ll be continuing to write to you every week.

Since being away from the city, I’ve written more poems than I can count. My nails aren’t even red (gasps). I’m wearing sweatpants and sweatshirts (I know—who am I?), and I’ve been diving deeper into my all-natural self.

As I told you before, I recently learned that my thousands of poems I’ve written over the years are organized into perfectly rhythmic formats. Well, I have around twenty fully finished demo songs, and there’s one in particular that I wrote, which is well... quite cheesy.

I won’t be pitching this song. It’s not Grammy material, but it’s maybe Hallmark gold. It’s the kind of song that plays quietly in the background of a farm-town romance flick. And honestly, I’m okay with that. Since I’m not pitching it, I’m releasing it under my name.

This song, Honey and Hay, was originally a poem, like all of my tracks. I wrote this when I was questioning whether or not I was meant to be in the city or the country. It’s definitely the city, but still, it’s a fun, cute song.

Itunes Link

Until next week, I’ll be writing, teaching myself to sing again, and exploring everything the world has in store for me. Maybe I’ll find the next version of myself somewhere between a love song and a job application, or perhaps I already have. Either way, I’ll keep chasing the kind of days that make good stories.

Whatever it is, I’ll be back here next week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

You deserve to feel safe walking into your grocery store, into your home, into your life. There are resources out there: the National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788), RAINN for sexual assault support (1-800-656-4673), and your local courthouse or legal aid office if you need to explore a protective order. title: So I'm Doing This Now
subtitle: A soft launch into my chaotic life, featuring dog meds, wrinkled wedding dresses, and one very sketchy nap.
body:
Hi there, I’m Sheridan.

I’m sick right now, so if this feels a little chaotic, it’s because my throat feels like crispy chicken tenders, and I’m writing this under five blankets with a mug of tea I’ve already microwaved twice. But I wanted to start this newsletter anyway… real-time, unfiltered, nothing polished. Just life as it’s happening.

So, what’s been going on?

My younger sister got married on April 11th. I drove from the East Coast to Minnesota with just me and my two dogs in the car. And no, I didn’t stop and get a hotel like my parents begged me to. I told them I would call when I was ready to stop for the night, and my dad would use his Hilton points; he has about a billion.

But if you know me… I didn’t call. I pulled over at a sketchy-ass truck stop in the middle of nowhere, took a three-hour nap, and woke up to frantic texts from my mom saying, “I hope you’re just snoozing at a sketchy truck stop and not dead.”

And honestly? It worked out. I woke up, still in the driver’s seat, in driving position, ready to go. No check-out. No wasted time. I swear by it.

Traveling solo with two dogs is a full production. Shadow has epilepsy, so I always keep a small jar of peanut butter in my purse to sneak him his meds — nothing gets past him except peanut butter.

I’ve turned my car into a rolling dog lounge. Big hammock in the backseat, their favorite blankets, toys, and their dog beds. I keep two seatbelt clips, one up front and one in the back, so when they want to stick their heads out the window, they are seatbelted in, and I’m not having a heart attack thinking they’ll launch themselves into traffic.

I keep a to-go cup and water bottles on hand at all times, and their food rides underneath the hamper in the backseat legroom so it stays temperature-safe. Not in the trunk, it gets too hot or too cold. Everything has a place.

Everything has a backup plan. It’s chaos, but it’s controlled.

I stayed two nights at my little sister Sophie’s college house in Winona, Minnesota. It was me, two dogs, and a bunch of college girls. I haven’t been in college in an actual decade, so it felt kind of hilarious. I forgot how chaotic it is. Zero structure, random kitchen supplies, everyone’s sleeping schedules are scattered as if it’s a shift job they’re alternating. It was weirdly nostalgic — like stepping into a version of myself I barely remember.

Also: I packed way too many clothes. But how am I supposed to know what vibe I’ll feel in five days? Or five hours? I need options. Comfy, hot, casual-chic, mysterious but approachable… all of them had to come. I wore like four things total.

Then we headed north for the wedding. Sophie rode with me. It was in central-northern Minnesota at this beautiful venue surrounded by little cabins. We each had our own cabin next to the venue, and it felt like something out of a movie. I was a bridesmaid. Sydney was glowing. Hunter looked like he’d been waiting his whole life to see her walk down the aisle. The whole thing was peaceful, warm, and just really… great.

Of course, no wedding happens without a little chaos. I somehow ended up on my hands and knees, steaming my mother’s mother-of-the-bride dress like it was my full-time job. No one assigned it to me. I just assumed the role. It’s the eldest daughter in me, unpaid labor, and wrinkle removal.

There were a lot of people there from the small town I grew up in. Some I was really happy to see. A few, I fully avoided. Let’s leave it at that.

I did my own hair and makeup for the wedding, obviously. I don’t trust anyone else to match my face vibe, and to be honest, I have to be extremely picky. After modeling throughout my teens and early twenties, my skin reacts to just about everything. It’s overly sensitive now, and I’ve learned the hard way that most products either make me break out or break down emotionally. So I’m meticulous.

Everything has to be clean, minimal, and non-irritating, and if it’s scented? Absolutely not.

I didn’t use concealer because I react to almost every single one I’ve ever tried. Instead, I went with BareMinerals’ Complexion Rescue Tinted Moisturizer, which gives me just enough coverage to look alive without suffocating my face. To finish it off and cut the shine, I layered on NYX’s Can’t Stop Won’t Stop mattifying powder — it’s one of the only powders I’ve found that holds without turning into chalk.

For hair, I kept it simple. I sectioned it into four horizontal layers and curled it with a half-inch barrel, one piece at a time. Once everything cooled, I sprayed it, gently brushed it through with a wide-tooth comb, gave it a shake, and then sealed it all with Aveda’s Air Control light-hold hairspray. It held up through wind, humidity, and bridal party chaos without turning crispy or stiff. I felt like myself, just more photogenic.

After the wedding, I drove to Tennessee to stay at my parents’ house for a few days. I was barely unpacked before I realized I was sick. My throat’s been killing me, I have no voice, and I’ve mostly been curled up in bed trying to drink enough tea to survive.

The good news is that my dogs are thrilled to be here. They have a huge yard, no city sidewalks, and no leashes. And honestly, it’s kind of perfect timing. If I had to be sick, I’m glad it’s here and not in our East Coast home with a very small backyard.

I was hoping to drive back tomorrow, but I’m not sure that’s happening. I feel like trash. So we’ll see. Maybe Friday. Maybe when I can talk without sounding like a dying Victorian child.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Some Things Are Easy
subtitle: Some things are easy. // I say that a lot— // life is easy, // and I mean it // when the room is quiet.
body:
Some things are easy.
I say that a lot—
life is easy,
and I mean it
when the room is quiet.

But other things—
the things with teeth,
a smile, and always something chipper to say.
I keep them under glass.

Those are hard.
The chains I put them in.
But I can’t let them out.
It’s a glass floor I pretend isn’t there.

Like softening corners
before corners cut me.
Like holding one thought
without letting it burn the house down.
Like recognizing who loves me
before they leave.

I’ve never known how to pick a friend.
They flicker like electricity—
I forgot to pay the bill,
but I also forgot to check on them.

What I was supposed to do
drives by, egging my home,
a reminder I’m not spirited enough.
I had no “Prom” night.
So every day they throw spirit like it’s mine.

Sometimes it’s fluorescent,
suburban joy that drives by.
They raise their hands and wedge in a smile—
I don’t wave.
I never learned how.

Instead, I win.
Different games.
They say, the harder ones.
But I can see these rules.

I walk into rooms and shadder them open,
yet I don’t know how to sit
with soft hands
and let the day hold mine.

The world is simple,
except when it isn’t.
And when it isn’t,
I close the latch and lock it with a key.

I disappear into work like it’s holy.
And every night I come home
to a house built like a chapel—
my footsteps echo on glass,
the floor polished clear
so even I can see God’s regret
reflected back at me.

Below it, the basement breathes—
faint and warm, something’s still alive.
Prom dresses in plastic.
Silverware set for ghosts.
A voice that knew when to ask, “Are you okay?”

Friendships slowly wilt as lilies in a vase,
milestones wrapped in dust while suffocating
from ribbons I’ve tied too tight.
I walk across it,
toes curled against thoughts of beneath—
Everything, not to look.

But when I fall,
I fall harder than the coffee.
My knees hit first.
Then my hands, pressed to the glass,
as if I might pray
to what I locked beneath me.

I was already beneath myself,
pressed against regret.
Staring into the sealed room
where the world’s wished versions of me
rot politely in corners.

I forget how to keep the doors closed.
Soon all I taste is metal.
I’ve bitten down too hard
on what I’ve always swallowed.

It is easy.
And it is not.
And I don’t know how to hold both open—
the door, and my breath—
without cutting both hands open.

s.g

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
The Official Poetry Collection of WSS

title: Starting Multiple Ventures At Once… And It’s Not Burning Me Out
subtitle: Why breaking every “focus on one thing” rule feels sane for this perfectionist workaholic; plus the real update on my books, screenplay, and secret projects
body:
I have been so incredibly busy building several different ventures at once. And I know exactly what you’re probably going to say, “Sheridan, your entire business blog is talking about how to exactly not do that and not burn out!”

While that is true… it also isn’t true…

I know that we like to provide ourselves, especially entrepreneurs, with rules in society to keep our sanity. And the level of gurus out there speaking out all the measurable constants your energy, your sleep, and your dedication need to consistently rest at is, well, overwhelming and certainly unhelpful.

Reminder: Artists are entrepreneurs.

In none of my previously posted pieces have I stated direct numbers for us to consider what is sane or insane for our productivity and sanity. If I have, please call me out — respond with a screenshot so we can both call myself a dumbass together, or I will call you a dumbass in return for sending something that doesn’t actually qualify.

I do believe that you can begin multiple ventures all at once. Just like you can have three new friends versus just one.

The other day, somebody said, well, not directly to me, but I responded in my own head, so I’ll share it with you here now — “I can’t imagine managing 1,000 people.” Immediately, I rebutted aloud in my head, “I can.”

My rebuttal wasn’t just because I do have experience overseeing a thousand people at one time; hospitality can do that for an executive. But it was because I am the type of brain that, unfortunately, must understand something at a small, medium, and large frame in order to feel like I know anything at all. Therefore, management and business were something I dove into very early on; in textbook readings, in my college classes, and in all my positions throughout my career.

What I think most people don’t understand is that managing twenty people at an exceptional level is no different than managing a thousand. When you’re running a team of twenty or fewer, your operational structure and the little holes in efficiency will not be as bright or as costly. But if you take that exact same management and operational system to a team of a thousand, the cracks, holes, and costs in efficiency will no longer be small; they are seen, often very easily.

As a manager, a lifelong team athlete, and a champion of new business, it kinda is the same, managing a team of twenty and a thousand. It’s the same only when the team of twenty has the management, the trust, the foundation, the training, and the efficiency to expand. That’s when it becomes the same in a team of a thousand.

So as a fellow perfectionist, a workaholic, and overall team player and leader, I have looked at management, operations, and building at such small, medium, and expansive frames, because without doing that, I wouldn’t feel confident or knowledgeable at all.

That is never to say there isn’t a frame I may have missed, or a little speck in the paint I didn’t know about. My perfectionism loves new information. But it’s to say that just as you can manage and operate a team of twenty or a thousand, you can start one or multiple ventures at the same time.

Today, March 18th, I’ve spent most of the day creating a new script — which I can’t reveal anything about yet — and revising another script. So I’ve simply been ranting and trying to explain to you why it’s okay, and rather sane of me, to start multiple ventures at once. I suppose I should fill you in on some of this information and validation regarding the multiple projects, huh?

There are two things I cannot specifically mention right now, but I’ll spill all the details that I can, okay?

I haven’t been as actively scouting for locations for my short film that is ready with a team prepped, because I have been swamped with new work.

My What Sheridan Said: Season One book is officially ready for printing and publishing. But oh my goodness, who knew little Miss Sheridan the Great could be so demanded by the world? So, I am currently negotiating and debating which publishers and printing companies to use.

I have two other books that I wrote several years ago. One is a fiction mystery aiming towards young adults, and the other is an economics textbook on the morals of thrifting — lol. As I have these ready to go, I want What Sheridan Said: Season One — Memoir of the Modern Heroine to be the first thing that is published. So, babe, I’m working on it. It will be here soon.

I’m still carving out my next poetry book, the big one that will include over 150 original poems, compared to the 35-plus that one very special original poem in the limited edition book that’s currently taking pre-orders.

Creating a full poetry book takes a tremendous amount of time, let me tell you! Phew.

Also, I was supposed to be on a few podcasts, but I unfortunately had other things pop up in the way. I suppose that is the one downside to building multiple ventures at once. But in reality, it prompts me to focus even more on what is valuable to my time and the growth of what I’m trying to achieve.

I’m crossing all my fingers and my toes that I will have more news about my new publications and ventures next week. I’m hustling, baby, I promise!

In other terms, life has been a lot more normal lately; minimal chaos, and it’s been slow with routine. I’m answering and sending too many emails, and I’m writing at a consistent level between ghosting for others and working on my portfolio pieces. But I’ve also been a bit stagnant. In that, I’m home or at work. I’m between my dogs, my loved ones, and work. There isn’t much else that has been filling my time, besides the casual free time of trash TV and playing tennis when the sun decides to be kind.

After years of running all different types of companies, managing anywhere from twenty to a thousand people, and chasing extremes in the name of getting better, this season feels like deliberate, grounded expansion. I’m applying everything I’ve learned about scalable systems, but now in the service of creative work that lights me up.

So with my new stack of normalcy, and starting at not the extremes in a brand new industry, I find myself content and happy.

I’m working on new things, I’m dabbling in multiple ventures at once, and I’m prioritizing my time to the level of value and achievement it will bring towards my sanity and my future.

title: Stay 50 Feet Away at All Times
subtitle: A protective order, a tired girl, and the reality so many of us carry in silence.
body:
I wanted to start off this week’s episode by acknowledging everyone who missed me, messaged me, supported me, and showed kindness during my few weeks away from you. I’ve been quite off, both professionally and personally, and during these past few Wednesdays, I wasn’t quite sure what to say to you, or what I could say to you.

For someone who does not hold a law degree, I, for one, have seen the courthouse too often this past month for my taste.

I have a court-ordered emergency protective order, and if you were to tell me this would be happening today, a month ago, I would probably smirk, laugh, and walk away. But here we are, just a girl with a judge-signed paper saying, ‘creepy man stay 50 feet away at all times.’

So how did we get here? Well…, as some of you know, professionally I’ve been an advisor to founders, business owners, and investors for some time now, and I was at a networking event around the DC area, looking for another potential client, or just looking to chat with others in the industry.

The networking event was at a nice, casual place with some outdoor and indoor areas. For security reasons, I won’t name the restaurant, but to say the least, there were around 40 attendees at the event.

When I arrived, I did my usual routine: scan the room, grab a drink, and introduce myself to a few people. That’s when I first met him. He was polite enough at first, said he was interested in my background, and asked for my card. We talked for maybe five minutes, surface-level, nothing memorable, and I moved on.

The next morning, I had an email from him. He framed it like he was interested in hiring me. His words were professional enough; he mentioned his company, referenced our conversation, and said he wanted to set up a time to discuss further. I replied back, thinking it was just another lead, another potential client.

But after that? Silence. No follow-up. No scheduling. Just… nothing.

Then, a couple of days later, I got a DM from him on Instagram. Something I had never given him. The message was not business-related—it was inappropriate. Nothing outright threatening, but definitely crossing the line. I didn’t respond. I didn’t even open it fully.

That should have been the end of it. But a week later, I went out with friends to a close neighborhood bar, and who shows up? Him. He wasn’t in my circle, from what I remember, not a member of this neighborhood, and yet somehow there he was. He tried to approach me, but my friends, who might as well lowkey double as my security team, blocked him and sent him away. I slipped out without giving him any attention, and we left as a group.

I didn’t think I’d hear from him again.

I was wrong.

The next morning, I ran into him at my local Trader Joe’s. A place I’ve shopped at every other day for a year, where I know the staff by name. He acted like it was a coincidence, tried to talk to me again. I brushed it off, told myself it was weird, but maybe random.

Until it happened again.

And again, at the same Trader Joe’s. The next few times, I avoided him at all costs.

Then I stopped going to Trader Joe’s, and I went to Giant instead. A day later, I see him outside my house. Then, the messages—they kept coming, kept getting stranger, and more dangerous. Texts this time, harassing, threatening, escalating. It was no longer about “wanting to see me” or “why didn’t I respond.” It turned into intimidation. Into anger that I wasn’t willing to give him my attention.

At that point, I knew this wasn’t something I could handle by myself. I went to the courthouse. I explained what had happened. I showed the messages, explained the encounters, and documented the pattern. And that’s how I ended up with a judge signing off on an emergency protective order.

Because sometimes, things don’t stop on their own. Sometimes, you need it in writing: stay away, crazy man!!!

Going through the process of getting a protective order has unfortunately awakened me to the news that most women I know, or randomly come across, also at some point had to get a protective order. It’s been a blessing in disguise to learn so early that I’m not alone in this situation. I’d rather this not be a common trend among the random beautiful women I meet throughout my day. So I digress, I’m tired. I’m tired of individuals in society who don’t understand that their speech, actions, and desires in this world are not just, not moral, and do not align with the values they are willing to bring to the table, to the partnership, to the working relationship, to the friendship, to society.

As for me? I’m still awkwardly trying to push my life forward, still working ‘dedicatingly’ hard, and I’m still yearning for something new. I’m not sure what the new is yet, whether it’s a new hobby, friend, hell, maybe even another dog (no, three is too much, I don’t need to be a crazy dog lady), but I will find it, even if it’s delayed a few weeks by Miss Sheridan handling BIZNASS.

To everyone reading this, I hope this sheds some light on how common things are, how unsafe most cities and surrounding areas are, and to everyone dealing with a similar situation, I hope you understand that you are not alone.

So, this is where I’ve been. I’ve been mentally fighting a battle, angry that I couldn’t share all of this with you in real time, and on top of that, do you remember the T-shirt I designed and told you to buy? Well, hell, I’m so glad you didn’t because mine came in, and I was getting ready to take photos to share with you so you could see how cute it is, but my god, that thing was so ugly. I set it on fire.

I’ll be removing the cropped tee from my online store soon. My life has just been absolutely insane this past month. But I’m so happy to be back with you, writing every Wednesday, sharing my week, my drama, and my life with you.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: The Cat, the Cabin, and the Claritin
subtitle: In her latest hideout, Sheridan faces betrayal, bugs, and a cat with mob-boss energy, all while trying to stay alive, glam, and on brand.
body:
When I left the city last week, I thought I was escaping chaos. I packed my life into storage, drove off with my dogs, and told myself this was a fresh start, a retreat, a spiritual cleanse, maybe even the soft-launch of a more peaceful, creative era. But here’s the thing: chaos is surprisingly portable. It fits neatly in the backseat next to a duffel bag and a half-empty Starbucks cup, and it has a nasty habit of following you no matter how far you drive. I’d left behind the man with the tracking app, the police reports, and the crumbling illusion that professionalism meant safety. What I hadn’t left behind was the exhaustion, the kind that seeps into your bones and makes silence feel like suspicion.

The safe house was deep in the woods, the kind of middle of nowhere where Google Maps gives up halfway down the road. It was small but charming in that “potential crime scene” way. The air smelled like pine and generational trauma. The stillness was so heavy it felt like the house was holding its breath with me. For the first twenty-four hours, I convinced myself it was peaceful. Then I realized peace wasn’t what I’d found. It was just a different kind of noise, one made up of insects with bad intentions and absolutely no respect for personal boundaries.

Within a day, I’d met creatures that I’m convinced do not exist in the scientific record. They were the kind of bugs that don’t just bite you; they make eye contact while doing it. One landed on my hand, stared me down, and I swear I saw God blink. Another had wings, teeth, and the confidence of a man with no car insurance. By day three, I’d stopped screaming and started negotiating. I am, as of this week, a bug diplomat. Please update my LinkedIn.

But the bugs were just the opening act. The real headliner was a black cat named Stephen. And when I say cat, I mean sentient landlord. He was tall, lean, and gave off the energy of someone who once owned a boat but lost it in the divorce. Every time I moved, he’d hiss, not aggressively, just enough to remind me I was on his property. He’d vanish for days and return with the same silent judgment as an IRS audit.

Now, I had been to this cabin before. I knew about Stephen. But somehow, in the mess of my move and my mental exhaustion, I forgot one crucial detail: I am violently allergic to cats. Twelve hours in, my lungs began to throw a tantrum, and my throat felt like it was trying to close for business. I was taking Claritin, three to five a day, washed down with resignation and coffee. My voice got raspier by the hour, which, admittedly, made me sound sexier (; , but the near-death part was less ideal.

Meanwhile, Stephen had decided his new hobby was psychological warfare. His main victim was Dino, my golden retriever/chihuahua, who has already declared war against the safe house’s tomcat. Stephen would sneak up in the middle of the night, tap Dino on the head, and vanish before Dino even opened his eyes. I’ve seen horror movies with less suspense. By 6 a.m., Dino and I were both traumatized and wheezing.

The air outside was merciful. I sat on the porch steps with both dogs, wrapped in a blanket, watching the sun make its slow, arrogant rise over the trees. For an hour, I just breathed, slowly. Inside, Stephen paced the windowsill like a mob boss checking his territory. I knew then that this wasn’t sustainable. I had to leave, for my breathing and for my sleep.

I went back inside, packed my things, and drove to safe house number two, farther out, cat-free, and, blessedly, bug-light. It’s been a few days now, and my breathing has returned to normal, which is to say I only choke on air when thinking about my career. I’ve been looking at local serving jobs, something simple and temporary. Nothing like being a hideaway waitress in a town where the only Wi-Fi is in a Cracker Barrel.

But it’s peaceful here. The quiet doesn’t feel eerie anymore; it feels deserved. I still lock the doors twice and check the windows three times, but the air feels different, cat-free, breathable, but also safer somehow, or maybe just unfamiliar enough to trick my body into relaxing. I don’t know how long I’ll stay or where I’ll go next, but I do know this much: as soon as the dust settles and I am no longer this strange man’s obsession, I’m going back to my life. My glam, high-heeled, positively chaotic life, the one where I belong.

Until then, I’ll be the most overdressed, overly perfumed woman this side of whatever county I happen to be hiding in has ever seen. Sequins at the grocery store, lipstick for no one but myself, champagne in a mug if I have to. I might be off the grid, but I refuse to go off-brand. If I’m going to be in hiding, I’ll be hiding in style. 💋

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: The Spy, the Storm, and the Slam I Didn’t Perform
subtitle: I almost read a poem. I definitely spun like a tornado. My dad made the news. And no, I’m not a spy (but thanks for asking).
body:
I was supposed to perform at a poetry slam this week. I had the piece. I had the dress. I had the nerve—until I didn’t. I was sitting in the second row, staring at the sign-up sheet like it had teeth. And then I chickened out.

But here’s why I’m glad I did.

The night opened with a local legend who’s been hosting these slams longer than some of us have been out of high school. He said something like, “Read the room,” and I did. What followed was one of the most profound nights of poetry I’ve ever witnessed.

The night was beautiful. Emotional. Transformative. A man who had recently been released from prison after 35 years—sentenced as a kid—stood up and shared work that felt like survival. He read poems that they wish someone had written to them when they were 14. It was devastating. It was healing. It was everything poetry should be.

Each person, one after the other, all with the most inspiring stories to share, got up and read the kind of poems that make you forget if you were inhaling or exhaling. Poems about the paths they walked, the violence they endured, and the wisdom they now write for the teenage versions of themselves. It was sacred. The whole night felt that way. The kind of sacred that doesn’t need a pulpit.

And I realized, my story, my trauma, valid as it is, wasn’t meant to compete with theirs. That night wasn’t mine to interrupt. It was mine to witness.

So I sat there for several hours, as one of the very few white people in the room, listening, understanding, and learning. Feeling everything. I was honored to be in that space. And as it ended, I walked out with even more respect for the kind of poetry that isn’t written for publication, but written for survival.

I didn’t perform because I didn’t need to. Because it wasn’t about me. And I don’t say that with self-deprecation, I say that with reverence, with the understanding that presence, when it’s quiet, and respectful, and intentional, is sometimes more sacred than spotlight.

That night reminded me of what poetry is at its core. Not a performance. Not a brand. Not even an art form. It’s a lifeline. It’s your truest version asking for help, for guidance, for clarity. It’s the thing you write when no one’s coming to save you, but somehow the writing saves you anyway.

And I’m better for hearing it.

That said, don’t worry. I’ll be back on stage. As you know, I’ve got thousands of poems to read, but I’ll know when my moment’s right.

In other news, someone found my burner phone again and asked—half joking, half dead serious—if I was a spy.

It’s not the first time. Every man I’ve dated, multiple friends, and now even random acquaintances have asked if I work for the CIA. I guess having multiple phones and encrypted emails makes people suspicious. But it’s not espionage—it’s just anxiety and a serious habit of keeping my private life private. If I were a spy, I’d be the worst one. You caught me. And I’d still deny it.

The truth is, my whole life trained me to move like a ghost. I spent long stretches in total isolation, not for fun, but because it was safer. I didn’t go to prom. I skipped college. I was managing people twice my age while my peers were sneaking into bonfires. And when you live like that long enough, you build boundaries like fortresses. I’m not antisocial, I’m just… unbothered.

People think I’m mysterious. I’m not. I’m just tired. I don’t want to explain myself. I don’t want to small-talk. I don’t want to play the part of “relatable girl” who lets people all the way in. I’ve spent years building a rich internal world. Sometimes, forever forgetting I’m supposed to invite people inside.

And while that solitude shaped my art, it also dulled my social skills. Or maybe not dulled—just rerouted them. I lead better than I collaborate. I monologue better than I chat. I love people, I do. I’m just very selective about whom I let interrupt the quiet I worked so hard to earn.

Also, let’s talk about my dad. The legend.

After a destructive storm swept through his little country town, my dad was the guy who showed up. Literally. He rallied neighbors, coordinated recovery efforts, and had the entire community back on its feet faster than the local government could blink. He’s now a local news story, town celebrity, and general badass (he always was).

FULL ARTICLE

The world needs more people like my dad. People who don’t wait to be asked. People who show up with a chainsaw and a group of dads ready to slash fallen trees!

Speaking of wild things, I also went indoor skydiving.

I thought I was going to pee myself. Like, no joke. I was so nervous that the instructors kept checking on me. My face apparently screamed this girl is about to lose it. But I held out. I waited. I studied everyone else’s technique. And when it was my turn, I stepped into that tunnel like a bat out of hell and held the strongest air plank of my life.

Then I spun. Like, violently. Apparently, I invented a new move. They called it “The Tornado.” I’m choosing to take that as a compliment. A metaphor, even. Uncontrolled, uncontainable, and somehow graceful in my chaos.

It’s fitting, really. I’ve never been the quiet breeze type. I enter things sideways, spin too fast, and leave people wondering what just happened—but somehow, I still land it.

Eventually.

That’s what this season feels like. A tornado with intention. I’m not trying to be still. I’m trying to move on purpose. Even if that movement looks like fear, like nerves, like spinning until I forget which way is up. Because somewhere in that chaos, I found clarity. I found a thrill. And I’d rather be flailing in flight than stuck on the ground pretending not to want it. And finally, a quick poetry update:

I’ve been writing. A lot. Most days, I crank out two or three poems. Most of them get cut. However, it’s been a consistent one outstanding poem per day. One-third isn’t too shabby, and at this rate, maybe I’ll already have my second and third collections ready by the time this one is published.

I’ve crossed 130 finalized poems now. The goal is 200. I know, you’re probably saying, “Sheridan, that’s a lot, you need to chill out.” Umm, what if I don’t want to? Most of the recent poetry books I’ve seen released are between 120 and 200 pages, so yes, I’ve made the cut. But the general cut isn’t Sheridan’s cut, okay? She’s a little hard on herself. So… I want extras—for the what-ifs, for the “this just can’t leave,” or the last-minute “I need to burn these twenty poems to the grounds of hell before they are public knowledge.”

Because here’s the thing: I’m not just writing for print, I’m writing for permanence. This collection is generations of art disguised as literature. And I want the final version to hit like the family secret you’re not supposed to know, the kind that stays with you whether you want it to or not. So if that means triple the drafts, late-night edits, or dragging poems through emotional purgatory before they’re allowed to exist on a page, so be it.

I’m not trying to be your favorite poet; I’m trying to be unforgettable.

And let’s be honest, I’ve never done anything halfway. Why would I start now? These poems aren’t just confessions. They’re timestamps. They’re proof. Of who I was, what I’ve witnessed, what I survived, and how I learned to tell the story before someone else tried to. So if the book ends up being thick enough to stop a bullet, good. Maybe it was meant to.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
WhatSheridanSaid.com

title: The Truth I’ve Been Swallowing for Years
subtitle: I was emancipated at 17, ghosted by my own blood, and raised by the fire of starting over. This is my beginning.
body:
A lot of things about me, my story, what’s happened, and what I sometimes still deal with are things I’ve kept hidden. Hidden from the world. Hidden from the people closest to me. Maybe because I’ve cared more about the scarcity of their story than the right to tell my own. Maybe I’ve cared too much about them and not enough about my own need to selfishly, unapologetically express who I am.

I am an expressive, creative person. Always have been. And I’m finally ready to embrace the chaos that’s shaped me. To share it all, even if it causes discomfort for the ones involved. Starting with my family.

I’m the black sheep. That title isn’t a metaphor; it’s a full-time role. Things were sometimes rocky, and I actually cut off my parents for five years. One day, everything had exploded, and I just… walked away.

It was hard, moving to Washington, D.C., on my own. But my parents always knew I’d leave. I had aspirations bigger than anything they could offer, demanding by age eight that everyone call me “Sheridan The Great.” So I was emancipated at 17, my parents sold my car to buy my sister a nicer one, and left me alone in a city that didn’t know me.

I made it work. I fought harder than anything for the career I wanted. But I was naive. I was alone. I didn’t get calls from my family, not even to ask how I was. My mom would call, but only every six months or so. And even then, it wasn’t about me. The calls usually ended with her saying, “I need you to contact me every day so I know you’re not dead from a terrorist attack.”

Eventually, I stopped calling my siblings. Due to a lack of answering, except for one sister. Though she and I never had a great relationship, I kept trying. In high school, I was such a social pariah that even she wouldn’t hang out with me, unless I paid her. Paid for her mall clothes, paid for her movie tickets, on top of giving her cash for simply being near me. When I moved away, our relationship became one-sided. I’d have to call. I’d have to perform. Play dumb, so she and her friends could laugh at me. And later, on a family vacation, she pretended to be sick just to avoid me. At that point, I had reached my limit, hoping that now we are both adults, it would be different. It wasn’t, and I was done.

A few months later, following the vacation, I was drowning in work in D.C. I told my family I couldn’t make it to my brother’s graduation party. It was the first time I’d let them down, and I spiraled. I mean full-blown panic attack. I turned off my phone for two hours just to catch my breath.

When I turned it back on, the first text I saw was from my dad saying, “Call me, or we are calling the police.”

And I thought, “You’ve called me how many times since I left?” We don’t have that kind of relationship. You emancipated me. You didn’t prepare yourselves for a daughter like me. You sent me off with no map, no compass, just the sheltered ideas of a family who didn’t understand what I needed.

So I didn’t call. I texted to say I was fine, that I couldn’t make it because of work. But that wasn’t enough. They convinced themselves it wasn’t me texting. Their first thought was that it was my “handler.”

Give me a fucking break.

They used control. They used threats. My mother hacked into my call logs and started contacting everyone I had spoken to. She told them I was being sold into sex trafficking. Or that I was dying of a thyroid disease. She begged them to tell her everything they knew about me.

I lost business clients, my friends were panicking calling me asking what the hell is going on. Then she changed my federal mailing address to hers.

A few weeks later, I took a well-earned vacation and flew to the Dominican Republic. During a layover in Miami, I was stopped in the airport by two police officers. “Ma’am, are you Sheridan Guerrette?”

“Yes… why?”

“We have a detective on the phone. He just wants to ask a few questions.”

”Is this necessary?”

”Maa’am, it’s just a few questions.”

They hand me the phone. I take it, press it to my ear, and it’s my mother. Screaming. No detective. No explanation. Just her voice, trying once again to get me to do more than message via text and Facebook.

If I hadn’t had the context, they might’ve arrested me for throwing a phone at two police officers. Because I fucking did. I tossed it back to the officers and stood firm, surrounded by a hundred strangers.

“That was not a detective. That was my mother. I was emancipated at 17. I am 21 years old. I have lived alone, paid my way, and built my life. She is not my guardian. Leave me alone.”

Everyone stared. The whole terminal froze.

Welcome to the Sheridan show.

It took five years of distance and unlearning to get to the place we’re in now. And honestly, we have all grown since then. I’m proud of the

progress we’ve made. The boundaries are strong. But it took years.

I remember trying to sit them down when I was 20, explaining that I won’t come home if I’m expected to follow a curfew of 10 pm. I told them I understood — they didn’t get the usual college transition, where I’d come home for summers or holidays. That never happened. I skipped college and jumped straight into my career. I was ready. I was educated. But they never prepared themselves for how to have a daughter like me, and nothing I could say would change that.

Those years were hard. There were times I needed my mom. I needed my dad. But the trust was gone, and the silence felt safer. I chose being alone over being controlled. And somehow, that choice brought me closer to who I really am. To who I had to be.

For a while, I only talked to my parents through Facebook Messenger. I didn’t want them to have my number; I’m sure you understand after that fiasco. If they sent something kind, something not ‘manipulative,’ I’d respond. I told them where I lived, worked, and who I even dated. Despite the version they told neighbors and distant family, I never ghosted. I communicated. I just did it on my terms.

I guess the reason my life has been private is that I try to hold myself to a high standard. I stand by my choices. Every single one of them. But the people around me haven’t always done the same. And for a long time, I didn’t know how to live out loud while also protecting myself from their decisions.

Things with my parents are better than I could have imagined. Though even when we’re all in the same room, I still feel like I’m not really there. I’m the eldest. The big sister. But I don’t feel like one of them. Maybe I’m not “Guerrette” enough. Or maybe… I’m just too much.

So, that’s how I’m feeling this week.

I’m in the mood to cut the leashes and be honest about who I am. About what I’ve survived. There are stories I’ll never share. But there are others, like this one, that might be exactly what someone needs to hear.

Because if I can be “too much” and still make it, so can you.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: The Universe Keeps Leaving Its Abandoned Things on My Doorstep
subtitle: A week of rescuing puppies, interviewing companies who weren’t ready for me, and remembering why love is Plan B and purpose is Plan A.
body:
I should warn you in advance that the universe appears fully committed to casting me as some wandering patron saint of misplaced dogs, because somehow, honestly, I don’t know how this keeps happening to me.

I found another puppy, this tiny German Shepherd mix with ears still too heavy for her head and an umbilical cord scab that tells me she hasn’t been alive long enough to understand that humans sometimes do the cruellest things without hesitation.

She was down by the creek behind the house, wedged between the brush and water as if she was debating which direction to run in that would hurt less. And of course, in the way my life has always unfolded, she looked at me with that little face, half hope, half apology, and my entire body responded before my brain could even negotiate options.

She glued herself to me instantly, tucked behind my ankles like she’d known me her whole life, and every time a car passed or the wind moved wrong, she pressed her entire weight against my calves as if she believed I was the final safe place on earth. Shadow, predictably, is already competing for custody of my lap, performing his dramatic wedge maneuver by planting his thirty-something pounds directly between us, shoulder first, sighing with that theatrical exasperation that only dogs, and insecure men, seem to master. Dino, my other pup (Golden Retriever/Chihuahua), is thrilled, though “thrilled” for him is somewhere between confusion and blind enthusiasm; he was grown in a lab, not a womb, so everything in his life feels like an experiment he’s participating in without informed consent.

But the baby, she’s soft in the way only frightened animals are soft, the kind of softness that presses itself into the crease of your knee and refuses to look up, afraid that if she lifts her face the world will rearrange itself back into the moment it abandoned her. I took her to the front yard, let her watch children on bikes and strollers rolling past, and other dogs being walked by parents who don’t yet realize their children will soon be adults who ask complex questions at inopportune hours, and still she would not take more than six inches of distance from my feet. And the moment a car approached, even one she couldn’t see or hear, she ran for me so quickly her paws scraped the concrete. That’s how I know she wasn’t homeless. She wasn’t wandering. She was dropped, left, and removed from the center of someone’s life without explanation. Some fears settle into the muscles before they ever reach the tongue, and she moved with that quiet, trembling knowledge.

This isn’t the first time I’ve stepped into the middle of someone else’s irresponsibility, nor the last. Houston gave me two Great Pyrenees puppies trapped on a second-story balcony in heat so thick it felt like being waterboarded. Those dogs were panting themselves into exhaustion, no shade, no water, and a nineteen-year-old owner who didn’t understand that double-coated dogs can’t cool themselves by sweating, that they were built for snow banks and northern air, not concrete that bakes to 140 degrees by noon. Their umbilical cords were infected, riddled with worms and fleas, and I remember thinking how strange it was that a species built for mountains and snow was suffocating in a city that didn’t care enough to learn the basics of their biology. I carried them out myself, told the kid plainly that I was taking his dogs, marched them straight into a vet clinic, and later drove them across the country to Minnesota, where snow breeds actually belong, to homes that would love them, to a place where the seasons still mean something.

Sometimes I think rescuing is just what my hands know how to do. Not because I’m good, but because I am physically incapable of walking past suffering without feeling like the air has been stolen out of my lungs. I rescue until my arms are tired, until my mind is tired, until I’ve redistributed whatever tenderness I have left so something else, someone else, can go on breathing a little easier.

And in the midst of all of this, the job interviews came and went like little tests of intention, each one its own small theater of confusion and opportunity. I won’t share details the way I normally might because I don’t trust spoken plans; they evaporate too easily. But I can tell you this much: I felt steady in myself, the way I do when I know I am speaking from the place where logic and instinct braid into certainty. I care about systems, about structure, about analytics that actually measure impact and not vanity; I care about whether a company knows what it needs or if it’s simply hiring because someone told them it was time to grow. Most companies don’t know. They think they do, but the gap between intention and comprehension is wider than anyone wants to admit.

So I interviewed them back. I asked them questions they weren’t expecting because I’ve sat at enough executive tables to know when something is missing, when a company is reaching for the wrong solution, when a startup is trying to hire an operations person, when what they really need is someone who can reengineer the entire internal skeleton they didn’t realize was crooked. And I felt proud of myself, not because I performed perfectly, but because I didn’t shrink. I didn’t pretend to know less than I do. I didn’t withhold the clarity that has taken me years and entire lifetimes of mistakes to earn.

I’ve never been driven by money for its own sake; I’m driven by meaning, by impact, by the kind of purpose that outlives a paycheck. Give me my expenses covered and one luxury shoe a month, and I’ll be fine, because the real value is in what you can build, what you can extend, what you can open for other people. Resources matter more than wealth. Knowledge matters more than salary. And when you understand that—truly understand it—the world rearranges itself around the quality of your intention.

Which brings me, reluctantly, to the truth that gets me in trouble the most: men are my Plan B. It’s not a joke, not some feminist stance or rejection of softness, it’s just the architecture of my life. I am a mother to two dogs, one special needs and one emotionally confused; I’ve lived most of my adult life in solitude, whether chosen or forced, and I am comfortable there in a way that frightens people who think companionship is proof of worthiness. The company I accept is exceptional because my solitude is exceptional. I don’t need a partnership to feel whole; I need alignment to consider sharing the space I built for myself.

My career, my mission, my eventual child—that’s Plan A. Adoption has always called to me extremely loudly. My dream was to be stable enough by thirty-five to take three to five years off and adopt a child who deserves a world much bigger than the one I grew up in. I don’t trust the American public school system. I don’t trust gatekept information. I don’t trust the careful curation of ignorance that was handed to me by the region, the culture, the system. I want my child to have access, not limitations. Opportunity, not containment.

And if a man cannot commit to that—to private school, to alternative education, to an ungatekept childhood—then he cannot commit to me. And therefore, he cannot commit to my children. I would rather raise a child alone with the full force of my ambition than raise one with someone who would diminish their world just because it’s cheaper, easier, or more common. I will not hand a child the smallness I had to break out of—the one shaped by geography and circumstance.

So yes, men are Plan B. But I should clarify: even the one I’m not letting myself overthink does not outrank the life I’m building, not because he is unworthy, but because I am Plan A. And the truth is, if he ever knew that, if he ever understood how rare it is for me to soften even a fraction of an inch toward someone, he might realize that being Plan B in my life is still more sacred than being Plan A in most people’s.

So here I am: rescuing dogs, interrogating startups, trying to decide where to plant myself next, writing too much, sharing more than I ever thought I would, letting you in slowly, deliberately, in the way someone like me only can, one layered truth at a time.

And maybe that’s the real thread of all of this—the rescuing, the questioning, the interviewing, the uprooting, the rebuilding. Maybe everything I’ve done this year has been one long attempt to protect whatever small part of the world still feels soft to me. Whether that softness takes the shape of a trembling puppy or a career I refuse to compromise or a future child who deserves a bigger world than the one I had, the instinct is the same: I move toward what needs shelter, and I move away from anything that tries to convince me that smallness is safety. I don’t believe in shrinking. I don’t believe in settling. And I don’t believe in pretending that I don’t want more, not more money, but more meaning, more intention, more resonance in the bones of my life.

I think that’s why I’m so careful now, why I’ve become almost deliberate to the point of secrecy when choosing the people I let orbit me. When you’ve lived most of your life in solitude, the smallest shift in someone’s energy feels seismic. You notice things others overlook—who flinches at responsibility, who rises to it, who meets you where you are, and who simply marvels from a distance because they’ve never learned how to step closer without trembling. People assume solitude makes you lonely, but I’ve found the opposite: solitude teaches you how to recognize real connection when it appears, not because it announces itself loudly, but because it arrives quietly and consistently, without forcing you to compromise any part of yourself. And in that way, the people I choose, even the one I’m trying not to think too deeply about, matter not because I need them, but because I recognize a softness in them that echoes something inside of me.

As I figure out where to go next, how to rebuild a life that has been dragged through more extremes than any one person should reasonably endure in a single year, I’m not rushing, I’m not forcing anything. I’m letting each day unfold with the same intuition that led me to every dog I’ve ever rescued and every crossroads I’ve ever walked toward with shaking hands but steady feet. I know that whatever corner of the world becomes mine next will make itself known in its own time, just like the people who are meant to be there when I get there. For now, I’m doing what I’ve always done: caring, choosing, building, observing, loving in my own strange way, and staying tethered to the kind of life that feels warm in the center of my chest.

Until next week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: This Is What Happens When You Don't Stay Small
subtitle: I Was Supposed to Disappear. Instead, I Made Headlines.
body:
There’s something surreal about becoming the main character in a place that hoped you’d quietly disappear. Some of you reading this may remember me from somewhere: the field, the fashion runway, the ballot, a random bar in a random coastal country, school, work, maybe the whispers, or a fallout. Or maybe you just recognize my name. Doesn’t matter.

Because this isn’t about you. It’s about me. And how I turned exile into empire.

But let’s zoom out for a second.

For the rest of you: Hi. I’m Sheridan. I’m a native Midwesterner with an adopted East Coast sass. I’m a writer, a founder, and soon a patented inventor. I once got knocked out cold on a soccer field by a team of girls who didn’t like that I told the truth about a coach. That was after I’d already switched schools. I’d already left the original one because they wanted to avoid a bullying lawsuit. After the girls I grew up with, who used to braid my hair and sleep over on weekends, turned cold and cruel the moment I stopped pretending to fit in.

By then, I’d already been the girl who was too ambitious, too expressive, too difficult to ignore. I was getting asked questions by adults that no teenager should have to answer. I was sitting in meetings meant for lawyers, defending my own safety like a junior attorney. I was scouted by modeling agents but was told, more times than I can count, that I was too fat, too short, too ugly.

I was designing business flyers for my first venture while other kids were sneaking into bonfires. I skipped prom and ran errands for seniors in my town instead. I dodged classmates in the Walgreens aisles like they were walking paparazzi landmines, legitimately snapping photos of me to post online for clout. I watched my mother lose the mayoral race by inches, again and again, and each time we got anonymous letters from town elders demanding we leave.

And by then, I had already survived enough whispers, side-eyes, and backhanded

compliments to last a lifetime. I left my hometown concussed, disillusioned, politically scorched, and still, somehow, undefeated.

When I first moved away, people were astonished by how gracefully confident I was in being myself, out loud for the world to see. I wasn’t afraid of being seen, judged, or perceived by any number of people. I found victory in sharing vulnerabilities, and used everything I went through as an honest badge worn on my heart and sleeve.

I wasn’t trying to prove anything other than that I am capable of anything I decide. I just knew that hiding had never protected me, so I stopped pretending it ever would. I shared my story before anyone could weaponize it. I aired the truths that others were too afraid to name. Vulnerability, for me, wasn’t weakness; it was armor. It was control. And it worked. I didn’t build my voice out of vanity; I built it because silence had nearly killed me.

And over time, I turned every insult, every dismissal, every rumor into material. Into fuel. Into proof. That I could survive a place that tried to bury me and still be kind-hearted. Still dangerous in my own way.

That’s the thing: they never expected me to stay soft. Or strategic. Or to reappear in their inboxes years later with a following, a company, a patent, and a platform. They never expected I’d make a life where my honesty, the very thing they tried to punish, would become my power.

Since then, I’ve built startups. I’ve closed them. I’ve built again. I’ve advised investors. I’ve led campaigns. I’ve closed runway shows and was the face of magazines, to then leave the modeling world behind. I’ve made it through things I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemy, and designed a life that no one thought I could have.

Now, I lead with that same honesty, because if I don’t, who else will?

I don’t write these things to impress anyone. I write because someone, somewhere, needs to hear it. Some girl or boy who’s just now realizing the cafeteria whispers are going to follow them into math class. Some young woman working a job that makes her question if speaking up is worth the backlash. Some kid who hasn’t yet learned that being different is a gift, because no one around them has survived enough to say it out loud.

I feel as though I have nothing to prove, and I’m finally letting myself rest. It feels powerful. In the stillness, I’m building again. Quietly. Strategically. With the kind of fire that doesn’t scream, more of a subtle simmer. I’m not telling you what I’m building. Not yet. But let’s just say: you’ll wish you had invested. I’m writing new poems and revisiting the thousands of old ones I have hidden away, to be published on my sites soon.

I’m not here to be palatable. I’m here to be proof. That you can walk away from a place that tried to shrink you, and never look back, except to wave and for the occasional wedding invite.

Because the truth is, I didn’t get here by playing nice. I got here by being cutthroat with the world about what I wanted and what I deserved. And that’s the most dangerous thing a woman can do, be fully herself, unwatered down, with a fucking plan.

The easy moments were rarely there. And still, some days when the weight of it all creeps in, I think about how many parts of myself I’ve had to fight to keep intact. I’m focused. I still care deeply. I still laugh too loudly. I still love way too hard. And I still believe there’s room for more, more of me, and what I have to share with you.

So now I live as if I owe it to every past version of myself who didn’t know if she’d make it out sane, and sometimes alive. I create for her. I work for her. I build for the girl who got knocked down eight times and still walked off the field with her name intact.

I lead for the ones coming up behind me. The ones who haven’t yet been bruised by the world, or who have, and are still figuring out how to rise. If I can leave a trail that makes their climb less lonely, I will. I already am.

That’s the plot twist. Not just that I made it, but that I’m not done. That I still write. That I still speak. That I still open doors, even the ones I’m told I’m not welcome through.

It was never just about making it out. It was always about making it matter.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: This Week I Drove 1,400 Miles and Cried in a Storage Unit
subtitle: How art dealers, fake résumés, and one very public panic attack humbled but not discontinued— my hot-girl era
body:
I drove back to the East Coast to check on my storage unit, grab a few warmer coats, and pick up a few shifts while I crash with friends. The plan was simple: a little serving gig to make some cash, maybe sell one of my paintings for a financial boost, and get a breather from the chaos of starting over. But life loves to humble me, and apparently, so does the economy.

The art market right now is absolute garbage. I have a lot of valuable work I’ve collected over the years, pieces I actually adore, but I figured I’d sell one I’m not totally in love with. Turns out a popular art dealer just held an entire auction of Vladimir Kush paintings three weeks ago, the same artist and signature as mine. So my timing was immaculate in the worst possible way. Life is funny like that: when the economy sucks, it doesn’t just suck financially— it sucks the joy out of beauty, too.

And yes, money doesn’t buy happiness. But financial stability? That buys sanity. Let’s not confuse the two.

Anyway, if you remember last week, I did, in fact, announce that I am F A M O U S, which is unfortunately still true. I used to be very well-known in my big, powerful city—everyone knew me whether they wanted to or not. Which is great when things are good, but not when you’re trying to quietly start over. So when I started applying for jobs again, I… left a few (okay, maybe a LOT) of details off my résumé. Nothing unethical, just enough to seem like a normal post-college girl trying to make rent and not a headline waiting to happen.

I landed an interview at a restaurant for a server position, in an area of the city I thought would know me a little less. A friend called in a favor. I showed up, hair tied back, minimal makeup, playing the part of someone who’d never been on the other side of the table before. I walk in, meet the general manager, and before I can even say “hi,” I can tell. She recognizes me.

Here’s the thing about hospitality: it’s a this side or that side industry. And I’ve always been on that side. Management, ownership, and the one who’s doing the hiring. So when you show up applying for a serving job, it’s like Kim Jong-un walking into Olive Garden asking for a W-2. The look on her face said it all.

I didn’t get the job.

I’ve had other offers since, but every one feels like it comes with strings. My career began as an assistant to a CEO and only went up from there— and as a young, beautiful, terrifyingly fertile woman, I’ve learned that ambition and attractiveness are apparently mutually exclusive. And yes, I could seek out female-led companies, and I do, but even that’s not foolproof. I mean, hell, I once had to cut off my college bestie after she tried scissoring me in my sleep and treating me like her sugar momma. Apparently, being hot and business-minded is most certainly a felony now.

In brighter news, though… I modeled again! I KNOW. It’s been forever since you’ve seen me in a magazine or on a runway, but this bad bitch (not an Instagram model, because I’m actually cool) is so back.

So, in preparation, they had my lashes done!

And yes, I know what you’re thinking—“Sheridan, your lashes are already perfect, why would you mess with them?” WELL, every other week, I am a complete dumbass who dyes her eyelashes at home using substances that could probably strip paint or kill your beloved cat. Also, black mascara and my sensitive skin don’t match; I look as if I just got off the field tackling someone. Which, by the way, I used to do. I played football as a kid—my nickname was The Beast. I once sacked a hefty boy who was nicknamed, The Fridge. I’ve been the same height and build since I was twelve. So whatever you’re picturing, yes, it’s correct.

I’m just a girl.

So before I lose my vision from harmful (and probably federally banned) chemicals, we got them done professionally. And now? They’re stunning. They feel so light, soft, and safe.

And maybe it’s poetic that my lashes finally look perfect while everything else feels like it’s falling apart. On that subject, let’s talk about panic attacks. I hate calling them that (it sounds too glittery), but that’s what they are. I don’t get them often, barely ever really— but when they come, they come hard. I haven’t had the most emotionally safe life; I dive into work every chance I get, and eventually, my body catches up and yells at me to take a couple of hours.

Last Wednesday was one of those nights. I’d had a brutal day, rejections, offers with strings, exhaustion, the kind of nothing-goes-right spiral— and I could feel it coming. I always can. It’s like this pressure building behind my ribs, the frog growing bigger in my throat, the cloud beginning to thunder in my head. I know I’ll need to be somewhere private soon, somewhere I can let it out for a few hours without disturbing anyone. But this time, I was staying at a friend’s house. And even though I tried to fight it, my chest started seizing like my ribs were trying to escape. I couldn’t breathe. Couldn’t stop crying. It looks like I’m dying and trying to apologize for it at the same time.

I hate being seen in that state and avoid it at most costs. It’s raw, messy, it’s human. When it was finally over, I didn’t feel enlightened or healed. I just felt emptied out. Like my body was saying, “See, I told you so.” My body basically had to short-circuit to remind me I’m still in here somewhere.

And maybe that’s what the past two weeks have been about, being reminded.

The art sale that didn’t happen, the job interview that went sideways, my white-trash-at-home lash care, all of it just pushing me back to the same truth I keep skipping over: I’m still rebuilding. I need people in my corner. I need to not go almost blind out of sheer determination to do everything myself. Sometimes the smartest thing you can do is call a friend, someone like Nande at Revenge Studios, because survival doesn’t always mean hustling harder. Sometimes it just means letting someone else take care of you for a few hours.

That’s what survival actually looks like. It’s not the highlight reel, it’s the messy rerun you didn’t plan to watch again but somehow keep replaying because the drama, the lesson, the truth, is just too good to skip.

And speaking of reruns, I’ve been bragging a lot lately about my poetry (as I should—Sheridan The Great Guerrette, American Writer and Poet). So I thought I’d give you a little taste. Over the past few weeks, I redid my website; it’s much prettier now, and it actually reflects what I’m working on: music, writing, everything alive and current. You’ll find more of my poetry there, but for now, here’s one that’s always stuck with me.

I wrote Lipped Pearls while in a strange, nostalgic mood. It’s about the performance of womanhood, the loneliness of it, the constant disappearing act. To me, it’s the quiet space between survival and self.

Lipped Pearls

So yeah, I missed last week’s episode, and I am really sorry I wasn’t here to write to you.

I also just needed to breathe. I needed to allow myself to be human.

But you already knew that about me. You’ve been watching me crawl through safe houses, botched interviews, and breakdowns like it’s a reality show with better lighting. You know I’ll make the economy sound poetic, the panic attacks sound cinematic, and the near-blindness sound romantic. That is just what I do, my God-given talent. You read, I unravel, and somehow we both end up entertained. 💋

So maybe next week I’ll finally sell the damn painting, or maybe I’ll hang it in my safe house’s living room as a monument to bad timing and great taste. Maybe I’ll take another job interview just to see who recognizes me first. Or maybe I’ll just keep driving, keep writing, keep turning my own mess and lessons into something worth reading.

And if you want to see what that chaos looks like when it’s dressed up and pretending to have its life together, go peek at sheridanguerrette.com. I finally updated it to match who I am now, still a little too ambitious, a little too emotional, and just self-aware enough to make it art. It’s part portfolio, part personality test, and very much me—equal parts business plan and beauty.

So don’t get too comfortable. I’ll be back next week with another story, another disaster, another reason for you to pretend you’re just here for the writing when we both know you’re really here for me.

Jokes aside, I want and need you in my corner.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: To The Girl Who Cries Wolf
subtitle: Scattering My Story Everywhere, and a Fiery Plea to Stop Crying Wolf Before It Costs
body:
I’m finally back home on the East Coast after bouncing between cities and borrowed guest rooms, and let me tell you, there’s nothing like the slap of humid July air to remind you where you belong. Dino barreled into me the moment I stepped through the door, tail wagging so hard I thought he’d take off, and Shadow greeted me with that slow, sleepy grin that says, finally you’re back. I’ve spent half my life chasing my internal deadlines and inspirations, and as much as I’ve loved the thrill of new skylines, coming back to my own walls feels like breathing again.

Since I last wrote, I’ve attempted to reshape old poems into songs. And honestly, some of these are hits. So with that being said, my poetry book is evolving in real time: pages once destined for shelves are now teasing with becoming a reality as a melody through your speakers. I’m pushing myself harder to be the fullest, most muchness version of Sheridan I can be. And I’ve realized that selfishly, I want my words in every corner of your life, in bookstores, in your speakers, on your television, maybe haunt some of your dreams 💋. It feels like one of my purposes is to scatter pieces of my story through different lenses, to all of you. I think that’s beautiful.

I came back to my little corner of the world just a few days ago, and now with my pups sleeping at my feet and the soft bug hum of an East Coast night outside my window, I’ve been thinking about vulnerability. I spent months feeling each city’s pulse under my shoes: writing poems in dim hotel lobbies, turning them into songs before the sun rose, and scribbling new plot lines of chapters between makeup checks on a night out. All that frolicking, and of course the self-reflection that ties alongside writing, it has has shown me how rare it is to feel truly safe. It seems rare these days for someone to have a radar that only tunes into genuine threats, and when you are that person, you lose patience for anyone exaggerating distress just to grab attention. So before I dive in, know that this isn’t another unsolicited life lesson; it’s a fire‑lit warning from a restless heart that’s trying to make sure you don’t get hurt.

Maybe a month ago, I was out with a few friends, a good night out, with laughter and music, and then my phone erupted with panic. My friend’s messages poured in like a storm: “Please help. Something’s wrong.” I could practically feel her heart pounding through the screen. I dropped everything, ready to sprint out the door, only to hear her voice, not breathless, not trembling, and not with terror. Instead, she asked if she could borrow something. In that moment, I saw it.

False alarms aren’t harmless; they chip away at trust and leave us vulnerable when it really counts. The boy who cried wolf learned this the hard way, and as I’m a big believer in you receive what you give to the world, please stop waving phantom distress flags. Someday, they may become true, and nobody wants that to happen. Honestly, we’ve all done it at some point in some form. We cry wolf because we’re craving care, but those 2 AM “help me” pings do more damage than you think.

Each false alarm chips away at trust. People begin to wonder if your next crisis will be genuine or just another drama plot line. Your frantic messages start going unanswered, and when you finally face real danger, be it a break‑in, an attack, or a medical emergency, you’ll be calling into the void.

There’s a better way. If you’re feeling lonely or overwhelmed at 2 AM, say so outright: “I’m anxious and could really use someone to talk to.”

If people continue to broadcast threats when there are none, sooner or later, there will be real danger, and nobody, not even you, will know what to do. People will learn to ignore your pleas, chalking them up to drama or attention‑seeking, and when you do face true evil, your scream may fall to no ears.

So please, save your alarms for moments that truly matter. Speak your fears honestly and don’t weaponize panic for attention. Your friends want to help; they just need to know when it’s life‑and‑death, and they need the honest version. Protect each other by protecting your own truth.

So please, everyone, stop this behavior.

Well, having just laid that all out there, ranted,

pleaded, and probably even ruffled some of your feathers, I’ll circle back to where we began. To the same home that reminds me how sweet a well‑earned sigh can be, it also fuels my urgency as a storyteller. I hope you find my words in a poetry collection, floating through your favorite playlist, etched on your TV screen, and know that I’m speaking from the place between my late‑night panics and my morning calm.

Now, I have my pajamas on, and I’m all washed up for bed.

Thank you for being with me while I face many fears and continue to be the most ‘Sheridan’ I can be. I’ll continue writing, living, sharing my many mistakes along the way, and now, go to sleep!

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: unChosen
subtitle: same light sits on the same corner of the floor
body:
The sun didn’t disappear
it just stopped reaching here.

The same light sits
on the same corner of the floor.

Nothing moves unless I do,
and even then it settles,
back as if I never touched it.

The air holds its breath,
the sound is borrowed,
but somewhere, things are changing
even if I’ll never see it.

s.g.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
