title: When Love Turns into a Blizzard
subtitle: My 2 a.m. rescue run through a snow-packed cul-de-sac—and the hard-earned rules you need when someone you care about threatens to end it all.
body:
July 30th:

I just drove across the country. I believe this may be the fourth or sixth time this month? I’m not sure I’ve lost track; all I know is that I got an oil change three weeks ago, and I’m already due for another one.

Now, I’m home, EXHAUSTED and collapsed into my bed.

But before I pass out, here’s the deal: tomorrow, Thursday, July 31, at our regular 9/8 Central time slot, I’ll be here, promise!

. . .

July 31:

Last Episode, I invited you into a moment that feels suspended in time: me, cramped in the backseat of my grandfather’s old car, hot leather pressing against my legs as the salty Maine air whooshed past a stuck window. It’s a memory that carries clarity, and one that I believe crept out because of my upcoming plans.

My great-grandfather recently passed away, and as his life was much longer than most anticipated, it was more of a celebration than a funeral. The celebration was on Tuesday in Northern Maine, just a few miles from the Canadian border, where every farm is Guerrette-owned, and the air somehow feels even cleaner than Tennessee’s. So yesterday, Wednesday, during our regular What Sheridan Said time slot, I was busy driving 1,000 miles across the country to get back home… once again.

I learned so much about my family while visiting Maine; we have our own cemetery, and we dig our own graves. Yes, you heard me right; it still hasn’t sunk in yet for me. The day before the funeral, my dad, his dad, and my brother went out to the cemetery and dug an eighteen-inch hole for great-grandpa’s ashes. And yes, I like to be dramatic; it was only eighteen inches deep, since he was cremated, but still? The Guerrettes dig their own graves. It is a true and dramatic statement.

I have so many lessons that are valuable to someone, if not many, and someday I will get to all of them. Adult life, adolescence, childhood, and, of course, my strange high school experience. Several of you have asked me to share some of these hard-earned lessons I walked away with from my chaotic and strange time in high school, and since this lesson has come up recently, as I was helping another friend, I’ve chosen which to share first on What Sheridan Said.

So, here is what to do if someone you care about threatens to hurt themself or end it all.

It was 2 a.m., and the world outside my window had melted into a five-foot snow bank while darkness only glowed from the stars. My phone buzzed: Wyatt, the boy next door who’d become my high-school boyfriend, typing in all caps, “IF YOU LEAVE ME, I’LL KILL MYSELF.” No argument, no fight, just the promise that my walking away would cost him everything.

I scrambled out of bed in half-zipped pajamas. I ran through the cul-de-sac like a white-washed battlefield, each step frozen with the question: What the hell do I do?

I started dating Wyatt sophomore year, just after middle school and freshman year had beaten me down with bullying and small-town whispers. In a place where everyone’s business is highway gossip, my family was the outsiders. Then this new boy moves in next door, a blank slate with no hometown rumors known to him, and suddenly, I’m the slow-burning Hallmark heroine. I was attracted to him because he didn’t bring any of my past to us.

We dated for maybe three or four months, and in that time, he did things like say, “I’m so glad I got you before you got hot.” I’m not sure how I suddenly got hot in that short amount of time, but okay. I remember one afternoon he told me to hop in the car for a “surprise date,” and three hours later, we were still barreling down country roads into nowhere. I had no clue where we were headed or why, no fancy dinner reservation, no promise of a sunset walk, just him, voice cracking, begging me not to trade him for bright city lights, saying I’m going to leave him soon, repeating how much better I am than him.

Soon, that became our pattern: midnight calls, knife shows, guilt trips. No adults ever stepped in. Someone must have known I was slipping out of my front door in slippers and tears, but nobody said a word.

Then came the Youth in Government weekend in St. Paul, where I roomed with Monica, my best friend since soccer tryouts. Friday night, over hotel-room fries, I confessed everything: the knives, the sobbing, the fear of breaking up because I’d be damned if guilt became my permanent roommate. We devised a Sunday-night “safe split” where he wouldn’t be alone, and I’d communicate with his closest friend.

The relief hit me like a sauna after a long winter: confidence replacing that icy knot in my chest, the burden I’d been carrying suddenly lifting off my shoulders. My mind snapped into focus, the plan felt bulletproof, and we actually smiled, because we were at peace, and we slid back into our weekend routine.

Youth in Government is a full-immersion mock state legislature and press corps where high-school students from every corner of America come together to write bills, hold mock trials, and report on all the drama. It isn’t some backyard theater; we’re talking real hotel-ballroom hearings, gavel-to-gavel debates in the morning, then sprinting down corridors with notepads in hand for the afternoon press briefing. I was one of the “journalists,” which meant I spent Friday scoping out trial rooms, scribbling quotes, and filing stories on everything from voting on faux bills to heated floor speeches about imaginary tax reform.

Saturday night, there was a dance for all the students in Youth in Government. We danced at the mock-government ball. I flirted with some kid named Ben and even gave him a kindergarten kiss at midnight, just to prove I was free.

Because it’s in the heart of the city, they lock the kids in the hotel after lights out and even before; you can’t just wander off into downtown traffic. Instead, you crash in twin beds with your roommate. Monica and I shared one of those rooms, complete with carpet that smelled vaguely of ambition and stale pizza.

Sunday morning, Monica had to sneak out for a Catholic service or face being grounded until graduation, and there was no way I was letting her wander those city blocks alone. So bleary-eyed and whispering like conspirators, we tiptoed past the chaperones, made it through the pews without a hitch, and slipped back into our hotel before anyone even noticed.

Double Oh Seven.

We took the long bus ride home, and by Sunday evening, Operation “Safe Split” was a go. I remember sitting Wyatt down in my mother’s office, my stomach a tangle of nerves. I needed it as much as air, but the second I spoke those words, my heart fractured all over again. The plan went as planned; he was surrounded by friends and family, and for the first time in months, I felt he was safe.

Monday morning arrived like a surprise trial I never signed up for. I hadn’t spoken to Monica since the bus ride home, yet there she was, the second I walked into the locker bank, shoulder-to-shoulder with Wyatt. A half-circle of their little clique and some of the “popular” crowd hovered around them, heads bowed in a hush that felt like a conspiracy, a conspiracy about me.

By the looks on their faces and their body language, I made the decision to walk past them and head to my locker. That’s when I saw it: anti-suicide notes plastered across every inch of my locker, then my gym locker, even my assigned desk. One had a giant teddy bear clutching chocolates and a tag that said, “Don’t kill yourself.” Throughout the next month, on my locker, on my assigned desk, I would receive anti suicide notes, which were left too out in the open to have any sense of real sincerity.

In that moment, Monday morning in the locker bank, I realized Monica and Wyatt had teamed up, spinning the lie that I was the one on the edge, not him. That “I was the one” threatening to harm myself, instead of the truth.

Monica was raised in a fiercely religious home, and with that, she convinced herself that my harmless Saturday-night kiss was a bigger sin than his midnight knife threats. Somehow, they managed to get every kid in school to believe I’d been the one trying to end it all, instead of the truth.

I knew if I tried to correct that story, I’d only give them more ammunition, and I’d rather lose a hundred friends than my own voice. I simply lowered my head, walked through the gauntlet of pity, and let them play villain. I never said a word, not a denial, not an argument, nothing. This battle wasn’t worth my strength, my time, or my focus. I chose silence because sometimes silence is the strongest boundary you can draw.

I’m proud of the way I handled it, even if I did lose many friends along the way. I’m a firm believer in moments like these, narrow down who is good for you, who is true, and who is not. And so, all those who taunted me, a girl they falsely thought was suicidal, showed me enough regarding who they were and the distance I wanted them from my life.

However, I’m sharing this because I want you to know: when someone tells you they’ll kill themselves, hurt themselves, or anything related, you don’t hesitate—you call 911. I wish I’d known that. I wish someone had pulled me aside and said, “Sheridan, this is not okay. We need to call for help.” That’s why I’m laying every detail bare, the 2 a.m. runs across frozen asphalt covered in snow, the “safe split” break-up plan, the locker-bank betrayal. Because maybe hearing my story will give you the guts to speak up, to draw a line, to demand real support before it’s too late. I want this to land in your heart and stay there, so you never feel alone in the snow like I did.

Resources:

  • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (U.S.) – call or text 988

  • Crisis Text Line – text HOME to 741741

  • NAMI HelpLine – 1-800-950-NAMI

And through all of this, the thousand miles driven last week, the graves we dug with our own hands in Northern Maine, the education of family roots… I’ve learned that some stories have to be told in full. Not so you can relive my chaos, but so that if you ever find yourself tiptoeing across a frozen yard in slippers at 2 a.m., you’ll remember you’re not alone. You have permission to call for backup, to set a boundary, to refuse guilt as currency.

When someone threatens to end it all or harm themselves, you don’t wait for permission; you call for help. You call 911, then you loop in a friend. You insist on real help. And you honor your own worth enough not to drown in someone else’s crisis.

Thank you for sticking with me through every detour, every soul-searching road trip, and every painful memory. I promise to keep sharing these hard-earned lessons so they can light a path for you or for someone else.

With fierce love and zero guilt.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: When The Angels Come Out
subtitle: On blue skies and letting this week be simple.
body:
I spent most of this week in my head, circling the same hallway, opening the same doors, finding the same empty rooms. I kept asking myself what I’m going to write about for this week’s episode, and then immediately not liking any answer I gave myself. I realized I haven’t felt good about much this week.

Then I looked outside. Gray. Heavy. The kind of sky that sits right on your shoulders. Oh, right. The angels are out.

When I was little, I was fully convinced clouds were angels. They only showed up when I felt sad; therefore, the clouds were there for me. Simple math for a spiritually dramatic kid who grew up going to church and took it all to heart. I’d have a string of cloudy days where I felt… off. Not crying, just muted. And then I’d wake up to a blue sky scrubbed clean, and I’d smile to myself, genuinely thinking, I don’t need the Angels today. I later learned they simply call this seasonal depression. I still like my version better. Where the clouds are Angels that only appear when I’m sad.

I did make myself go out this week. Last night, I went to the improv club downtown D.C. and saw Marcello Hernandez from SNL. He was great, sharp, charming, totally get why he’s on that stage. But the comic right before him? Unreal. I want to see that man everywhere. The whole room felt like a secret we were all good at keeping. Part of that is the rule: they lock your phone in a little felt pouch with a magnetic seal, and you keep it on you the whole show. It’s like a clothing security tag but for your screen; you tap it on a magnet on the way out, and it pops open. I loved that. I love rules that keep things alive. Some rooms need to be just a room. Every demographic got roasted. Equal-opportunity obliteration. It was hilarious, and it worked because no one was busy collecting evidence for the internet. We agreed to be there, together, without escape hatches. I want more of that, more spaces where the point is to be present, not to post.

On the writing front, I’ve been busy in the kind of way that makes time disappear. I officially have ten songs copyrighted, group registration for unpublished works is absolutely the move for a self-proclaimed starving artist. (I’m literally starving only because I forgot to make dinner; there’s lasagna in the microwave as I type this, please don’t judge me.) I grouped ten pieces into one application, hit submit, and exhaled. Since then, I’ve written four more songs and built demos I’m genuinely excited about. They’re stuck in my head, which is usually a good sign and also a gentle form of self-torture.

If you know me in person, you already know this: poetry has always been my engine. It’s how I think, how I move, how I make sense of anything. People tell me I even act poetic, quirky but elegant, somehow, like the sentences in my head are already broken into stanzas. I’m not a singer. I’m not a musician. I’m a writer. But songs are just poems that learned how to breathe on a beat, so we’re getting along just fine. I’m learning the tools, and once I have the bones, I can pop these out fast. They carry, they’ll sell. I know this because I’ve become so obsessed with this entire project that I’ve even begun to reverse-engineer several different artists’ brand era by era, benchmarked it against the arcs of their most successful peers to forecast the next album, and tailored my heartbreak song to fit that future silhouette exactly.

Hint: I have an obsessive, addictive personality.

The pivot from page to studio started in Nashville a month ago. I did a tiny social experiment: I took a poetry book to a bar and waited. A musician asked if I write, and within minutes, he was trying to turn one of my stanzas into a melody. I texted a friend, “Okay, this just happened. What do I do?” Then I spent the entire next day learning how to translate the thing I already do into songwriting structure. Verse. Pre. Hook. Bridge. The morning after, I sat down, obsessively, like a raccoon with a locked trash can, and two songs fell out of me. I sent them to my friend, and he was blown away. I’ve been getting faster and sharper ever since, just stacking skills and trusting my ear. (:

If you work in the industry and want to hear demos, please let me know! I’m just a girl who is turning her poems into killer songs. I want singers to cut these, make them their own. I want to be in the rooms where decisions get made, and songs get placed. I’m actively building those connections. Introduce me to the person who will fall in love with what I write, and I’ll show up prepared.

Back to the angels. It’s been cloudy and rainy the past few days, muggy in that way that makes your hair and brain both misbehave. I think that’s been the whole story behind the story. I spent two days scolding myself for not feeling inspired when the truth was simpler: the sky’s been low, which makes me a little low too. That’s not failure. It’s the weather. So I’m letting this week be simple. No grand thesis, no stunt. Just a small life update, a room where phones stayed quiet, a shirt that says what I’m too tired to explain, and some songs that make me feel like I’m finally translating myself.

If you needed the angels too this week, I see you. If you’ve got blue above you today, take an extra second with it, for both of us. Either way, we’re fine. We’ve got weather, and we’ve got words, and we’ll keep showing up until the sky remembers how to be bright again.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: When the Poem Is About Me
subtitle: Poetry, trauma, and plunging necklines: This poem might ruin your day, wreck your makeup, or fix your whole life.
body:
I’ve spent the week drowning in other people’s poetry, because apparently I enjoy torturing myself with the fear I’ll never measure up. Sometimes I’ve convinced myself of this, even though nobody’s seen my writing in years. It’s that maddening little voice whispering, “What if you’re not good enough?”

But I’m doing it anyway. Hell, it’s art, subjective. It’s who I am.

I’ve been writing poems since I was a kid. The first two that were published ran under anonymous names because I was mortified someone might actually read them. Unfortunately, I can’t even find copies of them anymore. I buried my name so deep, I outsmarted even myself.

Back in my Tumblr days (I know, throwback here), I used to post poems into the void, fully expecting no one to care. Soon, I started to gain a small following, then one day, a stranger messaged me asking if he could tattoo two stanzas of mine on his sleeve. I said yes. He sent a photo. I lost it. If you’re still out there: I love you. Please send another pic (:

I’ve always been the creative type. But creative people are often quiet about it until they’re brave enough to be loud. So here I am. Louder. Older. Maybe not ready, but I am willing.

Because this next chapter of my life is about sharing what I’ve been hiding. Not just for me, but for the younger version of me who was too scared to use her own name. And for the ones reading this now, who still are.

We’re working on small PR stunts. We’re building connections for a little tour. We’re plotting the kind of release that doesn’t just announce a poetry book, but lasts in your thoughts, makes a connection. But before any of that, before the mics and the lights and the business plan, I need to share it here, with you.

I’ll be testing pieces at open mics. I used to be the leading lady of a theatre, but this feels different. I’m not hiding behind a script, a character, or this fictitious character card announcing my whole life and persona as a strategy to finish the scene. It’ll be me, standing in front of strangers who are begging for something other than rhyming, cliche lines of heartbreak. I’m quite terrified.

And look, some of my poems rhyme. Some are about heartbreak, and I have cheesy ones too. But mostly, I live in rhythm, not rhyme. Multi-layered plotlines, sonnets, prose poems, little stabs of memory that drip and dry before the next verse hits. (Working on villanelles and pantoums too, in case you want the nerdy breakdown. 💋)

My poetry collection is one of darkness, heartbreak, as well as life and love, but not in the way that’s been done before. These aren’t recycled metaphors or stitched-up heartbreak haikus.

These are stories, some mine, some borrowed from the world around me, and held under a microscope until it cracked open and I saw what was real. It’s not always autobiographical, but it is always personal.

Some of the poems were written in the thick of it: breakups, betrayals, silence that screamed louder than words. Others came from years of watching, watching people love poorly, watching families fall apart at the dinner table, watching joy show up in the middle of pain like an uninvited guest that still knows your name. Some are prose poems, some sonnets, some built like little cinematic scenes with layered plotlines you don’t see coming. And yes, I’m experimenting with new styles and methods, because I love a challenge. And I love it even more when feeling slips into form and still comes out breathing.

This collection is broken into chapters: Dark, Breakup, Life, and Love, because I believe you have to walk through the first three to understand the last one. It’s not soft. It’s not sweet. But it is honest. It’s written for the people who keep going. It’s not meant to be liked. It’s curated to be felt.

Because love, real love, the kind that lingers in the bones and survives the fire, doesn’t arrive clean. It’s dragged in by the ankles, bruised and bleeding, wearing the face of grief and the perfume of hope. It shows up after the mirror has cracked, after your hands have bled from clawing your way back to yourself. As the opening poem says, “We understand”—not because we were handed peace, but because we fought for it with every last breath.

This book is for the ones who ran toward the light even with hell burned into their souls. For the girl crying in her car who still fixes her makeup before walking back into the world. For the man who remembers every word his father never said. For the friend you lost without closure. For anyone who’s ever had to decide what’s worth staying for. For the ones who have loved through strife and still call it love.

But before I read you this poem, let me tell you about the night I wore the most plunging neckline of my life, and felt safe doing it.

JK, first, the poem. (;

Here’s one that may still yet be revised (perfectionism), but I’m willing to share.

It’s called Some Things Are Easy.

« INSERT SOME THINGS ARE EASY POEM »

Anyway. After all that emotional excavation, I put on a dress and went out.

It was soft and loud all at once. I wore the most plunging neckline I own, and went out—and I mean an OG millennial style clubbing night out. In honor of Pride month, we hopped from one LGBT+ bar to the next in Washington, D.C., dancing, laughing, and existing. I didn’t get groped. I wasn’t leered at. I didn’t feel like prey. I was celebrated. I was adored. And it made me furious.

That was it. No performance, no pretending. Just a space not built for the male gaze, and a few people who made breathing feel easy. That’s what safety should feel like.

I don’t want to scream “it’s men’s fault” into the void. That’s too easy. It’s really society. It’s women who stay friends with men who abuse. It’s the guys who shrugs it off as a rumor. It’s the best friends, the families, the coworkers who know what he did, and still choose brunch. Still invites him. Still protects him.

And to be clear: some sins you don’t come back from. Not in a friend group. Not in a partner. Not in a business deal. Not in my life. Some violence is so deep no apology can make it social again. No remorse, no true change, never will be enough. That’s the truth.

We need to do better. And I don’t mean performatively. I mean for real.

If you made it this far, thank you.

Next week’s post will be another poem—or maybe a behind-the-scenes look into the making of this book, or just another drama venting session about all the random dramatic shit that happens in my life. Either way, I’ll see you next week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Where Are Your Hands
subtitle: Her shoulders stopped living near her ears...
body:
Her shoulders stopped living near her ears.
Weight did not send her elsewhere.
She does not know how to fake that.

She watched him step closer
and did not step back—
not because she wanted more,
because she does not know how to make less.

Her heart does not speak casually.
It does not survive being opened
and told it is misunderstood.
She cannot.

title: Where Your Hands Are
subtitle: Her body remembered things...
body:
Her body remembered things
she thought were gone.
Her shoulders stopped living near her ears.
Weight did not send her elsewhere.

She does not know how to fake that.
Does not know how to kiss
without meaning.
Alone that long,
her body stopped distinguishing
between touch and intent.

She watched him step closer
and did not step back.
Not because she wanted more—
because she does not know how
to make less.

Some people can survive almosts.
She cannot.
Her heart does not speak casually.
It does not survive being opened
and told it is misunderstood.

Do not take her hand.
Do not stop her world.
Do not touch what took her years
to let breathe again.

Because to her,
being held
is already a decision.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Why I’d Rather Melt Than Hit the Gym
subtitle: Confessions from a sweat-phone and the unexpected way silence fuels my biggest breakthroughs
body:
It’s another brutal week of summer, and every time I open my front door, I stop in my tracks and ask myself whether my sanity is really worth this heat. I actually don’t mind the sun beating down; give me a hundred degrees, and I will breathe through it without flinching. But sweat is a different story. If you didn’t know this about me, I refuse to go to the gym or do anything that might send moisture dripping down my back, because on the rare occasion that I do break a sweat, I want to tear my own fricken skin off. It is that itchy. I think I am allergic to my own sweat, and if that is not a perfect excuse to avoid public sweating, I do not know what is.

This week, I’ve caught myself wondering if I’m doing anything right; if what I’m doing is enough; if I’m on the right path. But the truth is, I think I think too much. Which is probably the main diagnosable cause of my life’s insistent writing. I’m trying to share more of my writing because I’m really, really bad at letting people in, trying to actually ‘sher’ Sheridan, haha. Anyone who’s crossed paths with me knows this: there have definitely been times when I’ve dropped off the face of the earth for six months or even a couple of years. I haven’t done that in a while, but I still go quiet for a few days at a time.

For all of you, I’m assuming quarantine was your first taste of true isolation, but by the time the world shut down, that solitude felt normal to me, even peaceful. I was so overworked and exhausted by my career that when I heard everyone was staying home, I smiled, turned off my phone, and slept for what felt like forever. In that moment, I experienced an unparalleled sense of peace.

On a lighter note, I finally indulged myself with the most beautiful leather-bound notebook. It has a wraparound cover, refillable inserts, and that perfect, slightly toothy paper that begs to be written on. Holding it transports me back to another century, complete with quill and ink. The only snag is that my current notebook still has a quarter of its pages blank. I adopted the three-morning-pages ritual from The Artist’s Way, a simple practice of writing three unedited pages before breakfast, closing the book, and never looking back. But lately I have been on fire, cranking out ten pages a day, mostly daydreams about cracking open that new journal. I cannot wait until the last page is filled so I can leap into the next one. And yes, I treated myself to a new gold pen. Every writer deserves a touch of shine in her hand.

Like I mentioned last week, I’ve continued to stay committed to producing more songs. My poems have always leaned toward rhythm rather than rhyme, so adapting them into verses and choruses feels almost like my second nature. And to continue branching out with people and writing, I did actually just get back from a local writers’ group held in a tucked-away library room. We gathered around and were given the prompt “Because I am here.” We had eleven minutes to capture a moment of utter peace without relying on nature descriptions. I admit that I bent the rule; I wove in both my emotions and a hint of Maine’s coastline because some memories demand their setting. Here is the passage that poured onto the page:

. . .

Because I am here, I peer out the window with only glass separating my face from the salty air, insisting I breathe it in. A tune I cannot name drifts through the speakers and then to my ears, though I recognize it the instant it begins. And when I hear it again, my body and all its senses are dragged back to the hot leather backseat of my grandfather’s car, where I shimmy my legs back and forth, trying to ease the burning sensation of leather cooked before it cooks me.

I try to push the window down to get a better listen to the ocean waving hello at me. The window doesn’t move. I tug at the stubborn thing; it refuses to budge. I turn forward where my father and his father share their love of the same music while sharing the same deep‑throat laugh.

“Dad, Grampie,” I say.

They turn as their laughter and music fade and say, “Yes, Sheridan,” and turn their attention toward me.

“Can I open my window?” I ask.

They smile, turn back around to face the front, and then my grandfather takes one hand off the steering wheel to push my window down.

I stick my head out the window and breathe in Maine’s air that had been following me, and I hear the ocean’s hello. I take a deep breath and whisper back, “Hello, Ocean.”

. . .

My mind drifts back to that exact moment whenever a certain feeling washes over me. It’s as if the chemical makeup of my brain shifts right back to that day. When I hear that one song, even though I can’t recall its name or hum its melody, I instantly recognize it. Within five seconds, I’m sitting in that spot again, hot leather and salty Maine’s coast air. I see every detail, hear every sound, smell the air, and feel every emotion all over again.

I remember crying in that moment, not out of sorrow, but because I knew I needed to preserve that moment forever. I sat, tears streaming, determined to memorize everything around me. I cataloged each sensation in my mind, as if I could freeze time and steal that moment for myself. I wanted to carry it with me, to have it on hand whenever I needed it.

So I sat and cried in the backseat while my father and his father shared the front, and I etched every sight, sound, and feeling into my memory. I captured that stolen moment and made it mine forever, so that no matter where I go or what I face, I can always return to that place of clarity, peace, and certainty.

That flash of memory reminds me why I write. It forces me to notice every crack of leather, every echo of laughter, and every inhale of salty air. It teaches me that genuine peace can be found in the smallest details, and that capturing those details is worth every ounce of discomfort…no sweat required. 💋

Thank you for reading through my sweaty confessions, my notebook obsessions, and my creative adventures. I promise to keep inviting you behind the scenes, even when I retreat into my own head.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Woman Compulsively Overshares, But People Somehow Still Don’t Know Anything About Her
subtitle: On safety, storytelling, and the strange art of surviving your own extremes.
body:
I owe you an update.

I know the drama began when I filled you in on my business stalker and my ongoing dilemma of finding a business owner, or investor, who’d rather work with me than date me. For my own court-ordered safety and my financial safety, I put everything into storage. Since then, I’ve been bouncing between friends and family, which I dramatically like to call my safe houses.

Thank you to everyone who reached out to me personally. As you know, I overshare with purpose, but there are things that simply aren’t smart, safe, or legally sound to share online.

I am very purposeful with what I say, with the tidbits of my life that I’ve shared so far. But as the title goes, you still know little about me.

I’m not saying that to downplay the relationship we’ve built through me writing to you, but because I am a multi-layered woman with too many sides to count. Sometimes the sides I choose to show, write about, or act on are intentional, for the outcome, the lesson, or the morality I’m trying to instill. Not because I think you need it, but because I believe the world does.

I’m writing to you because I know my morality is high, my ambition is among the stars, and my brain thinks in such a strange, wonderful way that the lessons I stumble across in life come at me with extremes. Earlier this year, I sat with myself and journaled religiously for a minimum of ten minutes every single morning, right after my eyes opened and my pups ran out to potty in the yard.

I sat with my lessons in storytelling. Every single one of Shonda Rhimes’s courses I sat through during COVID. Each textbook I read about persuasion, how to make someone eager to finish the story. How the extremes and the unexpected turn normalcy into humor, fear, and great storytelling.

I remember leaning back in the chair where I was writing. My two dogs were running through the open air on the side of the mountain that hugs both Tennessee and Georgia. And, like Signal Mountain itself, I was sitting there deciding whether I wanted to pay taxes on my own lessons, my own story, my own home.

It was in that moment that I decided I did— it was my extremes that I needed to share.

Perhaps I’m writing this much for selfish purposes. I’ve admitted that the world being infected by my words makes my insides warm. But I’ve always written this much, if not more, so it’s not that I’ve been writing more; it’s that I’ve been sharing more.

And I don’t think that’s selfish. What is selfish is the number of novels I snuck into the backyard bonfire in the countryside of Minnesota, so no one would ever read the anger and frustration I poured into those hundred-page manuscripts.

What’s selfish is stockpiling three shelves of an antique bookshelf with nothing but handwritten notebooks of poems and op-eds. What’s selfish is the number of days and weeks that have gone by where I’ve kept my mouth closed, convincing myself that my lessons and my life were too abnormal to share.

What makes beautiful television, a mesmerizing film, a story that takes over your soul, is not normalcy. It’s the breathtakingly beautiful decisions and devotion, the morality that cannot be shaken, no matter the circumstances. It’s the stories that encompass such extreme measures that we watch in awe and still manage to see a part of ourselves in them.

I hope this makes sense.

Cinderella had an evil stepmother, a fairy godmother, and a curfew of midnight—not a stepmother with minor boundary issues and a nice therapist she pays for.

It’s the stories with extreme circumstances that we read, listen to, and watch, where we find a slice of ourselves within them. A story built on normalcy rarely does that, and when it does, it’s usually because it’s visually or rhythmically poetic enough to use every other trick in the book to make you eager for the next line.

It’s an arousal. A tease, a pressure point, a climax, and the aftercare— unless, of course, you’re the show with the biggest cliffhanger in history that got canceled before the next season.

With all of this, and while actively going through an extreme situation, I decided it was truest to my mission, and my found purpose, to share as much as I can.

Because, if we’re being frank, cities are slowly breeding psychopaths whose eyes don’t flinch when they witness a murder from across the street. Populations are swelling on the thought that the more power you have, the more your desired shames are allowed to become small-circle secrets. And the sex industry has spread so far into daily life that its beginnings are starting to blur into corporate behavior.

This isn’t everyone, not every city, not every company, not every person—but it is happening.

And being a young woman who’s spent her career in male-dominated industries, I hear the same refrain from my colleagues: “As long as you’re this young, hot—and this fertile—Sheridan, this may keep happening.”

So yes, I know how to handle it. If that means packing up my things, renting a storage unit, and rerouting my entire life, so be it.

And that’s exactly what I did.

I had an employer who began lowering my pay and eventually stopped paying me when I refused to play along with his… tactics. Then came the networking prospect turned stalker. I hadn’t shared the employer part before because I wasn’t sure it was smart—but it’s the reality many women live in, especially when you’ve always been the one directly under the CEO.

Right now, I can’t speak on the loss of money.

But I haven’t heard or gotten any weird pings from my networking stalker, so I can go back to my city now. Still, finding something I can tunnel my ambition into feels more uncertain than ever. The small part of the world I thought was mine flipped upside down, and I’m not sure where my next little corner of it will be.

I’ve moved across the country several times now, and I’ve never been afraid of a new beginning. So I’m trying everything—taking small gigs in between, am contemplating trying to keep my business advisory alive, though it’s difficult when you’re in hiding, tucked away in the countryside with two pups, my laptop, and a shit ton of notebooks.

I’ve promised to share my writing more, so this week I released several different works, one of the many projects I’m dabbling in till I find my slice of the world again.

This piece is titled Why Modern Dating is Performance Art. It’s a generational philosophical piece on today’s dating culture and how trauma seeps into our sex and relationships.

Why Modern Dating Is Performance Art

This week, I also published a few poems. I’ll share my favorite of the few here.

Coke Without Ice

My poetry is often fiction, and yet sometimes it’s also painfully true. Either way, my poems are written with layered meanings for different readers. I started doing that when my sisters and friends kept snooping in my diary—I’d write decoy meanings to mess with them.

The habit stuck. I write so that someone, maybe you, will feel something real in it. Long enough to see yourself inside my extremes.

Because you still know little about me. But I think, slowly, you’re starting to.

P.S. I was a pirate for Halloween, and I did in fact steal your booty. Find this on Insta

Sheridan Guerrette

title: You Perverts, This One’s About Kisses
subtitle: Nitpicking, Free Memoir Downloads, Hottistic Reflections, Boyfriend Trauma, and the Exhausting Beauty of a Complicated Family
body:
I wanted to start by sharing some exciting news (and, admittedly, a little chaos). While Substack is still very much alive, growing, and home to all of our memberships, episodes, and bonus content, there is now a second platform.

She’s not a sister. Not a cousin. She’s an identical twin—right down to the three moles on her cheek.

What does that mean?

Why are we doing this?

As What Sheridan Said continues to grow, I wanted to build a home that I own independently—a place where the archive, community, and future of this project can live beyond any single platform. This gives readers more flexibility in how they follow along while ensuring the series remains accessible no matter where it grows next.

Whether you subscribe through Substack or WhatSheridanSaid.com, you’ll receive the same episodes, the same membership perks, and the same access. And if you’re a paid subscriber who would like access on both platforms, simply reach out, and I’ll be happy to grant it.

I’ve mentioned a bit before about the possible partnerships and sponsorships that I’ve been chatting back and forth with and heavily contemplating. After it all worked out, a former colleague stepped up and invested the money I needed to order my own first round of books, get a team for the promotional content, and honestly it gave me this big boost of confidence that what I’m doing here isn’t just right for me— other people see the value in it too, and that includes the space you and I are building together Wednesdays at 9/8 Central.

I need to pause this right now to tell you that while I’ve been typing, I’ve taken a pause every other paragraph, and I’ve gone back to editing and nitpicking my website like crazy. I’m taking little breaks just to obsess for another thirty minutes over one tiny flaw or some layout misalignment that’s driving me nuts. So if you could, I’d really appreciate it if you went and dug around on my new platform and gave me a compliment sandwich only. If you don’t remember from my previous episode, a compliment sandwich is when you compliment someone, then tell them something that needs fixing or that is wrong, and then hit them with another compliment right after. That would mean the absolute world to me right now. Thanks ♡.

My other writing updates: I’ve written one new poem since we last spoke, but I also shared a few that I found in an old notebook. If you remember my poem from earlier this year, Where Your Hands Are, well, if not, it’s right here if you want a quick refresher:

Where Your Hands Are

Now that you’re refreshed, I have been obsessing over a few of the lines in that poem and wanted to see what else I could do with it. I felt wrong plagiarizing myself— well, I suppose it’s not even remotely close to that when I’m taking my own art or words and turning them into a new painting or poem— though I find it disingenuous to not let you know and label it as a series connected to the original Where Your Hands Are.

The second poem of the series is named, I’m sure you could probably guess this one, ‘Where Are Your Hands.’ I’ll share it here instead of forcing you to click another button. ♡

Where Are Your Hands

Her shoulders stopped living near her ears.
Weight did not send her elsewhere.
She does not know how to fake that.

She watched him step closer
and did not step back—
not because she wanted more,
because she does not know how to make less.

Her heart does not speak casually.
It does not survive being opened
and told it is misunderstood.
She cannot.

s.g

The opening line is one that looped in my head; I had to repurpose it for this piece, while the idea for this piece as a whole came from not only my thread’s social feed.

As a ‘hottistic’ woman, I wasn’t able to wrap my head around the idea that you can kiss someone you don’t have romantic emotions for without wanting to barf immediately after. As much as I still don’t completely understand how somebody could, it took my heart a while to understand that others don’t have the same walls or emotional boundaries that I do.

And yes, I’m talking about a kiss, you perverts.

But the discussion I saw across my threads’ social feed was of new adults, ages 18 to 22, talking about the same thing I struggled to work into just understanding: that others aren’t like me. My first thought was to check the accounts posting. I hate to say that I was equally checking if it was an AI/spam account as if it were a real human who would be classified into the ‘incel’ demographic. The verdict is that they were normal humans.

I think this truly outs me for the fact that I am only judging others if I’m judging myself first. Ugh, well, alright, to end my thought, I’ve been obsessing over the line “Her shoulders stopped living near her ears.” Since I wrote it for the first poem in this series, and the chatter and discord across my social feed gave me the idea to write this poem, the second of its series.

Go figure— I’m still moving a million miles a minute. My brain hates slowing down a thought pattern, but I am resting, transitioning between projects to a walk to tennis, to lounging, or simply writing something stupid just for myself. As much as I’m probably still classified as a workaholic with my day-to-day routine and self-discipline I hold myself to, I’m incorporating many different things to keep me active, sane, and on top of that, I’ve been sleeping ten hours a night. Eye bags where?

Last week, I was absolutely slammed with dog watching, house sitting, ghostwriting, and overall sales. You know the number one thing I hate about starting new projects or companies or hustles? SALES.

Some say I have a temperament for a good sale, meaning my face can not bullshit you.

But a bad sale? That would be me, face redder than my hair, sweating, palms and fingers twitching, I’ve lost my balance, and through a fake smile, I say, “Yes, sir! This medicine is backed by doctors, and I’ve witnessed it save thousands firsthand.”

“You don’t say?”

My face is now redder than hell and my voice and guilt wreaks that I’ve entered it myself and am crawling out as I crumble and say, “No sir! I don’t! I’m lying, this company kills thousands, and the doctors aren’t medical doctors,” sobs get increasingly more teary, “and, and.. they tell us to say that but they have doctorates in economics not medicine!”

To say the least, I have no poker face, and it’s extremely painful for me to lie. So the only sales I’m currently partaking in are good sales, my sales, my positive growth for myself and those around me!

I have to fill you in… something happened over the weekend, it also completely outs me for yet again being dramatic and possibly not sane, but when do I let that stop me from shutting up?

I told you in the last episode what happened with my last boyfriend, why it’s been so long since I’ve been in another relationship, and the absolutely chaotic out-of-nowhere sister wives bullshit he tried pulling on me. Well, let’s just say that I’m a little territorial, a little sensitive, and maybe over-the-top dramatic. So, when I dove into the creative industry at the end of 2025, I had hoped to meet some amazing people, but I didn’t think I’d meet someone who not only works in the creative industry but is as much of a business mind as I am. And that he’d be my boyfriend?

We didn’t meet because we worked together; we met because, well, I slid into his Instagram DMs. I know. At least it’s not Raya or Hinge, ok?

I’m sure you’re asking, “Sheridan, what the hell happened over the weekend?”

Well, my boyfriend is a really talented actor, and over the weekend I watched him act on set, where he, on script, had a romantic interest and a major scene ending with a kiss. To say the least, I left the second their hands touched, and have categorized myself as not sane enough to watch my man pretend to be with another woman, even if it’s professional, even if it’s scripted, even if its 100% fake, and we live together and he gives me all the reassurance I could possibly ask for. I am very much still not sane enough to watch that.

After I calmed down, my face went from red back to its regular pale, and I could no longer see stars or red. I said to him, “I will support you in your acting career, but I will probably never be sane enough to watch you act, even in the most professional environment, with a romantic interest.”

He laughed and instantly said, “For both our sakes, I won’t take a Heartthrob acting role again.”

So yes, over the weekend, I learned that I am not sane enough to watch my boyfriend act romantically on set with another woman, and I learned once again that I made the right choice sliding in his DMs.

(for now…… DUN DUN DUN!!!!!!!!)

Jokes aside, I have another reassuring and positive point of my relationship I’d love to share with you! We are moving into a new place together, so the next two weeks will be even more chaotic than normal. I’ve moved so many times now that I’m not afraid of this transition, but it will feel nice, not chaotic, and restful when we finally have our place together and sleeping under our new roof.

I’m building a new life, a new home around all the things I enjoy, and with an open avenue to allow more positives in. My parents live in the middle of Tennessee, which, if you aren’t aware, my entire immediate family is still in the frozen tundra state of, what was it? oooh yeaaah.. Riiiight, Minnesooota. I didn’t forget Minnesota, I just wanted to throw in my Fargo accent for old times’ sake.

But this new life I’m building isn’t too far from them. I can still take a long drive over for free weekend dog care (I do this a lot), and it’s a new sense of safety knowing I have family within a drive’s reach if Bigfoot were to break into my home and take all my money and food, versus being across the entire country with all help a two-day drive away. That’s not to say that I didn’t choose that several times over, because I certainly did; I wanted to move to D.C. for as long as I had cognitive thoughts and memories.

If you have ever moved across the country by yourself, to an unfamiliar community, with your family thousands of miles away, I think you understand. Safety that’s given and safety that’s earned hit two different spots. It’s a beautiful thought to be across the country from where I was raised (I bust out my minx coat at 55 degrees, therefore I can not go North again) and still have a sense of safety that there is at least some family, safety that’s given, nearby.

This isn’t to say and discredit those who helped me, stood by me, and offered safety given and not earned, but I’m speaking in regards to blood is bred and others are met.

But I want to open this to a new discussion; there is a large portion of my family scattered across the country in parts I have yet to live in, and perhaps hope to someday. It’s been a bit difficult, I know that I’m dramatic, over the top, dare I say… extreme? But my family’s ideologies, politics, and morals have been scattered from all ends of the spectrum that half of the time I must remain Switzerland in order to continue a relationship with that family member. This isn’t saying that I don’t shut down statements, and I certainly can not lie or hold a poker face, as discussed before, but I’ve had to act smart in what I share, in how I question someone, and how I can respond to get someone to see what they just said is fucked up on their own.. because if I do it myself.. who knows how long until they want to speak to me again.

I’m sure your family is like this. I see many families like this. Divided, fighting, and going over the topics not allowed at a gathering prior to entering the door, like a Vampire that needs an orientation first. It’s exhausting, sad, and I wish I had relationships with many of my family that’s chosen their deserved boundaries to be away. If you’re reading this, some of you do, would you hear me if I said I was just a little kid and I’d love to get to know you?

I know family stuff like this is heavy, and I’m sure a lot of you reading this get it. The constant tiptoeing, staying Switzerland just to keep the peace, watching ideologies fly across the table while you try not to blow everything up… It’s exhausting and honestly kind of sad sometimes. I wish things were simpler with the ones who’ve set their boundaries and stepped back, and often even the ones who didn’t. If any of you are reading this and you’re one of those people, just know that a huge part of my heart is still open even when the rest of me is dramatic and extreme about everything else.

Whew… that was a lot to unload on a Wednesday evening. Between the website transition, waiting on the books, my sales meltdowns, the very not-sane acting-set moment, moving in with my boyfriend, and all the family feelings I can never quite keep inside— I basically just dumped my whole brain onto the page… but hey, what else is new. Thanks for sitting through all my rambling and oversharing.

I’m excited about what’s coming next, even if it’s messy and chaotic for a while. New platform, new home, new chapters, and hopefully a little more peace mixed in with all the noise. If you’ve been here since the beginning, I appreciate you more than you know. I’d love to hear from you if the new site needs a compliment sandwich, or if you just want to say hey— I really do read every single one.

Until next Wednesday… keep surviving your own version of dramatic life, protect your sanity, and be gentle with your heart.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette

title: Your Body is Trying to Tell You Something
subtitle: How paying attention to my chakras changed the way I deal with anxiety, vices, and the urge to shut down— and how you can start reading your signals.
body:
Tonight’s episode won’t be a normal episode. I flew to LA on Monday for a last-minute trip, witnessed the Emmys, learned so many amazing things, and met many amazing people. Then later, flew to Hawaii for a much-needed mental reset.

At the moment, my rear end is sitting on the beach of Honolulu, my toes digging into the sand, and the birds of the beach wondering if my laptop tastes good. Where once only the Hawaiian royalty were allowed on this beach—it was their playground. So as gate-kept as this beach once was, unfortunately tonight’s episode will also be rather gate-kept from our usual time slot of Wednesdays at 9/8 Central Chicago. A much-needed vacation. Here we are, the next day, Thursday at 9 PM Oahu, HI time.

I have some exciting news to share with you all. I have several new episode drafts, but they aren’t the right fit for today. This is what seemed most fitting to send out.

I haven’t slept much this week. We can attest to a total of ten hours slept throughout the past five collective days. My mental stamina has been rather depleted.

I’m hearing whispers this week is the witches’ week, the week of transformation, and for those like me that have lain wide awake with their brain still pulsing on random facts and problems I need to solve, I browse through what others might have to say on social media—those that are also unfortunately still awake at 6 AM on a Tuesday night as I.

According to the Internet, it’s witches’ week. Lilith just moved into the sidereal Sagittarius house and is working with the deity Nirriti, who is known to soothe the throat chakra of silenced spiritual women, the vulnerable truth-tellers.

In astrology, Lilith refers to Black Moon, rather than a planet. It’s the focus on the empty side of the Moon’s orbit. It’s a place of exile, raw appetite, and the self that refuses to submit. In Abrahamic folklore, she is Adam’s first wife, who left Eden, leaving him alone. She’s known for representing the part of you that can’t be tamed, an appetite you are ashamed of, the woman who would rather run away than obey. Lilith moving into Sagittarius just means the points have aligned in Sagittarius’s flavor for blunt truth-telling and wanting it all. (If you can’t tell, I’m a Sagittarius.)

Nirriti is the Vedic Goddess of decay and dissolution, the underside of order. She comes from some of the oldest Hindu scriptures, and she’s not the nicest one by far. She personifies things falling apart, the rotting, the bad luck, the grief, the sharp edge you forgot was still inside of you. Those who practice and pray to Nirriti, the deity, most of the time it’s for her to leave them alone.

I’ve never considered myself a witch, a rock practicer, an avid churchgoer, or even a fully committed Christian, but I have always considered myself a “woo woo.”

Growing up, I was surrounded by one religion, one way of thinking, one sense of life. As a young girl finding new routes, discovering new religions, new practices, new cultures, and ideas, I’ve always tried to consider everyone’s beliefs, “woo woo” or not, to try and have a better understanding of myself, my mind, my body, and the world around me.

To give credit where credit is due, our computers cannot operate without a quartz crystal rock. That’s right—a rock. The ocean is the largest mass of anything accumulated on this planet, and yet the moon, the stars, and the alignment of the galaxy tell her, the ocean, exactly where she can go.

Manifestation, when done right, is only Newton’s law. Saying a poem, then lighting a candle, or taking a sip of wine, is a form of that.

In all three Abrahamic religions, we have interchangeable stories—the same people but with a different outlook on it, the same mantra for peace, and forever the human evils that turn a mantra for peace and light into control and ego.

In Hinduism, chakras are a higher topic of conversation, which I find wildly interesting. It was the first thing that I studied that showed true evidence that mental and physical health are deeply interconnected. Through the connection of spiritual practices and black-and-white science, over the past decades we have learned that a bruised chest can mean a bruised identity, a stutter can mean stress chooses to sit at the throat, an anxious person has their paranoia choose their host in dizziness and perhaps nausea, and guilt makes your cheeks red hot.

There are seven chakras: the root of your spine, lower abdomen, upper abdomen, center of the chest or your heart, between your eyes or more commonly known as the third eye chakra, the top of your crown, and my topic of conversation, the throat chakra.

The body, the mind, and the soul are deeply interconnected. Those who question Christianity’s baseline often argue that the Holy Trinity—God, Jesus, and the Holy Spirit—acts simply as a mirror for creating peace throughout your body, mind, and soul, your own personal Holy Trinity.

If you’ve had emotional strain, stress, any type of mental block, or unnecessary bridge this week as I have, I want you to pay attention the next few days to each of your seven chakras. Do you feel tension at the top of your crown, or a flustered feeling at the bottom of your stomach? Which chakra points light up, tighten, or become more rigid when you’re depleted, stressed, or anxious? Have you developed any habits or vices like I that are subconsciously targeting that exact chakra?

Even just talking about my throat chakra, I feel it tighten, yelling at me not to say another word, allowing only carbon dioxide to leave my tongue. My battles with kicking smoking nicotine, the harsh Diet Cokes I crave early in the morning and right after my 2 pm slight downhill. My recurring nightmare of not being able to scream when I need to the most. I mean, hell, I was a full-blown thumb sucker for the first thirteen years of my life. In honor of soothing my throat chakra, I’ll tell you such an embarrassing story of mine. It took me years to connect all of these memories, habits, vices, and soothing techniques I’ve used throughout my life. This utterly embarrassing one screams that my chakra of choice has been, and may always be, my throat.

I’ve always been rather anxious until I lap to a feeling of competence. My social skills, my friend circles, still could use a few more laps. At the young ages of 12 and 11, I had a few friends, but I wasn’t one of the “townies,” so I felt anxious making new friends, wondering if I even did fit in, and what that may even look like. Times I would get so anxious I’d want to run and hide, and as a closet thumb sucker, maybe just one hit would make me feel better. Just around the corner of the hallway, past my class and the next teacher’s class, and make the right-hand turn, you’ll see a little door, usually unlocked. “Janitor” read the sign just outside the door. I opened it just a crack so I could slide in, kept the lights off, and crouched down in a tiny janitorial closet next to the mop and buckets of cleaning materials. I’d pull out my thumb, take a hit, take a few breaths, and return back to class.

Imagine if I were to get caught. Brittany or Meredith opening the janitor’s door to find little Sheridan crouched down, anxious, scared, getting just one hit of her thumb in so she can calm back down and return to class. Thank Jesus I was never caught.

But I did that. I snuck into the janitor’s closet so I could suck my thumb for a second when the day got too loud for me.

My throat chakra has tightened this week, the witches of online spooking with me that I may truly be a part of this community, the eerie fortune cookie that was a thousand percent differently printed than every other fortune cookie at PF Chang’s—no numbers, no logo, no little TM, nothing. Inside the fortune cookie was a little piece of paper, blank on one side, with a slightly too-small font on the other reading in Times New Roman, “How you connect business and art will impress your colleagues and bring you into the next light.”

Did I cry at PF Chang’s? No, almost. I blinked the one tear away and tightened my posture before it became a reality on my cheek; I definitely put too much blush on.

I’ve always been rather woo-woo. I saw my first ghost in a church service and burst into tears. I won the flat-screen TV at my prom raffle because I was repeating in my head, “The TV is mine, I have it in my hands.” Then it was. I have a certain pattern of dreams that arrive to me telling me the future. I know when someone’s staring at me from behind with ill thoughts, sexual, or just simply looking. I understand energy, frequency, and feel these at depths I can’t truly explain.

I’m not going to transcend this series into teaching you how to astral plane, or other magical whimsical shit, but I think I need to talk more about these practices, how they helped me better understand myself, and how you can take practices from different “woo woo” things to a practice or habit that feels right for you.

My throat chakra hates me right now. But this is because I need to jump; I need to scream at the top of the hill with all my lungs, and let the world know I am here. I’m still trying to kick the nicotine, and after going a few days without it, my sanity, the throat chakra, scratched and scratched until I gave it what it wanted.

It’s not another vice I need, but to understand how my body will allow my throat to soothe without smoking. So I thought this episode would be sharing the honest journey I’m on right now. I’ve studied chakras, read too deep into pagan practices, I respect the rock girls, and I feel a sense of peace when looking over the three Abrahamic religions of the world. But my research has just been picked back up, as my personal Holy Trinity is craving a new sense of direction.

The discomfort I’ve been describing—the throat tightness, the thumb sucking, the nicotine pull, the urge to scream—all are clear telltale signs my throat chakra is in need of new techniques, new practices, a new healthy way to be soothed. Over the next few weeks, I’ll be exploring what this means to me, what works, and what is just plain silly. If you’re interested, I’d love to share the journey with you.

Please let me know if you enjoyed this episode. I know it’s different than what we usually see from my feminine poetic rants, but as I’ve continued to grow within this series, I’ve been searching for what value, lesson, something I can give back to you. I think maybe this is it.

More next week.

xo,
Sheridan Guerrette
